title: The Wire: Baltimore, HBO, and the Making of a Landmark Series

the_wire.name: The Wire
the_wire.desc: An American crime drama created by David Simon for the cable network HBO, broadcast in five seasons of sixty episodes between 2 June 2002 and 9 March 2008. It follows a long police investigation into a West Baltimore drug organisation, telling the story from both sides at once — the detectives and the dealers given equal weight and equal complexity — and each season adds another failing city institution: the police, the docks, City Hall, the schools, the newspaper. Its argument is that individuals are largely powerless against the institutions they serve. Widely named among the greatest television series ever made, it received only two Emmy nominations in its entire run and won neither.

season_1.name: Season One (2002)
season_1.desc: Thirteen episodes broadcast between 2 June and 8 September 2002. A makeshift police unit assembled from officers other commanders wanted rid of builds a wiretap case against the Barksdale drug organisation in West Baltimore. The season establishes the show's method: the dealers are given as much screen time, interior life and internal politics as the detectives, and neither side is presented as simply right.

season_2.name: Season Two (2003)
season_2.desc: Twelve episodes broadcast between 1 June and 24 August 2003. The focus shifts to the Port of Baltimore, where too few ships call for the number of men on the union rolls, and a stevedores' union official lets a smuggling ring move containers through the docks untouched in order to fund lobbying that might bring the work back. Its subject is the disappearance of unionised manual work and what fills the space it leaves.

season_3.name: Season Three (2004)
season_3.desc: Twelve episodes broadcast between 19 September and 19 December 2004. Two attempts at reform run in parallel and both fail: a police major quietly stops making arrests in three abandoned blocks to see whether concentrating the drug trade reduces violence elsewhere, and a drug organisation's second in command tries to convert its profits into legitimate property development. The season also introduces the city's electoral politics.

season_4.name: Season Four (2006)
season_4.desc: Thirteen episodes broadcast between 10 September and 10 December 2006, following four West Baltimore thirteen-year-olds through a year of middle school as each is sorted toward a different future. It sets the school system's manipulation of test scores against the police department's manipulation of crime figures as the same behaviour. Most often named the show's finest season, and the one for which its writers won the 2008 Writers Guild award.

season_5.name: Season Five (2008)
season_5.desc: The final season, ten episodes broadcast between 6 January and 9 March 2008 and the shortest of the five. It adds a fictionalised version of Simon's own former employer, the Baltimore Sun, to the show's map of institutions, and sets a reporter who invents quotes against a detective who invents a serial killer preying on homeless men in order to unlock funding for a real case he has been denied.

prequel_shorts.name: The Prequel Shorts
prequel_shorts.desc: Three short vignettes set before the events of the series, filmed during production of season five and released through HBO On Demand: When Bunk Met McNulty, Young Omar and Young Prop Joe. They were later included with the complete series DVD box set.

the_target.name: The Target
the_target.desc: The series premiere, broadcast 2 June 2002, running 62 minutes. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Clark Johnson. It opens on the killing of a corner hustler called Snot Boogie and ends with a detective's complaint to a judge forcing a case nobody in the department wants.

the_pager.name: The Pager
the_pager.desc: The fifth episode of season one, broadcast 30 June 2002. Teleplay by Ed Burns from a story by David Simon and Burns, directed by Clark Johnson. The drug organisation stops using telephones the police can listen to and switches to pagers carrying numbers mapped onto a clock face; breaking that code falls to the one officer his colleagues consider too incompetent to be trusted with patrol duty.

the_wire_ep.name: The Wire (episode 1.06)
the_wire_ep.desc: The sixth episode of season one, broadcast 7 July 2002, and the only episode to share the series title. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Ed Bianchi. The murder of a man connected to the robber Omar Little gives the stalled detail its first real lead.

the_cost.name: The Cost
the_cost.desc: The tenth episode of season one, in which an undercover drug purchase arranged to reach the top of the Barksdale organisation is rushed into place by commanders impatient for results. It goes wrong, and Detective Kima Greggs — the investigators' best source of street information — is shot and badly wounded in the car.

cleaning_up.name: Cleaning Up
cleaning_up.desc: The twelfth episode of season one, teleplay by George Pelecanos from a story by David Simon and Ed Burns. A sixteen-year-old lookout who asked to leave the drug trade is shot by the two friends he grew up beside, on orders from above — the first of the penultimate-episode deaths Pelecanos was handed in every season thereafter.

all_prologue.name: All Prologue
all_prologue.desc: The sixth episode of season two, and the only one of the sixty to carry a joint four-way writing credit rather than the usual story-and-teleplay split. D'Angelo Barksdale — the drug kingpin's nephew, serving twenty years and starting to consider cooperating with police — is strangled in the prison library on his uncle's partner's orders, the death staged as a suicide. Shortly before, he argues in the prison book group that Gatsby cannot outrun what he was, which is his own case exactly.

backwash.name: Backwash
backwash.desc: The seventh episode of season two, teleplay by Rafael Alvarez, a Baltimore native who had worked around the port. Detectives take evidence cloned from the union's computer to their sergeant, and the union treasurer's son — a young dock worker treated as a joke by everyone on the waterfront — shoots a smugglers' associate dead behind a warehouse counter after being cheated once too often.

bad_dreams.name: Bad Dreams
bad_dreams.desc: The eleventh episode of season two, teleplay by George Pelecanos. Frank Sobotka, the union treasurer who has been letting a smuggling ring move containers through the docks in exchange for money to lobby for the port's revival, decides to tell the federal investigators everything — and walks under the interstate to meet the smugglers' people knowing what is likely waiting.

port_in_a_storm.name: Port in a Storm
port_in_a_storm.desc: The season two finale, broadcast 24 August 2003, running 63 minutes. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns. The case closes against the dock workers who moved the containers while the organisation that filled them clears out of Baltimore on a federal tip-off — and it is the only episode directed by Robert F. Colesberry — the executive producer who had shaped the show's visual method since the pilot, for whom this was a directing debut, and who died six months later, on 9 February 2004, from complications of cardiac surgery.

time_after_time.name: Time After Time
time_after_time.desc: The season three premiere, broadcast 19 September 2004. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Ed Bianchi. It opens with the demolition of the Franklin Terrace towers, the symbolic clearing of the ground the Barksdale organisation stood on.

dead_soldiers.name: Dead Soldiers
dead_soldiers.desc: The third episode of season three, teleplay by Dennis Lehane, his first for the series. A homicide detective dies suddenly and the squad holds a wake for him at their bar, the body laid out in dress blues on the pool table — a scene written for the show's own executive producer, Robert Colesberry, who played the character and had died seven months before the season began. The title also refers to the empty drug vials littering West Baltimore's pavements.

hamsterdam_ep.name: Hamsterdam
hamsterdam_ep.desc: The fourth episode of season three, teleplay by George Pelecanos. The three abandoned blocks where a police major has secretly suspended drug arrests acquire the name the whole city then uses: dealers herded there mangle a patrolman's sneer that their commander has built an Amsterdam. The major also stands before a hall of residents and refuses to promise them anything will improve.

straight_and_true.name: Straight and True
straight_and_true.desc: The fifth episode of season three, broadcast 17 October 2004. Teleplay by Ed Burns from a story by David Simon and Burns, directed by Dan Attias. The experiment becomes operational: uniformed officers are ordered to escort dealers into the tolerated blocks, and a major discovers his own men will carry out an instruction he cannot put in writing. Meanwhile a former enforcer, out after fourteen years, finds he can no longer pull a trigger.

middle_ground.name: Middle Ground
middle_ground.desc: The eleventh episode of season three, broadcast 12 December 2004. Teleplay by George Pelecanos from a story by David Simon and Pelecanos, directed by Joe Chappelle. The drug organisation's two leaders spend a last night together on a rooftop, each having already arranged the other's destruction — one by giving the police his partner's whereabouts, the other by telling a wronged enforcer where to find him. It drew the series' first Emmy nomination, for writing, and lost.

boys_of_summer.name: Boys of Summer
boys_of_summer.desc: The season four premiere, broadcast 10 September 2006, teleplay by David Simon. It introduces four West Baltimore thirteen-year-olds in the last fortnight of their summer holiday, before a school year that will sort each toward a different life, and opens on a young drug enforcer buying a replacement nail gun while discussing its load with a hardware assistant who has no idea what it is for. It won the 2007 American Cinema Editors award.

home_rooms.name: Home Rooms
home_rooms.desc: The third episode of season four, teleplay by Richard Price. The school year begins and the former policeman discovers that a classroom cannot be commanded the way a street corner could — order has to be negotiated rather than imposed — while the police department and City Hall manoeuvre over a murdered state's witness neither wants to own.

corner_boys.name: Corner Boys
corner_boys.desc: The eighth episode of season four, teleplay by Richard Price. A university researcher and a retired police major separate the school's most disruptive thirteen-year-olds into a classroom of their own and start asking them how their neighbourhood actually works. The answers are more sophisticated than the curriculum, and include Namond Brice's charge that the city does what the corner does and calls only one of them animal.

thats_got_his_own.name: That's Got His Own
thats_got_his_own.desc: The twelfth episode of season four, teleplay by George Pelecanos. The season's penultimate hour takes each of the four thirteen-year-olds past the point at which school could still have caught him: one loses his foster home to arson, another is passed to a high school that will not help him, and every consequence the year has been assembling arrives at once.

final_grades.name: Final Grades
final_grades.desc: The season four finale, broadcast 10 December 2006 and running 78 minutes, the second longest episode of the series. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Ernest Dickerson. The four thirteen-year-olds the season has followed arrive at four different futures — a suburban adoption, a group home, a drug corner and the street — while police open the boarded-up houses where a drug crew has been hiding its murder victims.

more_with_less.name: More with Less
more_with_less.desc: The season five premiere, broadcast 6 January 2008, teleplay by David Simon. Its title is the instruction handed down in the same hour to two institutions — a police department told to cut costs and a newspaper told the same by out-of-town owners — and the season is ten episodes on what each does to comply.

unconfirmed_reports.name: Unconfirmed Reports
unconfirmed_reports.desc: The second episode of season five, teleplay by William F. Zorzi, a former Baltimore Sun political reporter. The paper's buy-outs start removing experienced staff, and a detective denied the resources for a real murder case begins staging evidence to invent one that will be funded — two institutions responding to scarcity by manufacturing what they cannot obtain.

transitions.name: Transitions
transitions.desc: The fourth episode of season five, teleplay by Ed Burns. Three removals in one hour, each arranged by people who benefit: the drug wholesaler who supplied the whole city is shot in his own kitchen by the younger boss he had mentored; the police commissioner is levered out of office by a political deal; and a retired robber is drawn back from Puerto Rico by a killing designed to reach him.

clarifications.name: Clarifications
clarifications.desc: The eighth episode of season five, broadcast 24 February 2008. Teleplay by Dennis Lehane from a story by David Simon and Lehane, directed by Anthony Hemingway. Omar Little — the robber who had spent five seasons holding up drug crews and become the most feared man in West Baltimore — is shot dead buying cigarettes in a corner shop by a child, mid-sentence, with no music and no build.

late_editions.name: Late Editions
late_editions.desc: The ninth episode of season five, teleplay by George Pelecanos — the last of the penultimate episodes he was handed in every season. Michael Lee, a teenager recruited into the drug organisation at thirteen, shoots the young enforcer who brought him in, having worked out from her own instruction that she was sent to kill him. The illegal wiretap finally produces arrests.

series_finale.desc: The series finale, broadcast 9 March 2008, running 93 minutes and the longest episode of the series. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Clark Johnson, who had also directed the pilot. Nothing is resolved; everyone is replaced. A reporter who invented his stories collects a Pulitzer, a transactional major becomes police commissioner, a teenager takes up the dead robber's shotgun, and a boy who could not hold school or corner work takes his first shot of heroin in a scrapyard.

david_simon.name: David Simon
david_simon.desc: The creator of The Wire. He spent over a decade as a crime reporter at the Baltimore Sun, then wrote two books of immersive reporting — a year inside the city's homicide squad, and a year on a drug-ridden street corner — both of which became television before he created a series of his own. He ran The Wire as showrunner, executive producer and head writer for all five seasons, and was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship, the American 'genius grant', in 2010.

ed_burns.name: Ed Burns
ed_burns.desc: Edward P. Burns, born 1946, co-creator of The Wire's world though not named on its created-by card. He spent around twenty years as a Baltimore police detective, first in homicide and then building long-term wiretap cases against drug organisations — the patient, paperwork-driven method the series dramatises — and afterwards taught in a city middle school. Both careers went directly into the show: his casework into its police procedure, his classroom into the fourth season about four thirteen-year-old boys.

george_pelecanos.name: George Pelecanos
george_pelecanos.desc: Washington crime novelist, born 1957, author of The Big Blowdown and A Firing Offense. He wrote seven teleplays for The Wire, at least one in every season, and produced the third. Simon placed his scripts in the penultimate slot of all five seasons, where four of the five put their principal death.

richard_price.name: Richard Price
richard_price.desc: American novelist, born 1949, whose books Clockers and Lush Life cover the same ground as The Wire — drug crews, the detectives working them, and the neighbourhoods both operate in. Reviewers had spent two seasons comparing the series to Clockers before Simon and Pelecanos approached him at a reading and recruited him. He wrote five episodes between the third and fifth seasons, including the hour in which a separate classroom finally asks four thirteen-year-olds how a corner actually works.

dennis_lehane.name: Dennis Lehane
dennis_lehane.desc: Boston crime novelist, born 1965, author of Mystic River. He joined The Wire's writing staff for the third season and wrote three episodes, one per season thereafter — including the hour in which the series' most recognisable character, the robber Omar Little, is shot dead in a corner shop by a child, mid-sentence and without ceremony.

rafael_alvarez.name: Rafael Alvarez
rafael_alvarez.desc: Baltimore native and former Baltimore Sun colleague of David Simon, with years of working knowledge of the city's waterfront — its unions, its checkers, and the paperwork a shipping container can disappear through. That experience fed directly into the second season, and he wrote or co-wrote three of its episodes as well as compiling the series' official companion book.

william_zorzi.name: William F. Zorzi
william_zorzi.desc: Political journalist who covered Maryland state politics for the Baltimore Sun, where David Simon was a crime reporter on the same paper. He joined the writing staff for the third season and supplied the reporting behind the show's City Hall material — how endorsements are traded, how a police commissioner is removed by negotiation rather than sacking — and appears on screen in the final season as a Sun reporter under his own name.

joy_lusco_kecken.name: Joy Lusco Kecken
joy_lusco_kecken.desc: Baltimore native and independent film-maker who wrote for each of The Wire's first three seasons, and returned to the final one as a director, sharing that episode with her husband Scott Kecken. Her teleplays include the hour in which thirteen dead women found in a shipping container stop being a statistical problem and acquire names, effects and a route.

david_mills.name: David Mills
david_mills.desc: Television writer and producer, 1961 to 2010, a former investigative journalist at the Washington Post who wrote for Homicide: Life on the Street, NYPD Blue and ER. He was David Simon's earliest television collaborator and later wrote for The Wire's fourth and fifth seasons. He died of a brain aneurysm during production of Treme.

eric_overmyer.name: Eric Overmyer
eric_overmyer.desc: Playwright and television writer who had worked with David Simon years earlier on the NBC police drama Homicide: Life on the Street. He wrote two episodes of The Wire's fourth season — the election hour and the one in which a boy's cooperation with police destroys his foster placement — and then co-created Treme with Simon, about New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina.

kia_corthron.name: Kia Corthron
kia_corthron.desc: Playwright and novelist from western Maryland, whose single Wire credit is a fourth-season episode in which each of four thirteen-year-old boys is shown the ceiling on what he will be permitted to become — and a former policeman turned teacher recognises his school's weeks of test drilling as the same manipulation of figures he watched police commanders perform.

chris_collins.name: Chris Collins
chris_collins.desc: Television writer who joined The Wire as a staff writer on its fourth season and took his first solo teleplay credit in the fifth — the episode in which the Baltimore Sun offers its reporters buy-outs while a drug organisation has a rival's adviser killed. He shared in the writing staff's Writers Guild nomination for that final season.

melnick_choksey.name: David H. Melnick & Shamit Choksey
melnick_choksey.desc: David H. Melnick and Shamit Choksey, credited jointly with a single first-season teleplay and nothing else on the series. Their episode suspends the police investigation for a full day to show the rival drug organisations as neighbourhood institutions, fielding basketball teams against each other with serious money staked on the result.

robert_colesberry.name: Robert F. Colesberry
robert_colesberry.desc: Film producer and director, 7 March 1946 to 9 February 2004, an Academy Award nominee for producing Mississippi Burning. He was The Wire's executive producer from the pilot and the crew's authority on how the show should look and move, directed the season two finale, and played the recurring role of Detective Ray Cole. He died of complications following cardiac surgery, weeks before season three began shooting.

nina_kostroff_noble.name: Nina Kostroff Noble
nina_kostroff_noble.desc: Television producer, born 1959, who produced all five seasons of The Wire and is David Simon's long-standing producing partner at Blown Deadline Productions, the company behind everything he has made since The Corner. She was named on the directorial team that took the series' only Directors Guild award.

karen_thorson.name: Karen L. Thorson
karen_thorson.desc: Television producer who joined the production as a co-producer in 2001, while the pilot was being prepared, and worked on all five seasons. She had previously produced Homicide: Life on the Street and The Corner, making her one of the continuous threads running through David Simon's Baltimore work.

clark_johnson.name: Clark Johnson
clark_johnson.desc: Actor and director who had starred as Detective Meldrick Lewis on Homicide: Life on the Street, the NBC series adapted from David Simon's first book. On The Wire he directed the pilot and the series finale — the two bookends — and appears on screen in the fifth season as Gus Haynes, the Baltimore Sun city editor who tries to stop a reporter inventing his stories.

joe_chappelle.name: Joe Chappelle
joe_chappelle.desc: Director and producer on The Wire throughout its run. His credits include Middle Ground, in which a drug organisation's two leaders spend a last night on a rooftop each having already arranged the other's destruction, and More with Less, the final season premiere that issues the same budget instruction to a police department and a newspaper in one hour.

ernest_dickerson.name: Ernest Dickerson
ernest_dickerson.desc: Cinematographer turned director, best known for shooting Spike Lee's early features including Do the Right Thing. His Wire credits include the third season finale, in which a police major's experiment in not arresting drug dealers is bulldozed and he is demoted on the day he retires.

anthony_hemingway.name: Anthony Hemingway
anthony_hemingway.desc: Director promoted from inside the production, having worked as a first assistant director on four first-season episodes before being given episodes of his own. His credits include Clarifications, in which Omar Little — the robber who had spent five seasons holding up drug crews — is shot dead in a corner shop by a child.

ed_bianchi.name: Ed Bianchi
ed_bianchi.desc: Directed four episodes of The Wire: the season one hour that shares the series' title, in which the police wiretap finally goes live after six episodes of legal groundwork; the season two premiere that opens on thirteen bodies found in a shipping container; the second-season episode that follows; and the season three premiere, which begins with the demolition of the high-rise blocks where most of the drug trade had been conducted.

dan_attias.name: Dan Attias
dan_attias.desc: Directed four episodes of The Wire across four seasons, and won the 2009 Directors Guild award for dramatic series direction for the last of them, Transitions — the only individual industry award the series ever received. That hour removes three figures at once: a police commissioner, a drug wholesaler, and a robber's retirement in Puerto Rico.

charles_dutton.name: Charles S. Dutton
charles_dutton.desc: Actor and director who grew up in Baltimore and served time for manslaughter before training as an actor. He directed all six parts of The Corner in 2000 — Simon and Burns's miniseries about a year on a drug-ridden West Baltimore street — having initially wanted nothing to do with the project, and won an Emmy for it. That collaboration is what persuaded HBO to commission The Wire.

alexa_fogel.name: Alexa L. Fogel
alexa_fogel.desc: Casting director on The Wire, responsible for a company mixing established stage actors with Baltimore locals, former offenders and people with no acting experience at all. Her work on the first season drew a Casting Society of America nomination, and the practice of hiring people who had lived the material is one of the reasons the series is taken as documentary-like.

dominic_west.name: Dominic West
dominic_west.desc: English actor Dominic West played Detective Jimmy McNulty in the starring cast of all five seasons. McNulty sets the series in motion by complaining privately to a judge that his department will not investigate a drug organisation's murders, and nearly ends it by inventing a serial killer preying on homeless men to unlock the funding his real case has been refused.

idris_elba.name: Idris Elba
idris_elba.desc: Sir Idris Elba, the English actor who played Stringer Bell in the starring cast of the first three seasons — the drug organisation's second in command, who runs it as a business, takes economics classes at a community college and tries to move the money into property development. The role made his reputation in America; he was appointed OBE in 2016 and knighted in the 2026 New Year Honours for his work with young people, having co-founded the Elba Hope Foundation and campaigned against knife crime in Britain.

wood_harris.name: Wood Harris
wood_harris.desc: Wood Harris played Avon Barksdale in the starring cast of the first three seasons: the head of a West Baltimore drug organisation who thinks of himself as a soldier rather than a businessman, valuing held territory and personal standing above profit — the conviction that eventually destroys his partnership and his organisation.

michael_k_williams.name: Michael K. Williams
michael_k_williams.desc: Michael K. Williams, 1966 to 2021, played Omar Little — a robber who makes his living holding up drug crews rather than dealing, working to a rule that nobody outside the trade is harmed. He carries a shotgun, whistles as he walks so that corners empty before he reaches them, refuses to swear, and is openly gay. Recurring from the first season and in the starring cast from the third, the part is routinely named among the finest in American television.

sonja_sohn.name: Sonja Sohn
sonja_sohn.desc: Sonja Sohn played Kima Greggs in the starring cast of all five seasons: a narcotics detective shot and badly wounded in the first season during an undercover drug buy rushed by pressure from above. She returns to street work rather than take a desk, and is the officer who eventually reports a colleague's fabricated serial killer to their commander.

lance_reddick.name: Lance Reddick
lance_reddick.desc: Lance Reddick, 1962 to 2023, played Lieutenant Cedric Daniels in the starring cast of all five seasons: the commander given the central investigation because his superiors expect him to close it quickly and quietly, who instead protects his detectives' slow work for five years. Promoted to commissioner at the end, he resigns rather than falsify the city's crime statistics.

clarke_peters.name: Clarke Peters
clarke_peters.desc: Clarke Peters played Detective Lester Freamon in the starring cast from the second season on: an investigator of unusual ability who had spent thirteen years and four months exiled to the pawn shop unit for embarrassing a commander. His method is to follow money and paperwork rather than make arrests, and it produces both the drug case and, later, the bodies hidden in empty houses.

wendell_pierce.name: Wendell Pierce
wendell_pierce.desc: Wendell Pierce played Bunk Moreland, a Baltimore homicide detective, in the starring cast of all five seasons. He is the closest friend of the detective who drives the series' central investigation and its most consistent critic, disapproving of almost everything his partner does while continuing to work beside him.

andre_royo.name: Andre Royo
andre_royo.desc: Andre Royo played Bubbles in the starring cast of all five seasons: a heroin addict who survives by scavenging scrap metal and by informing for the police, whose knowledge of every corner in West Baltimore makes him more useful than the department's own equipment. The series withholds his real name, Reginald Cousins, until its fourth year, and ends with him a year clean and invited to eat upstairs at his sister's table rather than in her basement.

larry_gilliard_jr.name: Lawrence Gilliard Jr.
larry_gilliard_jr.desc: Lawrence Gilliard Jr. played D'Angelo Barksdale in the starring cast of the first two seasons — the drug kingpin's nephew, who cannot stop registering what the family business costs other people. That makes him first useless to the organisation and then a danger to it; sentenced to twenty years, he is strangled in prison on his uncle's partner's orders, the death staged as a suicide.

jd_williams.name: J. D. Williams
jd_williams.desc: J. D. Williams played Preston 'Bodie' Broadus from the pilot to the fourth season finale, in the starring cast from the third season. Bodie starts as teenage muscle and works up to running a corner of his own; when a more ruthless organisation takes West Baltimore he keeps working the same ground out of loyalty to an outfit that no longer exists, and is shot on it.

jamie_hector.name: Jamie Hector
jamie_hector.desc: Jamie Hector played Marlo Stanfield in the starring cast of the fourth and fifth seasons: the young drug boss who takes West Baltimore by refusing every convention the trade runs on. What he wants is not money but that his name should frighten people, and the series ends with him free and wealthy, slipping out of a business reception to provoke a street fight with two teenagers who have no idea who he is.

gbenga_akinnagbe.name: Gbenga Akinnagbe
gbenga_akinnagbe.desc: Gbenga Akinnagbe played Chris Partlow, chief enforcer to the drug boss Marlo Stanfield, in the starring cast for the fifth season. Partlow's method is what makes the organisation almost impossible to prosecute: he seals victims inside Baltimore's boarded-up empty houses with quicklime and nails the boards back, so the killings never appear in the city's murder figures at all.

felicia_pearson.name: Felicia Pearson
felicia_pearson.desc: Baltimore-born performer, born 1980, who played Snoop, a fictionalised version of herself, from the third season on. She grew up in foster care, was convicted of second-degree murder as a teenager, and was cast after meeting Michael K. Williams in a Baltimore club.

robert_f_chew.name: Robert F. Chew
robert_f_chew.desc: Robert F. Chew, 1960 to 2013, was a Baltimore actor and acting coach who played Proposition Joe — the East Baltimore drug wholesaler who treats the trade as a business rather than a war — in all five seasons, one of very few figures from the drug world present from the first episode to the last. Chew coached many of the show's young local actors offscreen, including all four of the boys the fourth season follows; he died of heart failure at his home in Baltimore, aged 52.

chris_bauer.name: Chris Bauer
chris_bauer.desc: Chris Bauer played Frank Sobotka in the starring cast of the second season: treasurer of a stevedores' union at a Baltimore port with too few ships calling to employ its members. He lets a smuggling ring move containers through the docks untouched, and spends the money lobbying politicians to dredge the canal and reopen the grain pier — trying to buy back the work rather than enrich himself.

paul_ben_victor.name: Paul Ben-Victor
paul_ben_victor.desc: Paul Ben-Victor played Spiros 'Vondas' Vondopoulos in the starring cast for the second season: second in command of the smuggling operation running heroin, stolen cargo and trafficked women through the Port of Baltimore. He does all the talking so the man above him need never appear, and is courteous to everyone including the people he is arranging to have killed.

pablo_schreiber.name: Pablo Schreiber
pablo_schreiber.desc: Pablo Schreiber played Nick Sobotka, a Baltimore stevedore with a union card and too few shifts to afford a flat of his own, who carries much of the second season's argument about the disappearance of unionised manual work. He moves stolen cargo and then drugs for a smuggling ring, enters witness protection when the case collapses, and reappears in the final season at the unveiling of a waterfront memorial to his uncle.

james_ransone.name: James Ransone
james_ransone.desc: James Ransone, 1979 to 2025, was a Baltimore-area native who played Ziggy Sobotka — the union treasurer's son, a young dock worker treated as a joke by everyone on the waterfront, whose escalating attempts to be taken seriously end with him shooting a man dead behind a warehouse counter. Ransone was later cast by Simon and Burns in Generation Kill, and was found dead in Los Angeles in December 2025, aged 46.

amy_ryan.name: Amy Ryan
amy_ryan.desc: Amy Ryan played Beadie Russell, a port police officer whose ordinary job is checking seals on shipping containers. She opens one with a broken seal and finds thirteen dead women inside, which starts the second season's investigation and pulls her into homicide work several ranks above anything she has done.

aidan_gillen.name: Aidan Gillen
aidan_gillen.desc: Irish actor Aidan Gillen played Tommy Carcetti in the starring cast from the third season on: an ambitious white councilman who wins the mayoralty of a majority-black Baltimore by encouraging a second black candidate into the race to split the vote, then refuses state money for the city's schools because accepting it would damage his own run for governor.

robert_wisdom.name: Robert Wisdom
robert_wisdom.desc: Robert Wisdom played Major Howard 'Bunny' Colvin in the starring cast of the third and fourth seasons: a police commander who, after thirty years, concludes that drug arrests have never changed anything on his streets, and quietly stops making them in three abandoned blocks to see what happens. Violent crime falls; he is demoted on the day he retires.

jim_true_frost.name: Jim True-Frost
jim_true_frost.desc: Jim True-Frost played Roland 'Prez' Pryzbylewski, in the starring cast for the third and fourth seasons. Banned from street duty after blinding a boy in a stop, he turns out to have an unexpected gift for reading codes and phone records, and becomes the reason the wiretap works. After killing a plainclothes colleague by mistake in a dark alley he resigns and becomes a middle-school mathematics teacher.

john_doman.name: John Doman
john_doman.desc: John Doman played William Rawls, the homicide commander and later deputy police commissioner, in the starring cast of all five seasons. Rawls exists to embody the department's only real measure — the proportion of murders officially recorded as solved — and to treat every new body first as a question of whose figures it will damage.

frankie_faison.name: Frankie Faison
frankie_faison.desc: Frankie Faison played Ervin Burrell, Baltimore's police commissioner, in the starring cast of the first four seasons. His hold on the job depends entirely on delivering acceptable crime figures to City Hall, so he obstructs any investigation likely to take years or embarrass a politician — and is removed by a negotiated deal when a new mayor needs someone to blame.

deirdre_lovejoy.name: Deirdre Lovejoy
deirdre_lovejoy.desc: Deirdre Lovejoy played Rhonda Pearlman, the assistant state's attorney attached to the police investigation, in the starring cast of all five seasons. She is the lawyer who must persuade a judge to authorise each wiretap and then make the resulting case survive in court, and she ends the series appointed a judge herself.

seth_gilliam.name: Seth Gilliam
seth_gilliam.desc: Seth Gilliam played Ellis Carver from the pilot onward, in the starring cast from the third season: an officer who begins as a corner-clearing brawler and is changed by a single question from his commanding major — name one person living on the streets you have policed for years. He cannot, and spends the rest of the series learning the names.

domenick_lombardozzi.name: Domenick Lombardozzi
domenick_lombardozzi.desc: Domenick Lombardozzi played Thomas 'Herc' Hauk, in the starring cast from the third season. Herc's instinct is always force and shortcuts, in a series about patient investigation: he loses a surveillance camera worth thousands of dollars, then invents an informant to justify a warrant, and between them those failures collapse a case the department had spent a year building. He leaves the police to work for the defence lawyer who represents the drug organisations.

reg_e_cathey.name: Reg E. Cathey
reg_e_cathey.desc: Reg E. Cathey, 1958 to 2018, played Norman Wilson in the starring cast of the fourth and fifth seasons — a newspaperman turned political operative who runs Tommy Carcetti's mayoral campaign and then advises him in office, and the aide willing to tell the mayor plainly when a decision is about his own ambition rather than the city. Cathey had earlier appeared in The Corner, and won an Emmy in 2015 for House of Cards; he died of lung cancer, and David Simon announced his death publicly.

chad_coleman.name: Chad L. Coleman
chad_coleman.desc: Chad L. Coleman played Dennis 'Cutty' Wise in the starring cast for the fourth season: a drug organisation's enforcer released after fourteen years in prison who goes out on one job, finds he can no longer pull the trigger, tells his old boss the work is not in him any more, and opens a boxing gym for neighbourhood boys instead.

glynn_turman.name: Glynn Turman
glynn_turman.desc: Glynn Turman played Clarence Royce, mayor of Baltimore. He first appears presiding over the demolition of the city's high-rise public housing blocks, staged as urban renewal, and last appears having lost the primary to a challenger he never took seriously, reduced to making introductions for a lobbyist.

michael_kostroff.name: Michael Kostroff
michael_kostroff.desc: Michael Kostroff played Maurice Levy across the run of the series, in the starring cast for the fifth: the defence attorney who represents every major drug organisation in Baltimore in turn, and who ends the series exposing an illegal police wiretap, collapsing the state's case, and negotiating his client's freedom.

neal_huff.name: Neal Huff
neal_huff.desc: Neal Huff, a New York stage actor, played Michael Steintorf in the starring cast for the fifth season — the mayor's chief of staff, the aide who carries the instructions nobody will put in writing, including the demand for lower crime figures that makes the police commissioner resign rather than falsify them. Huff later played the clergy-abuse survivor Phil Saviano in Spotlight, the newspaper film directed by Tom McCarthy, who had played the reporter inventing his stories in The Wire's own newsroom season.

tom_mccarthy.name: Tom McCarthy
tom_mccarthy.desc: Actor and film director Tom McCarthy played Scott Templeton in the starring cast for the fifth season — a Baltimore Sun reporter who invents quotes and sources, is promoted and given a Pulitzer for the invented work, and is never caught. McCarthy later directed and co-wrote Spotlight, about reporters doing the opposite.

michelle_paress.name: Michelle Paress
michelle_paress.desc: Michelle Paress played Alma Gutierrez, a junior reporter at the Baltimore Sun, in the starring cast for the fifth season. She does the night calls and door-knocks while a colleague invents quotes and wins a Pulitzer for them; she backs her city editor against him and is moved to a suburban bureau for it.

tristan_wilds.name: Tristan Wilds
tristan_wilds.desc: Tristan Wilds played Michael Lee, the most capable and most guarded of four West Baltimore thirteen-year-olds followed through a single school year. Michael hides an abusive household from every adult who offers help, takes a drug crew's protection in exchange for having his abuser killed, and ends the series holding up dealers with a shotgun in the manner of the robber the show spent five years building up.

jermaine_crawford.name: Jermaine Crawford
jermaine_crawford.desc: Jermaine Crawford played Duquan 'Dukie' Weems, the gentlest and most academically able of the four boys whose thirteenth year the fourth season follows. Dukie's household sells his clothes for drug money and his teachers wash and feed him at school; promoted into a high school by a system counting test scores rather than readiness, and unable to hold either school or street work, he is last seen injecting heroin in a scrapyard.

maestro_harrell.name: Maestro Harrell
maestro_harrell.desc: Maestro Harrell played Randy Wagstaff in the fourth and fifth seasons, one of the four schoolboys at the centre of the fourth. Randy runs a sweet-selling business from his locker and unknowingly passes on a message that arranges a murder; when he tells a teacher and then a police officer, the police let his cooperation become known, his foster home is firebombed, and he ends up in a group home.

julito_mccullum.name: Julito McCullum
julito_mccullum.desc: Julito McCullum played Namond Brice, the loud, soft-centred son of an imprisoned drug enforcer and one of four thirteen-year-old boys the fourth season follows. His mother expects him to earn selling drugs as his father did; he is the only one of the four to escape that future, adopted by a retired police major.

isiah_whitlock_jr.name: Isiah Whitlock Jr.
isiah_whitlock_jr.desc: Isiah Whitlock Jr., 1954 to 2025, played Clay Davis across all five seasons and in the starring cast for the fifth: a Maryland state senator who takes money from developers, drug dealers and his own constituents' campaign funds alike. Prosecuted in state court, he casts himself to the jury as a man redistributing money to the poor and is acquitted. Whitlock's elongated delivery of a single profanity became the character's signature and followed him through five Spike Lee films; he died in New York after a short illness.

corey_parker_robinson.name: Corey Parker Robinson
corey_parker_robinson.desc: Corey Parker Robinson played Detective Leander Sydnor, in the starring cast from the third season on — a young officer recruited into the special investigative unit because he is good at the patient, unglamorous work the department otherwise has no use for, and who ends the series as one of the few still trying to build a real case.

delaney_williams.name: Delaney Williams
delaney_williams.desc: Delaney Williams played Sergeant Jay Landsman across the series — the homicide supervisor who runs the squad's chart of open and closed murders and makes decisions accordingly. The character carries the name of a real Baltimore detective Simon had written about, who himself appears in the show playing a different officer.

michael_b_jordan.name: Michael B. Jordan
michael_b_jordan.desc: Michael B. Jordan played Wallace, the sixteen-year-old lookout whose guilt over a killing he unwittingly set in motion leads him to ask to leave the drug crew — and gets him shot by his own two closest friends on their bosses' orders. Jordan was fifteen when cast, having auditioned for the tougher part of Bodie and been judged a better fit for Wallace; it was his breakthrough role, and he appeared in all thirteen first-season episodes before a film career that included Fruitvale Station, Creed and Black Panther.

michael_potts.name: Michael Potts
michael_potts.desc: Michael Potts played Brother Mouzone in the second and third seasons — a fastidious, bow-tied enforcer brought down from New York to protect the Barksdale organisation's most profitable ground, the high-rise public housing blocks, from the robber who had been raiding them. He reads intently between acts of violence and speaks with elaborate politeness.

anwan_glover.name: Anwan Glover
anwan_glover.desc: Anwan Glover, a Washington go-go musician, played Slim Charles — hired muscle rather than family, which is exactly why he survives every organisation that employs him. He moves from the Barksdales to the city-wide dealers' association, fires the last significant shot of the series, and observes immediately afterwards that it was for nothing.

hassan_johnson.name: Hassan Johnson
hassan_johnson.desc: Hassan Johnson played Roland 'Wee-Bey' Brice, the Barksdale drug organisation's most prolific killer, who accepts a life sentence and confesses to murders he did not commit so that the men above him survive. Years later, from prison, he overrules his own wife and gives their son away to a retired police officer, to keep the boy out of the trade.

method_man.name: Method Man
method_man.desc: Clifford Smith, the rapper performing as Method Man, played Melvin 'Cheese' Wagstaff across all five seasons: a dealer working for his uncle, the East Baltimore wholesaler who supplies most of the city. His disloyalty escalates from betraying his own crew to giving up his uncle's whereabouts to a rival, and he is shot mid-sentence at the wholesalers' final meeting.

tray_chaney.name: Tray Chaney
tray_chaney.desc: Tray Chaney played Poot Carr from the pilot: a low-level corner dealer who takes part in killing his own closest friend on orders and is visibly diminished by it. He serves fifteen months, returns to selling on the same ground, and is the only member of the original crew still alive and out of prison at the end — last seen selling trainers in a shoe shop.

hbo.name: HBO
hbo.desc: An American subscription cable network which, because subscribers pay directly rather than advertisers, could commission drama with no obligation to attract mass audiences. It commissioned and broadcast The Wire, renewing it year by year on critical standing despite viewing figures that stayed modest and fell further in the final season, and allowed it to end on its creators' terms rather than be cancelled mid-story.

blown_deadline.name: Blown Deadline Productions
blown_deadline.desc: David Simon's production company, run with his producing partner Nina Kostroff Noble, through which every Simon television project since The Corner has been made — The Wire, Generation Kill, Treme, Show Me a Hero, The Deuce, The Plot Against America and We Own This City, almost all of them for HBO. It is the reason the same Baltimore crew, casting director and production designer recur across two decades of work, and why a Simon series looks and moves unlike anything made around it.

homicide_book.name: Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets
homicide_book.desc: David Simon's 1991 work of narrative non-fiction, written after a year spent inside the Baltimore Police homicide unit with the detectives' cooperation. It won the 1992 Edgar Award for Best Fact Crime, supplied characters and cases to the NBC series Homicide: Life on the Street, and is where Simon learned the material and the access that everything since has been built on.

corner_book.name: The Corner: A Year in the Life of an Inner-City Neighborhood
corner_book.desc: The 1997 book by David Simon and Ed Burns, reported over a year spent at the open-air drug market at Fayette and Monroe Streets in West Baltimore, following the residents of one corner under their own names. It was the pair's first collaboration, became an HBO miniseries in 2000, and established the reporting method that The Wire then turned into fiction.

truth_be_told.name: The Wire: Truth Be Told
truth_be_told.desc: The official companion to the series, compiled by staff writer Rafael Alvarez, containing essays by David Simon, George Pelecanos and William F. Zorzi, accounts of all sixty episodes, and interviews with cast and crew. It was published while the show was still running and is a primary source for how the series was made.

generation_kill_book.name: Generation Kill (book)
generation_kill_book.desc: Evan Wright's book drawn from his time embedded with a United States Marine Corps reconnaissance battalion during the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and the source for the HBO miniseries of the same name.

we_own_this_city_book.name: We Own This City (book)
we_own_this_city_book.desc: Justin Fenton's account of the corruption of the Baltimore Police Gun Trace Task Force, reported for the Baltimore Sun and published as a book, and the source for the 2022 HBO series.

homicide_tv.name: Homicide: Life on the Street
homicide_tv.desc: NBC police drama that ran seven seasons and 122 episodes between January 1993 and May 1999, developed by Paul Attanasio from David Simon's book about a year spent observing Baltimore's homicide detectives. Simon left the Baltimore Sun to write and produce for it; it was his apprenticeship in television and where he met several people he would later hire for The Wire.

corner_tv.name: The Corner
corner_tv.desc: Six-part HBO miniseries broadcast between 16 April and 21 May 2000, adapted by David Simon and David Mills from Simon and Burns's book about a year on a drug-ridden West Baltimore street corner, and directed by Charles S. Dutton. It uses the real names of the people whose year it dramatises, won three Emmys, and is what persuaded HBO that Simon could carry a Baltimore series of his own.

generation_kill.name: Generation Kill
generation_kill.desc: Seven-part HBO miniseries broadcast in 2008, written by David Simon, Ed Burns and the reporter Evan Wright from Wright's own embedded account of a US Marine reconnaissance battalion during the 2003 invasion of Iraq. It was the first Simon and Burns project after The Wire, and applies the same method — institutional detail, no heroes — to a military unit.

treme.name: Treme
treme.desc: HBO drama co-created by David Simon and Eric Overmyer, four seasons broadcast between 2010 and 2013, following musicians and residents of a New Orleans neighbourhood rebuilding their lives in the months and years after Hurricane Katrina. It applies the method Simon developed on The Wire — institutional detail, no heroes, a city as the real subject — to a different American disaster.

show_me_a_hero.name: Show Me a Hero
show_me_a_hero.desc: Six-part HBO miniseries from 2015, written by David Simon and William F. Zorzi from Lisa Belkin's book about Yonkers, New York, where a federal court order to build public housing in white neighbourhoods destroyed the career of the young mayor who had to carry it out. It applies the show's method — institutions, not villains — to a fight over housing rather than drugs.

the_deuce.name: The Deuce
the_deuce.desc: HBO drama co-created by David Simon and George Pelecanos, three seasons broadcast between 2017 and 2019, about the rise of the pornography business around New York's Times Square in the 1970s and 1980s. Richard Price, also a Wire writer, wrote for it — one of several projects reassembling the same writing staff on different subjects.

plot_against_america.name: The Plot Against America
plot_against_america.desc: Six-part HBO miniseries broadcast between 16 March and 20 April 2020, created by David Simon and Ed Burns from Philip Roth's alternate-history novel and starring Winona Ryder, Zoe Kazan, Morgan Spector and John Turturro. It is the only Simon project not drawn from journalism, and drew a single Emmy nomination, for cinematography.

we_own_this_city.name: We Own This City
we_own_this_city.desc: Six-part HBO limited series from 2022, created by David Simon and George Pelecanos and directed by Reinaldo Marcus Green, about the real Baltimore police squad convicted of robbing the people it policed. Shot in Baltimore with a substantial number of Wire actors returning, it dramatises as documented fact what the earlier series had argued as fiction.

way_down_in_the_hole.name: Way Down in the Hole
way_down_in_the_hole.desc: Song written by Tom Waits for his 1987 album Franks Wild Years, a gospel-blues warning to keep the devil down in the hole. It was The Wire's title theme in a different recording each season; permission from Waits arrived only shortly before the first air date, with a Cowboy Junkies track held in reserve.

tom_waits.name: Tom Waits
tom_waits.desc: Singer-songwriter who wrote Way Down in the Hole for his 1987 album Franks Wild Years, itself developed out of a stage production he mounted with Chicago's Steppenwolf Theatre Company. His own gravelled recording, rather than any of the four covers, opens the second season, and permission for the song arrived so late that a Cowboy Junkies track had been prepared as the fallback.

blind_boys_of_alabama.name: The Blind Boys of Alabama
blind_boys_of_alabama.desc: Gospel group formed in 1939 by pupils at a school for blind children in Talladega, Alabama, first performing as the Happy Land Jubilee Singers and not recording until 1948. Their version of Way Down in the Hole opens all thirteen first-season episodes and plays over the closing montage of the series.

neville_brothers.name: The Neville Brothers
neville_brothers.desc: Grammy-winning New Orleans rhythm and blues group whose brass-inflected reading of Way Down in the Hole opened the third season — the season that begins with the Franklin Terrace towers coming down and the trade scattering into the streets around them.

domaje.name: DoMaJe
domaje.desc: Five Baltimore teenagers — Ivan Ashford, Markel Steele, Cameron Brown, Tariq Al-Sabir and Avery Bargasse — who recorded the title theme specially for the fourth season, the only one of the five arrangements commissioned rather than licensed. That season follows four Baltimore thirteen-year-olds through a school year, so the year about children is opened by children.

steve_earle.name: Steve Earle
steve_earle.desc: American singer-songwriter, himself in long-term recovery from heroin addiction, who recorded the fifth-season title theme and appears across the series as Walon — the recovery-meeting sponsor who keeps turning up for Bubbles, the addict informant, and who is one of very few characters offering help that is not conditional on something.

blake_leyh.name: Blake Leyh
blake_leyh.desc: Music supervisor for The Wire, who chose the music heard on screen and enforced the show's rule that it must be diegetic — playing only where a character could plausibly be hearing it, from a car radio or a bar jukebox, never as a score telling the audience what to feel. He also composed the instrumental that closes every episode.

the_fall.name: The Fall
the_fall.desc: The instrumental piece that plays over the closing credits of every episode of The Wire, composed by the show's music supervisor Blake Leyh. Unlike the title song, which was re-recorded by a different artist for each season, it never changed across all sixty episodes.

baltimore.name: Baltimore, Maryland
baltimore.desc: A port city on the American east coast, of roughly 650,000 people when The Wire was made, and the subject of the series rather than merely its setting. It has lost close to forty per cent of its population since 1960 as manufacturing and shipping work disappeared, leaving thousands of abandoned row houses, an entrenched heroin trade and, through the years the show was broadcast, more than 250 murders annually in a city of that size. Simon treats these institutions and conditions, not any individual, as the story's real protagonist.

baltimore_sun.name: The Baltimore Sun
baltimore_sun.desc: Baltimore's daily newspaper, where David Simon worked the crime beat for over a decade and where two of his later writers, William F. Zorzi and Rafael Alvarez, were also reporters. Its buy-outs and shrinking newsroom under out-of-town ownership become the fifth season's subject, with a fictionalised version of the paper added to the show's map of failing institutions.

baltimore_police.name: Baltimore Police Department
baltimore_police.desc: The city force whose homicide unit David Simon spent a year observing for a book, and in which Ed Burns served some twenty years as a detective. Its culture of measuring commanders by the proportion of murders officially recorded as solved, its wiretap cases and its internal politics supply the show's police material almost directly.

melvin_williams.name: Melvin Williams
melvin_williams.desc: Melvin Douglas Williams, known as Little Melvin, 1941 to 2015: the Baltimore heroin trafficker who dominated the city's trade from the 1960s and was credited with helping calm the 1968 riots. David Simon covered his prosecution for the Baltimore Sun, and Williams became one of the models for the drug organisation at the centre of the series. After his release he worked as a community activist, and Simon cast him in The Wire as the Deacon — the church elder whose judgement a police major trusts more than his own commanders'.

donnie_andrews.name: Donnie Andrews
donnie_andrews.desc: Larry Donnell Andrews, 1954 to 2012, a West Baltimore stick-up man who robbed drug dealers and kept to a rule of never involving women or children. He turned himself in for a murder, served eighteen years, was paroled in 2005, became an anti-crime advocate and consulted on The Wire, also appearing in it as a character named Donnie.

fran_boyd.name: Fran Boyd
fran_boyd.desc: Denise Francine Boyd, 1956 to 2022, one of the central figures reported in Simon and Burns's book and miniseries The Corner, which followed a year in the life of a West Baltimore drug corner using its residents' real names. She came out of addiction to work as an addiction counsellor in the city, and later worked on The Wire's production.

jay_landsman_real.name: Jay Landsman
jay_landsman_real.desc: Baltimore homicide sergeant and one of the most vivid figures in Simon's book about the unit, whose name, manner and turn of phrase were given to a fictional sergeant on The Wire. Landsman himself appears in the series as a different officer — a lieutenant in the Western District — so that the man and his fictional namesake are on screen in the same programme.

ed_norris_real.name: Edward T. Norris
ed_norris_real.desc: Edward T. Norris, commissioner of the Baltimore Police Department from 2000 to 2002 and afterwards head of the Maryland State Police, who was convicted of a felony in 2003 and served six months in federal prison. He then appeared on The Wire as a homicide detective under his own name — one of many local figures cast from the world the series dramatises.

gun_trace_task_force.name: The Gun Trace Task Force
gun_trace_task_force.desc: A Baltimore Police plainclothes squad whose officers were convicted from 2017 of robbery, racketeering and overtime fraud — police stealing from the citizens they were policing. Its exposure is the subject of We Own This City, and it is the real-world case that arrived fifteen years after The Wire had argued in fiction that the department's incentives would eventually produce exactly this.

peabody_award.name: Peabody Award (2004)
peabody_award.desc: An award for electronic media administered since 1940 by the University of Georgia's Grady College of Journalism, judged by a board of critics, scholars and practitioners against a single stated criterion — excellence — rather than by the industry that makes the work. The Wire received one in 2004, and it is among very few institutional honours the series collected while it was still on air; its reputation was largely built after it ended.

emmy_nom_middle_ground.name: Emmy nomination, Outstanding Writing (2005)
emmy_nom_middle_ground.desc: The first Emmy nomination in the show's history, in 2005, for Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series. It went to Middle Ground, the third-season episode in which a drug organisation's two leaders spend a last night together on a rooftop, each having already arranged the other's destruction. It lost.

emmy_nom_finale.name: Emmy nomination, Outstanding Writing (2008)
emmy_nom_finale.desc: The second and last Emmy nomination The Wire received, in 2008, again for Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series and again unsuccessful. Across five seasons the series was never nominated for outstanding drama, nor for any performance, and its two writing nominations are the entirety of its Emmy record.

wga_award_2008.name: Writers Guild Award, Dramatic Series (2008)
wga_award_2008.desc: The Writers Guild of America's award for Television: Dramatic Series, won in 2008 for the fourth season and shared by the whole credited writing staff. It is the most significant competitive award The Wire received, and it went to the season about a middle school — the year the series is most often said to be at its best.

wga_nom_2009.name: Writers Guild nomination, Dramatic Series (2009)
wga_nom_2009.desc: A second Writers Guild nomination for Television: Dramatic Series, for the fifth and final season, citing eight credited writers — David Simon, Ed Burns, George Pelecanos, Richard Price, Dennis Lehane, David Mills, William F. Zorzi and Chris Collins. Unlike the previous year's award for the fourth season, it did not convert.

dga_award_2009.name: Directors Guild Award (2009)
dga_award_2009.desc: The Directors Guild of America's award for dramatic series direction, won in 2009 by Dan Attias for Transitions — the fifth-season episode in which a police commissioner is levered out of office, a drug wholesaler is shot in his own kitchen, and a retired robber is summoned back from Puerto Rico by a killing designed to reach him. It is the only individual industry award the series ever won.

tca_heritage_2008.name: TCA Heritage Award (2008)
tca_heritage_2008.desc: An award from the Television Critics Association, given to programmes judged to have lasting cultural significance, presented to The Wire in 2008 — four months after the series had already ended. It was the show's only win from ten TCA nominations across its run.

afi_top_ten.name: AFI Top Ten Television Programs
afi_top_ten.desc: The American Film Institute names ten outstanding television programmes each year. It listed The Wire three times — in 2003, 2006 and 2008 — recognition that mattered because the series was otherwise almost entirely ignored by awards bodies, receiving only two Emmy nominations in five years and winning neither.

naacp_image_noms.name: NAACP Image Award nominations
naacp_image_noms.desc: Sixteen nominations across the run from the NAACP Image Awards, which honour work by and about people of colour, in drama series and acting categories — none of which converted, including Michael K. Williams for outstanding supporting actor in 2009. For a series carried by one of the largest black casts on American television at the time, the shut-out sits alongside the Emmy record as its other conspicuous absence.

ace_eddie_2007.name: ACE Eddie Award (2007)
ace_eddie_2007.desc: An award from the American Cinema Editors, the editors' professional guild, for the best edited hour-long series on non-commercial television. The Wire won it in 2007 for Boys of Summer, the fourth-season premiere that follows four thirteen-year-olds through the last weeks before a school year that will sort each of them toward a different life.

corner_emmys.name: Emmy Awards for The Corner (2000)
corner_emmys.desc: Three Primetime Emmys won in 2000 by The Corner — the six-part miniseries Simon and Burns made from their book about a year on a drug-ridden West Baltimore street corner — for Outstanding Miniseries, Outstanding Directing and Outstanding Writing. The contrast with what followed is stark: The Wire, made by the same men about the same city, received two nominations in five years and won neither.

edgar_1992.name: Edgar Award (1992)
edgar_1992.desc: An award given by the Mystery Writers of America, in its Best Fact Crime category, to David Simon's book Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets — the account of twelve months he spent shadowing Baltimore's homicide detectives. It was his first professional recognition, and the book became an NBC drama two years later.

evan_wright.name: Evan Wright
evan_wright.desc: Evan Wright, 1964 to 2024, an American journalist who reported on subcultures for Rolling Stone and Vanity Fair. He spent the 2003 invasion of Iraq embedded with a United States Marine Corps reconnaissance battalion, published the reporting as the magazine series The Killer Elite — which won a National Magazine Award — and then as the 2004 book Generation Kill. He co-wrote the HBO adaptation with David Simon and Ed Burns, the only occasion the pair have built a series with the reporter whose work it came from rather than from their own; Simon called his contribution to the scripting and filming elemental.

artios_nom_2003.name: Artios Award nomination (2003)
artios_nom_2003.desc: A nomination from the Casting Society of America for the first season's casting — recognition of a company assembled from established stage actors, Baltimore locals with no professional experience, and people who had lived the lives being dramatised, including a woman cast as a version of herself after a conviction for murder.

war_on_drugs.name: The War on Drugs
war_on_drugs.desc: The show's most direct political argument, stated by a police major: call something a war and everyone starts behaving like warriors, until the neighbourhood you are supposed to be policing becomes occupied territory. David Simon put the same case to President Obama at the White House in 2015 — that what drugs do not destroy, the war on drugs is ripping apart — and the five principal writers made it explicit advocacy in a 2008 magazine essay urging jurors to refuse to convict in non-violent drug cases.

institutional_dysfunction.name: Institutions Consume Their Own
institutional_dysfunction.desc: The idea David Simon has described as the series' governing one: that modern institutions — police departments, unions, city halls, schools, newspapers — reliably sacrifice the individuals inside them to their own survival, and that this happens without villainy, through people making locally sensible decisions. Every other theme in the show is a particular case of it.

juking_the_stats.name: Juking the Stats
juking_the_stats.desc: How institutional self-protection looks in practice, and the show's own phrase for it: managing the measurement instead of the problem. Police reclassify robberies as larcenies and let rapes disappear from the books, because commanders are promoted on the share of crimes recorded as solved. A former officer turned schoolteacher recognises the same thing in a school suspending teaching for weeks to drill children for the one test it is judged by — 'I've been here before.' The newspaper does it too, chasing prizes rather than reporting.

death_of_work.name: The Death of Work
death_of_work.desc: The disappearance of the industrial jobs that once sustained working-class Baltimore, and what fills the vacuum. It drives the second season's docks entirely, and underlies every corner in the series: the drug trade is the employer of last resort in an economy with nothing else on offer.

education_vs_corner.name: The School and the Corner
education_vs_corner.desc: The fourth season's contest between two systems that both educate, put most sharply by Namond Brice: we do the same thing as you, except when we do it it is oh my God these kids are animals, and that is hypocritical. Zenobia Dawson gives the other half of it in Colvin's separate classroom — we got our thing, but it's just part of the big thing — which is the show's argument that the corner is not outside the city's economy but inside it.

decline_of_journalism.name: The Failure of the Press
decline_of_journalism.desc: The final season's subject: a newsroom thinned by buyouts and run by out-of-town management that asks for more with less and then for a Dickensian aspect, meaning a human angle rather than a reported explanation. Gus Haynes checks a reporter's copy and is moved to the copy desk for it, while Mike Fletcher's weeks with a homeless veteran produce the story management claimed to want and nobody treats as the answer.

the_code.name: The Game and the Code
the_code.desc: The unwritten rules the drug trade claims to run on: who may be robbed, who may be killed, what a soldier owes the organisation that employs him, and that civilians are left alone. The robber Omar Little, giving evidence in court, puts it as an equivalence — he holds up drug dealers with a shotgun, the defence lawyer does the same thing with a briefcase, and both live off the trade. The series measures the code's collapse by who replaces him: a boss who negotiates nothing, and a child who was never taught the rules at all.

race_and_class.name: Race, Class and the Disposable City
race_and_class.desc: The series' account of a majority-black American city in which race and class determine which neighbourhoods are policed, which schools are funded and whose deaths are investigated, told largely through black characters at a time when American television very rarely did so.

limits_of_reform.name: The Limits of Reform
limits_of_reform.desc: What happens to people who try to fix things from inside: a major who suspends the drug war in three blocks, a commander who will not falsify figures, an editor who insists on checking facts. Each reform works and each is destroyed, usually by the institution it was meant to serve.

tragedy_form.name: Tragedy, with Institutions as the Gods
tragedy_form.desc: The show's declared literary shape: Greek tragedy in which the implacable forces overhead are not Olympian deities but police departments, city governments and market economies, and in which characters are destroyed for their virtues as reliably as for their faults.

surveillance.name: Surveillance and the Wiretap
surveillance.desc: The slow, paperwork-bound police work the series is named for. A wiretap is not a decision but a legal process: officers must first show a judge that every ordinary method has failed, then justify each renewal, and the drug organisations adapt continuously — from payphones to pagers with numbers mapped onto a clock face, then to disposable mobiles, and finally to picture messages of a clock face that no wiretap can capture at all. Most of the investigators' time goes on affidavits, logs and waiting.

critical_standing.name: Critical Standing
critical_standing.desc: The Wire's position in critical opinion, which grew steadily after it ended: it is routinely placed at or near the top of lists of the greatest television series ever made, by outlets including Rolling Stone, Entertainment Weekly, the Guardian and the BBC, and is frequently discussed as a novel in televised form.

low_ratings.name: Low Ratings
low_ratings.desc: The Wire never had a large audience. Viewing figures fell rather than grew across its run and dropped further in the fifth season, and HBO renewed it year by year on critical standing rather than commercial performance — a decision a network funded by advertising could not have made, and the reason the series was able to finish on its creators' terms.

dvd_afterlife.name: The Afterlife on Box Set and Streaming
dvd_afterlife.desc: The audience The Wire never had while broadcasting arrived afterwards, through DVD box sets and later streaming. Its serialised structure — episodes that make little sense out of order and refuse to recap — had worked against it on weekly television and worked for it once viewers could watch several hours at a time, which is why its reputation is largely posthumous.

academic_courses.name: University Courses on The Wire
academic_courses.desc: By 2010 The Wire was being taught as course material at Harvard, Duke and Middlebury, in sociology, law and media studies departments — used as a case study in urban poverty and institutional failure rather than as a text about television, which is a rare position for a drama series to occupy.

drug_law_letter.name: The Wire's War on the Drug War
drug_law_letter.desc: An essay published in Time in March 2008, days after the series ended, in which its five principal writers — Simon, Burns, Pelecanos, Price and Lehane — declared that if called for jury duty in a non-violent drug prosecution they would vote to acquit regardless of the evidence. It converts the show's argument from drama into direct political advocacy, urging jurors to refuse to enforce a law they consider unjust.

barack_obama.name: Barack Obama
barack_obama.desc: The forty-fourth President of the United States, who named The Wire one of the greatest pieces of American art of recent decades and Omar Little his favourite character, first as a candidate in 2008 and repeatedly afterwards.

obama_conversation.name: The White House Conversation (2015)
obama_conversation.desc: A recorded discussion at the White House in March 2015 between President Obama and David Simon about the drug war, criminal justice reform and what the series had argued, released publicly by the administration seven years after the show ended.

all_the_pieces_matter.name: All the Pieces Matter (oral history)
all_the_pieces_matter.desc: Jonathan Abrams's 2018 oral history of The Wire, assembled from interviews with the cast, writers and producers, and the fullest first-hand account of how the series was made.

agnieszka_holland.name: Agnieszka Holland
agnieszka_holland.desc: Polish film director and Academy Award nominee, known for Europa Europa and In Darkness, and among the most prominent film-makers The Wire recruited. She directed three episodes between 2004 and 2008, including the hour in which a drug organisation's second in command finally admits to his partner that he had the partner's nephew killed in prison.

timothy_van_patten.name: Timothy Van Patten
timothy_van_patten.desc: Directed three episodes of The Wire, one in each of the first three seasons, including the first-season finale in which the drug case ends in plea bargains and the police unit that built it is broken up. He worked extensively on The Sopranos and Boardwalk Empire in the same years.

clement_virgo.name: Clement Virgo
clement_virgo.desc: Jamaican-Canadian film and television director, known for the features Rude and Brother. He directed two first-season episodes of The Wire: the one giving the detail's best investigator his backstory — thirteen years in a dead-end posting — and the one in which a teenage lookout who asked to leave the drug trade is shot by the two friends he grew up with.

brad_anderson.name: Brad Anderson
brad_anderson.desc: Film and television director whose Wire credits include The Cost, the first-season episode in which an undercover drug purchase — arranged under pressure from commanders before the investigators were ready — collapses, and the detective sitting in the car, Kima Greggs, is shot and badly wounded.

seith_mann.name: Seith Mann
seith_mann.desc: Director who came up through The Wire's own production crew rather than being hired from outside. He directed the fourth-season hour in which a former policeman takes over a middle-school mathematics class and finds he cannot command a room of thirteen-year-olds the way he once cleared a street corner, and a fifth-season episode following a wounded robber through a city where every crew is hunting him.

alex_zakrzewski.name: Alex Zakrzewski
alex_zakrzewski.desc: Directed two episodes, one in the third season and one in the fourth. The first ends an officer's police career with a single shot fired at a colleague in a dark alley; the second, a year later in story time, finds the same man teaching mathematics and recognising his old department's habits in how the school handles its test scores.

uta_briesewitz.name: Uta Briesewitz
uta_briesewitz.desc: German cinematographer who shot The Wire's early seasons and set the visual rule the production kept afterwards: available light, static or slow cameras, and no shot that tells the audience how to feel. The result looks closer to documentary than to television drama, which is precisely the effect Simon wanted.

vincent_peranio.name: Vincent Peranio
vincent_peranio.desc: Vincent Peranio, born 1945 in Baltimore, production designer on The Wire. He built his career designing sets for John Waters and is counted among the Dreamlanders, Waters's regular ensemble of cast and crew; he had already designed Homicide: Life on the Street and The Corner for David Simon before this. His knowledge of the city determined where the series shot and how those places were dressed — the derelict row houses, the low-rise courtyards, the union halls — so that the setting reads as documentary rather than construction.

the_buys.name: The Buys
the_buys.desc: The third episode of season one, teleplay by David Simon. It introduces Omar Little, a robber who holds up drug crews rather than dealing, walking a corner with a shotgun under his coat. It also contains the chess lesson in which a crew chief explains his own organisation to two teenage dealers through the board — the king is never taken, the pawns go first, and nobody in between is ever promoted.

one_arrest.name: One Arrest
one_arrest.desc: The seventh episode of season one, teleplay by Rafael Alvarez. The investigators make their first arrests using what they have heard on the wiretap, which looks like progress and is the opposite: it tells the drug organisation exactly how closely its phones are being listened to, and the line goes quiet.

game_day.name: Game Day
game_day.desc: The ninth episode of season one, teleplay by David H. Melnick and Shamit Choksey. The police investigation stops for a day so that the rival West Baltimore drug organisations can be seen as neighbourhood institutions: they field basketball teams against each other, recruit ringers, and stake serious money on the result. It is also where detectives finally get a look at the man they have spent half a season unable to identify.

the_hunt.name: The Hunt
the_hunt.desc: The eleventh episode of season one, teleplay by Joy Lusco Kecken. A detective has been shot during an undercover drug purchase, and the department's response — city-wide raids, drugs displayed for cameras, every agency in Baltimore on the scene — demonstrates that the only emergency it recognises is one involving its own, and destroys the patient case that caused it.

sentencing.name: Sentencing
sentencing.desc: The thirteenth and final episode of season one, teleplay by David Simon. The case ends in pleas rather than trials: the organisation's leader takes seven years, his nephew twenty, and an enforcer confesses to murders he did not commit so that everyone above him survives. The police unit that built the case is then broken up and its detectives returned to the squads that gave them away.

ebb_tide.name: Ebb Tide
ebb_tide.desc: The season two premiere, teleplay by David Simon, which opens on the water rather than the street corners and moves the series to the Port of Baltimore. It introduces the stevedores' union, its dwindling shifts, and the port police officer whose routine check of a broken container seal turns up thirteen dead women inside.

hard_cases.name: Hard Cases
hard_cases.desc: The fourth episode of season two, teleplay by Joy Lusco Kecken. Thirteen women found dead in a shipping container stop being a statistical problem the police are trying to hand to another agency and acquire names, belongings and a route — the turn coming from a letter in a foreign language found among their clothes.

duck_and_cover.name: Duck and Cover
duck_and_cover.desc: The eighth episode of season two, teleplay by George Pelecanos.
