Detective Jimmy McNulty, exiled to harbour patrol after going over his commanders' heads, hits bottom — a failed reconciliation with his ex-wife and a drunken car crash — while the stevedores' union runs out of ways to fund the lobbying that might bring work back to the docks.

storm_warnings.name: Storm Warnings
storm_warnings.desc: The tenth episode of season two, teleplay by Ed Burns. The two investigations the series has been running in parallel — smuggling through the Port of Baltimore, and a war over West Baltimore's drug corners — turn out to be one case, while the smugglers, already tipped off by a corrupt federal agent, stay a step ahead of everyone listening to them.

all_due_respect.name: All Due Respect
all_due_respect.desc: The second episode of season three, teleplay by Richard Price — his first for the series. A young and unusually ruthless drug crew announces itself in West Baltimore, and after an officer is shot in the face during an undercover drug purchase, the district's commanding major stops running such operations altogether and begins privately considering something no American police commander does: giving up on arrests in part of his district.

homecoming.name: Homecoming
homecoming.desc: The sixth episode of season three, teleplay by Rafael Alvarez. Avon Barksdale is released from prison expecting to reclaim the drug corners he ran, finds a younger and more violent crew holding them, and chooses to fight rather than accept his business partner's argument that the money is now in property. The season's war starts here.

moral_midgetry.name: Moral Midgetry
moral_midgetry.desc: The eighth episode of season three, teleplay by Richard Price. Stringer Bell finally admits to his partner Avon Barksdale that he had Avon's nephew killed in prison — the confession the partnership does not survive. The title comes from a patrolman's verdict on the police major who has quietly stopped arresting drug dealers in three abandoned blocks.

mission_accomplished.name: Mission Accomplished
mission_accomplished.desc: The season three finale, broadcast 19 December 2004. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Ernest Dickerson. The police get three wins in one hour — the arrest-free blocks bulldozed, the drug case closed, the major responsible broken — and the corners are left exactly as they were, which is what the ironic title refers to.

soft_eyes.name: Soft Eyes
soft_eyes.desc: The second episode of season four, teleplay by David Mills. A former police officer, now teaching mathematics at a Baltimore middle school, is told that a classroom is like a crime scene: it shows you nothing unless you look at it with soft eyes — stop trying to control what you see and let the room tell you what is there.

refugees.name: Refugees
refugees.desc: The fourth episode of season four, teleplay by Dennis Lehane. It follows the four thirteen-year-olds the season is built around through their first weeks of the school year, while a heroin addict enrols the teenage boy living with him by falsely claiming to be his uncle — two sets of adults trying to get children into classrooms from opposite ends of the city.

margin_of_error.name: Margin of Error
margin_of_error.desc: The sixth episode of season four, teleplay by Eric Overmyer, directed by Dan Attias. It runs a Baltimore election day almost in real time — polls, church halls, ward workers — and ends on Tommy Carcetti, the white councilman who has just won the mayoralty of a majority-black city by splitting the vote against the incumbent, alone with the size of what he has taken on.

unto_others.name: Unto Others
unto_others.desc: The seventh episode of season four, teleplay by William F. Zorzi. The new mayor-elect starts discovering what he has inherited and what he owes, while Randy Wagstaff — a thirteen-year-old who told a police officer what he knew about a murder — finds that being useful to the police is beginning to be dangerous. In prison, the robber Omar Little stabs an assailant in front of a full landing as notice to the rest.

know_your_place.name: Know Your Place
know_your_place.desc: The ninth episode of season four, teleplay by Kia Corthron, her only script for the series. Each of the four thirteen-year-old boys the season follows is shown the ceiling on what he can become, and a former police officer turned schoolteacher recognises his school's weeks of test drilling as the same trick his old commanders played with crime figures.

misgivings.name: Misgivings
misgivings.desc: The tenth episode of season four, teleplay by Eric Overmyer from a story by Ed Burns and Overmyer. Word that Randy Wagstaff spoke to the police spreads through his school and neighbourhood, and reaches the foster home that is the only stable household he has — the point after which nothing in the season can be undone.

a_new_day.name: A New Day
a_new_day.desc: The eleventh episode of season four, teleplay by Ed Burns. The separate classroom for the school's most disruptive children starts visibly working, and the school system decides that is not a sufficient reason to keep paying for it — because the room's pupils are the ones whose test scores drag the averages down. A new mayor, meanwhile, meets what a predecessor called his first bowl of shit.

not_for_attribution.name: Not for Attribution
not_for_attribution.desc: The third episode of season five, teleplay by Chris Collins, his only script for the series. Marlo Stanfield moves against the older wholesaler whose supply line feeds every crew in Baltimore, having a blind bar owner tortured and killed as bait to draw out the robber who has been raiding him. In the same hour the Sun offers its reporters buy-outs. The title is the journalistic formula for information given on condition the source is not named.

react_quotes.name: React Quotes
react_quotes.desc: The fifth episode of season five, teleplay by David Mills. A detective who has invented a serial killer preying on homeless men — purely to unlock the overtime and wiretap funding his real case has been refused — gives the fictional killer a telephone, and a Baltimore Sun reporter supplies a call he never received. The title is newsroom jargon for the quotes gathered in reaction to someone else's story.

the_dickensian_aspect.name: The Dickensian Aspect
the_dickensian_aspect.desc: The sixth episode of season five, teleplay by Ed Burns. The title is the managing editor's instruction to his newsroom — find the Dickensian aspect, meaning a human angle on the city's poverty — and the episode's point is that this is asked for instead of the reporting that would establish whether any of it is true. Meanwhile a wounded Omar Little moves through a city where every crew is hunting him.

took.name: Took
took.desc: The seventh episode of season five, teleplay by Richard Price. State senator Clay Davis, on trial for stealing from his own campaign funds and from constituents, testifies in his own defence — casting himself as a man who redistributed money to the poor — and talks the jury into acquitting him. In the same hour a detective telephones a reporter posing as his invented serial killer. Dominic West, who plays that detective, directed the episode.

marlyne_barrett.name: Marlyne Barrett
marlyne_barrett.desc: Marlyne Barrett played Nerese Campbell, president of Baltimore's city council: a machine politician who trades her influence with the city's ministers and council members for a promise of the mayoralty, outlasts two mayors, and collects the office when the second leaves for the governorship.

michael_willis.name: Michael Willis
michael_willis.desc: Michael Willis played Andy Krawczyk, a downtown property developer who takes money from anyone — including a drug organisation's second in command, whose investment he pockets while delivering nothing. He is standing on his own half-built development site when that man is shot dead there.

melanie_nicholls_king.name: Melanie Nicholls-King
melanie_nicholls_king.desc: Melanie Nicholls-King played Cheryl, the partner of Detective Kima Greggs and mother of the son they have together by donor insemination. She wants the settled household the two had agreed on; Greggs, after being shot on duty, chooses to go back to street police work instead, and the relationship does not survive that choice.

frederick_strother.name: Frederick Strother
frederick_strother.desc: Frederick Strother played Odell Watkins, a veteran black state legislator whose endorsement decides Baltimore elections. He delivers his constituency for the sitting mayor until the mayor breaks a funding promise and quietly runs a candidate against an ally of his — then sits out the primary and endorses the challenger, which is the swing that decides it.

christopher_mann.name: Christopher Mann
christopher_mann.desc: Christopher Mann played Tony Gray, a black city councilman encouraged to run for mayor by his friend and colleague Tommy Carcetti. The encouragement is a calculation: with two black candidates splitting that vote, a white councilman can win a majority-black city. Gray loses badly and his career ends.

benjamin_busch.name: Benjamin Busch
benjamin_busch.desc: Actor, writer and former Marine Corps infantry officer Benjamin Busch played Officer Anthony Colicchio — the aggressive patrolman who supplies the mocking nickname for his commander's experiment in not arresting drug dealers, and who is eventually written up by his own sergeant for dragging a substitute teacher out of a car. Busch also worked on the production as a second unit director.

brian_anthony_wilson.name: Brian Anthony Wilson
brian_anthony_wilson.desc: Brian Anthony Wilson played Detective Vernon Holley, a Baltimore homicide detective. His significant act comes late: he reluctantly helps a colleague reopen the murder of the robber Omar Little and breaks down the false statement that had framed Omar for an earlier killing — accepting that reversing a case already recorded as solved will damage his own figures.

michael_salconi.name: Michael Salconi
michael_salconi.desc: Michael Salconi played Michael Santangelo, a Baltimore homicide detective, in the first season and again in the fourth. His deputy commissioner offers him a choice — inform on a colleague's movements or lose his place in the squad — and transfers him out to a uniformed post regardless once he has complied.

peter_medak.name: Peter Medak
peter_medak.desc: Directed The Buys, the third episode of the first season, in which the robber Omar Little first walks a drug corner with a shotgun under his coat, and a crew chief teaches two teenage dealers chess by explaining their own organisation through it — the king never taken, the pawns used up first, nobody in between promoted.

slapstick.name: Slapstick
slapstick.desc: The ninth episode of season three, broadcast 21 November 2004. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and George Pelecanos, directed by Alex Zakrzewski. McNulty and Prez answer an officer's call for help, turn up the wrong alley, and Prez shoots a plainclothes detective dead — the mistake that ends his police career and sends him to a classroom.

old_cases.name: Old Cases
old_cases.desc: The fourth episode of season one, broadcast 23 June 2002. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Clement Virgo. It contains Lester Freamon's account of thirteen years and four months filing index cards in the pawn shop unit, and the crime-scene sequence in which McNulty and Bunk reconstruct a shooting using no word but one profanity.

collateral_damage.name: Collateral Damage
collateral_damage.desc: The second episode of season two, broadcast 8 June 2003. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Ed Bianchi. Thirteen women are found dead in a shipping container, and a deputy commissioner calculates aloud that taking the case would drop the share of murders his detectives record as solved from 51.6 to 39.4 per cent — so he spends the episode trying to give the bodies away.

wire_soundtrack.name: ...and all the pieces matter
wire_soundtrack.desc: The five-years-of-music compilation drawn from The Wire, released by Nonesuch in 2008 as the series ended. It collects all five recordings of the title theme alongside music heard on screen and passages of dialogue, and is the only place the whole set of openings sits together.

justin_fenton.name: Justin Fenton
justin_fenton.desc: Baltimore Sun crime reporter who covered the federal prosecution of the Gun Trace Task Force — a city police squad convicted of robbing the people it policed — and turned the reporting into the 2021 book We Own This City, which Simon and Pelecanos then adapted for HBO. He holds the same beat Simon had held a generation earlier.

calvin_ford.name: Calvin Ford
calvin_ford.desc: Boxing trainer at Baltimore's Upton Boxing Center, a former drug-trade figure who turned to coaching young fighters from the same neighbourhoods, and the acknowledged real-life model for Dennis 'Cutty' Wise — the released prisoner who finds he can no longer kill for the organisation and opens a gym instead.

milco_mancevski.name: Milčo Mančevski
milco_mancevski.desc: Macedonian film director, best known for the feature Before the Rain, who directed a single episode of The Wire: the first season's Game Day, which suspends the police investigation for a day to show rival drug organisations fielding basketball teams against each other, with serious money staked on the result.

steve_shill.name: Steve Shill
steve_shill.desc: British television director who made four episodes of The Wire across its first three seasons. They include the aftermath of a detective shot during an undercover drug buy and the department's furious, useless response; the hour in which a police major concludes that arrests change nothing and stops making them; and the prison library killing of the drug boss's nephew, staged to look like a suicide.

leslie_libman.name: Leslie Libman
leslie_libman.desc: Television director whose Wire credit is Homecoming, the third-season episode in which the head of the West Baltimore drug organisation is released from prison to find a younger, more violent crew holding the selling ground he considers his, and chooses to fight for it rather than take his business partner's advice and leave the trade for property development.

thomas_j_wright.name: Thomas J. Wright
thomas_j_wright.desc: Director whose single Wire credit is Backwash, the hour that turns the second season. Two detectives take evidence cloned from a stevedores' union computer to their sergeant, and the union treasurer's son — a young dock worker treated as a joke by everyone on the waterfront — shoots a man dead behind a warehouse counter.

rob_bailey.name: Rob Bailey
rob_bailey.desc: Directed two episodes: Storm Warnings, the second season's most watched hour at nearly three and a half million viewers, and Dead Soldiers, which contains the homicide squad's wake for one of its own — the body laid out in dress blues on the bar's pool table while the detectives drink around it.

elodie_keene.name: Elodie Keene
elodie_keene.desc: Directed Hard Cases, the second-season episode in which thirteen women found dead in a shipping container stop being a statistical problem for the police and acquire names, effects and a route — the turn coming from a letter in a foreign language found among their clothes.

christine_moore.name: Christine Moore
christine_moore.desc: Directed two episodes of The Wire. Soft Eyes takes its title from advice given to a former police officer starting work as a schoolteacher — look at the room the way you would look at a crime scene, and it will show you what is in it. Reformation, two seasons earlier, brings a New York enforcer back to Baltimore hunting the man who shot him.

jim_mckay.name: Jim McKay
jim_mckay.desc: Independent film-maker, director of the feature Girls Town, whose Wire credit is Refugees — the fourth-season episode that follows four thirteen-year-old boys into the school year that will sort each of them toward a different future, and one of the very few hours of the series with almost no police work in it.

the_detail.name: The Detail
the_detail.desc: The second episode of season one, broadcast 9 June 2002. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns, directed by Clark Johnson. The special police unit is assembled from the officers each squad most wants to lose, and in the same hour the one witness who testified truthfully against the drug organisation is shot dead in the street.

lessons.name: Lessons
lessons.desc: The eighth episode of season one, broadcast 28 July 2002. Teleplay by David Simon from a story by Simon and Ed Burns. The investigators seize a courier carrying a state senator's campaign cash and are ordered to hand it straight back — the case's first collision with money it will not be permitted to touch — and the robber Omar Little delivers the series' most quoted line, that a man who comes at the king had best not miss.

hot_shots.name: Hot Shots
hot_shots.desc: The third episode of season two, broadcast 15 June 2003. Teleplay by David Simon, directed by Elodie Keene. Detectives travel to Philadelphia to interview a ship's crew — the unglamorous canvassing that putting names to thirteen bodies actually requires — while the union treasurer's son and nephew begin stealing containers on their own account. The title is police slang for narcotics deliberately poisoned to kill an informant.

undertow.name: Undertow
undertow.desc: The fifth episode of season two, broadcast 29 June 2003. Ziggy Sobotka loses his prized Camaro to drug dealers who will not accept his explanations, one of the humiliations that accumulate until he shoots George Glekas.

stray_rounds.name: Stray Rounds
stray_rounds.desc: The ninth episode of season two, broadcast 3 August 2003. Teleplay by David Simon, directed by Tim Van Patten. A firefight over Bodie Broadus's failing corner kills a child indoors with a stray round; Ziggy and Johnny Fifty run a caper that costs the Greeks real money; McNulty goes undercover in a brothel; and Agent Koutris, working for the Greek, seals Glekas's file and tips the organisation off.

back_burners.name: Back Burners
back_burners.desc: The seventh episode of season three, broadcast 7 November 2004. Teleplay by Joy Lusco from a story by David Simon and Lusco, directed by Tim Van Patten. Avon Barksdale tours the West Baltimore corners he is fighting for and finds them under police pressure and barely worth holding, while his younger rival has quietly stopped holding corners at all and become a wholesaler. The epigraph is a bar owner's: conscience do cost.

reformation.name: Reformation
reformation.desc: The tenth episode of season three, broadcast 28 November 2004. Teleplay by Ed Burns from a story by David Simon and Burns, directed by Christine Moore. Two teenage dealers find a body they were not meant to find, and a New York enforcer — shot a year earlier on a lie told by the man who hired him — returns to Baltimore and forces a member of the robber's crew to give up his location.

alliances.name: Alliances
alliances.desc: The fifth episode of season four, broadcast 8 October 2006. Teleplay by Ed Burns from a story by David Simon and Burns, directed by David Platt. It is the last episode to show all six neighbourhood boys — the four the season follows, plus two others — together as a single group, and the one in which a heroin addict finds the teenager living with him working a drug corner instead of attending school, and is beaten in the street for interrupting the sale.

gloria_muzio.name: Gloria Muzio
gloria_muzio.desc: Stage director whose single Wire credit is Lessons, the first season's hour about political money: the investigators seize a courier carrying a state senator's campaign cash and are ordered to hand it straight back — the case's first collision with money the department will not let them touch.

david_platt.name: David Platt
david_platt.desc: Director whose Wire credit is Alliances, the fourth-season episode in which Bubbles — a heroin addict who informs for the police — finds the teenage boy living with him working a drug corner instead of attending school, and is beaten in front of bystanders by the boy's customer for interrupting the sale.

scott_kecken.name: Scott Kecken
scott_kecken.desc: Documentary film-maker who directed Not for Attribution with his wife Joy Lusco Kecken; the pair made We Are Arabbers, a film about Baltimore's horse-drawn produce vendors, before either worked on the series.

kate_sanford.name: Kate Sanford
kate_sanford.desc: Film and television editor who cut episodes of The Wire across all five seasons — the only editor to work on every year of it — and won the American Cinema Editors award for the fourth-season premiere, Boys of Summer. She went on to edit two more David Simon series, Treme and Show Me a Hero, winning a second Eddie for Treme, and later worked on Boardwalk Empire and The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel.

geraldine_peroni.name: Geraldine Peroni
geraldine_peroni.desc: Film editor, 1953 to 2004, best known as Robert Altman's closest collaborator — she cut eight of his features and was nominated for the Academy Award for editing The Player. She edited episodes of The Wire's first two seasons and died during the run of the series, aged 51, while working on Brokeback Mountain; the third-season episode Back Burners is dedicated to her memory.

thom_zimny.name: Thom Zimny
thom_zimny.desc: Editor on The Wire's first three seasons, who had already won an Emmy in 2001 for cutting a Bruce Springsteen concert film. He became Springsteen's regular film-maker, directing the documentaries Wings for Wheels and The Promise about the making of Born to Run and Darkness on the Edge of Town.

eagle_egilsson.name: Eagle Egilsson
eagle_egilsson.desc: Icelandic cinematographer, born 1966 in Reykjavík, who shot seven episodes of The Wire's third season. He has been nominated four times by the American Society of Cinematographers, and since 2011 has worked mainly as a television director, on Nikita, Fringe and Gotham.

russell_lee_fine.name: Russell Lee Fine
russell_lee_fine.desc: Director of photography on eighteen episodes of The Wire between 2006 and 2008 — more than any other cinematographer on the series — meaning he shot most of the school season and effectively all of the final one, sustaining the available-light, static-camera look Uta Briesewitz had established at the start.

hd_remaster.name: HD remaster controversy
hd_remaster.desc: The Wire was broadcast in the 4:3 shape of a pre-widescreen television set. When HBO rescanned all sixty episodes from more than 8,000 reels of 35mm negative for high definition in 2014, it recomposed them to 16:9 — cropping the top and bottom of every frame. Viewers argued this overrode the framing its directors and cinematographers had chosen; HBO's answer was that the series had been shot 16:9 from the start as future-proofing, with only the later seasons composed for 4:3.

links.details: The first season sets the terms: a wiretap case against a drug organisation, run by a detail assembled from the officers each unit wanted rid of, against commanders who want it closed.
The second season moves to the port and the disappearance of industrial work, arguing that the drug trade is what fills the space left when a city stops making things.
The third season puts reform on trial twice over — a district commander's tolerated zones and a drug lord's attempt to go legitimate — and destroys both.
The fourth season follows four thirteen-year-olds through a school year, and is the season most often named as the show's peak.

The fifth season adds the newspaper, setting a detective's invented serial killer against a reporter's invented quotes, and closes the series by replacing each figure with a younger version of himself.
The three prequel vignettes are supplementary pieces of The Wire, filmed during the fifth season's production and set years before the series begins.

The Target establishes the pattern the whole of season one follows: a murder nobody wants investigated, a detective who goes outside the chain of command, and a detail assembled as a punishment rather than a resource.
The Pager is where the two sides begin adapting to each other: the drug crew stop using phones the police can listen to, and the investigators have to find someone able to read what replaces them.

The episode sharing the series title is where the wiretap finally goes live, six hours into a season spent showing what listening to a phone legally actually requires: surveillance logs, a judge's signature, and evidence that the target cannot be reached any other way.
The Cost is season one's turning point, in which the detail's push for a quick result gets an undercover officer shot and converts a patient case into a departmental emergency.
Cleaning Up is season one's penultimate hour and its moral centre, the organisation tidying away the one person who could not carry what he had seen.
All Prologue gives season two its thesis in a prison book club discussion of Gatsby, and then kills the man making the argument that a person can put his past behind him.
Backwash is where season two's comedy of humiliation turns: Ziggy Sobotka's attempts at respect end in a warehouse with a gun, and the season's outcome becomes fixed.
Bad Dreams is the second season's penultimate hour, the point at which Frank Sobotka's choice between the union and the Greeks is finally taken out of his hands.
Port in a Storm closes season two with the case made and useless: the enforcers arrested, the organisation intact, and the man who ran it walking through an airport unidentified.

The season opens on the demolition of the Franklin Terrace high-rises, the public housing towers that were the Barksdale organisation's most profitable selling ground. Staged by the mayor as urban renewal, it destroys the ground the organisation stood on and scatters its trade into streets the police have never mapped.
Dead Soldiers gives season three its wake for Ray Cole, the sequence in which the homicide unit buries one of its own and the production buried Robert Colesberry.

This is the episode in which the third season's experiment gets its name: dealers christen the three blocks where police have stopped making arrests after an officer sneers that it is like Amsterdam. The trade concentrates there, the surrounding neighbourhoods empty of dealing, and the district's crime figures start to fall.

The episode runs the season's two returns in parallel: a drug boss released from prison expecting his territory back, and a police district quietly withdrawing from the streets it has policed for decades — one man reclaiming ground as another gives it up.
Middle Ground is season three's penultimate hour and the series' most complete piece of tragic construction, two men spending a last night on a rooftop after each has already destroyed the other.
Boys of Summer resets the series for season four around four eighth-graders in their last free weeks, and introduces the vacant houses without explaining what they are for.
Home Rooms starts season four's school year and establishes its central discovery, that a classroom cannot be commanded the way a corner can.
Corner Boys is season four's pivot, the separate classroom finally asking the boys how the corner works and getting an answer more sophisticated than anything the curriculum contains.

That's Got His Own is the fourth season's penultimate hour, in which the consequences the year has been assembling all arrive at once: a foster home burns, a boy is taken into police custody, and the school hands on a pupil it knows the next institution will not help.
Final Grades closes season four by opening the vacant houses, killing the last Barksdale soldier standing, and delivering three of the four boys to the institutions that will not hold them.
More with Less sets season five's terms in its title, an instruction issued to a police department and a newspaper simultaneously, and follows what each does to comply.
Unconfirmed Reports is where season five's two fabrications begin, a newsroom short of reporters and a detective short of resources each arriving at the same solution.
Transitions clears season five's board in a single hour, removing a police commissioner, a kingpin and a newsroom veteran and replacing each without difficulty.
Clarifications kills season five's most mythologised character in a corner shop without ceremony, and then has the morgue attach the wrong name to his body.
Late Editions is season five's penultimate hour, in which the illegal wiretap finally produces the Stanfield arrests and Snoop is shot by the boy she helped recruit.
-30- closes the series by installing a successor in every vacated role, which is the show's final and least consoling argument about what actually persists.

David Simon created The Wire, a five-season HBO drama broadcast between 2002 and 2008 about the drug trade, police work, politics, schools and journalism in Baltimore, and ran it as showrunner, executive producer and head writer throughout. The on-screen created-by card names him alone, though the show's shape came equally from his collaborator Ed Burns, a former detective and teacher.

Ed Burns supplied the wiretap casework and the classroom experience the series was built from and shares story credit on the pilot and many later episodes. He is routinely described as co-creator, though the on-screen created-by credit belongs to David Simon alone.

Simon spent over a decade as a crime reporter at the Baltimore Sun; Burns spent twenty years as a Baltimore police detective and then taught in a city middle school. They met while Simon was covering one of Burns's drug investigations, and the pairing of a reporter's method with an insider's knowledge underlies everything they have made together — the book and series The Corner, The Wire, Generation Kill and The Plot Against America.
HBO commissioned The Wire and broadcast all sixty episodes between June 2002 and March 2008, renewing it season by season despite ratings that fell rather than grew.

Blown Deadline made The Wire for HBO across all five seasons, running the production out of Baltimore itself rather than a studio, which is why so much of the crew and so many of the minor performers were local.

Beyond creating it, Simon ran the series day to day: he hired the writers, broke the story for every season, wrote or co-wrote the majority of episodes, and defended a show that never found a large audience through five annual renewals HBO could reasonably have declined.
Nina Kostroff Noble produced all five seasons of The Wire, handling the Baltimore production alongside David Simon.
Robert F. Colesberry was executive producer of The Wire from the pilot until his death in February 2004, and the crew's principal authority on how the show should look and move.
Karen L. Thorson joined as co-producer in 2001 while the pilot was being prepared and produced all five seasons of The Wire.
Alexa L. Fogel cast The Wire, assembling a company that mixed established stage and screen actors with Baltimore locals, former offenders and people with no acting background at all.
Blake Leyh was music supervisor on The Wire, working with David Simon on the choice of title theme and enforcing the rule that music be heard only where a character could actually be hearing it.
Producers Robert F. Colesberry and Karen L. Thorson were married from 1992 until his death in 2004; he was The Wire's executive producer and she produced all five seasons.
David Simon and Nina Kostroff Noble are the producing partners behind Blown Deadline Productions and have made every Simon series together since The Corner.

The series is set and was filmed entirely in Baltimore, a port city on the American east coast that lost most of its manufacturing and shipping work in the second half of the twentieth century. Simon's stated subject is the city itself rather than any character in it — each season examines a different institution within it, and the same streets recur across all five.
The three prequel vignettes were made under David Simon's production during the fifth season and released through HBO On Demand.
HBO distributed the three prequel vignettes through its On Demand service while the final season was broadcasting, and later included them with the complete series box set.

Simon's teleplay for the opening episode establishes the whole series: a witness recants in open court, a detective complains privately to a judge that the murders are not being investigated, and the judge's phone call forces the police to assemble the special unit the next five years follow.
Ed Burns wrote the teleplay of The Pager, turning his own experience of drug crews defeating surveillance into the episode's spine.

Simon gave the series its own title in this episode, the point at which the investigators finally get a wiretap running on the drug organisation's phones — six hours into a season spent showing how much paperwork, surveillance and judicial permission that single step requires.
Pelecanos's first script for the series established the pattern Simon kept for five seasons: give him the penultimate hour, because that is where the season's cost is paid.

Alvarez, who had worked around the port and written for the Sun, drew the episode's stevedore detail from the docks themselves — the union computer, the checkers' routines, the paperwork a container can vanish through.
Pelecanos's teleplay gives Frank Sobotka a last working day of grievances and paperwork, and ends it with a walk toward men he has known for twenty years.
David Simon wrote the teleplay of Port in a Storm, closing out the port investigation and the Sobotka family with it.
Simon wrote the season three premiere's teleplay, whose opening image — a controlled demolition staged as civic renewal, with a mayor at the podium — sets the season's terms before a word of plot.
Dennis Lehane wrote the teleplay of Dead Soldiers, his first script for the series, containing the homicide unit's wake for Detective Ray Cole.

Burns's teleplay is the one that makes the experiment operational: uniformed officers are ordered to escort dealers into three derelict blocks where no arrests will be made, and a major discovers his own men will carry out an instruction he cannot put in writing.
George Pelecanos wrote the teleplay of Middle Ground, the script that killed Stringer Bell and drew the show's first Emmy nomination.
David Simon wrote the teleplay of Boys of Summer, introducing the four boys in the last weeks before school starts.
Price wrote Home Rooms, his first script of the school season, in which the department's manoeuvring over a murdered witness runs alongside a teacher losing control of a room.
Price's Corner Boys teleplay gives Namond Brice the charge of hypocrisy — that the city does what the corner does and calls only one of them animal.
Pelecanos's teleplay takes each of the four boys past the point at which the school could still have caught him, and hands the finale a set of outcomes rather than a crisis.

Simon's teleplay closes the school year with the season's quietest scene: a teacher watching a third of his class manage the standardised test adequately, having spent weeks drilling them for it instead of teaching, and being pleased.
Simon's teleplay for the final season premiere is the one that hands the newsroom its instruction and the police department the same one, in the same hour, from different mouths.

Zorzi's teleplay gives a detective his first act of outright fabrication — rearranging a dead man's body to suggest a killer who does not exist — and plays it as a small technical problem being solved rather than as a moral crossing.
Burns's Transitions teleplay is built on succession: an office vacated, a supply line taken over, and a man called back from retirement by a killing meant to reach him.
Lehane's Clarifications teleplay is the last of his three, and gives the series' most quoted figure an ending in a shop with a packet of cigarettes and nobody watching.
George Pelecanos wrote the teleplay of Late Editions, the last of his penultimate-episode scripts, in which Snoop is killed and Marlo is arrested.
David Simon wrote the teleplay of -30-, closing the series with the montage that installs a successor in every vacated role.

Simon's contribution to the pilot's story is a reporter's instinct for the telling detail: the frightened witness who changes his testimony, and the opening scene in which a man who robbed a street dice game every week was allowed to keep playing, because — as the witness explains over his body — this is America.
Burns supplied the institutional half of the pilot — what a commander does when a judge telephones him, and how a unit gets built out of the officers nobody wants.

Simon and Burns built this episode around code-breaking: the drug crew communicate by pager using numbers mapped onto a clock face, and the man who cracks it is the one officer his colleagues consider too incompetent to be trusted with street work.
The Pager turns on breaking the Barksdale code, and the clock-and-pager arithmetic in it is the craft Burns had used building real wiretap cases against Melvin Williams.

Simon broke the title episode with Burns around a single legal threshold — the moment a judge signs a wiretap order — after which everything the investigators have gathered becomes usable in court, and before which none of it is.
Burns broke the title episode with Simon; the affidavit granted at its end is the document he had spent twenty years learning how to write.

Simon and Burns broke the second season finale around what survives Frank Sobotka: the Greeks walk, Nick goes into protection, and the case closes with the men who moved the containers rather than the men who filled them.
Burns's half of the second season finale is procedural: what a port case can actually charge when the organisation above it has been warned and gone.

Simon broke Time After Time with Burns, introducing in one hour Cutty Wise finishing a fourteen-year sentence, Slim Charles as Stringer's new enforcer, and Marlo Stanfield holding ground nobody has yet contested.
Burns co-broke Time After Time; the season's argument, that scattering a trade does not reduce it, is the lesson he had watched the department relearn every few years.

Simon's half of the finale is what happens to each institution's paperwork: a school year signed off with its test averages intact, a police case closed on a man already dead, and a mayor briefed on figures nobody in the room believes.

Burns broke the finale around the arithmetic of the vacant houses: every body recovered becomes a fresh unsolved murder, so the detectives who solved the puzzle are punished by the only measure the department keeps.

Simon and Burns broke -30- as a set of replacements rather than resolutions: Templeton takes a Pulitzer, Valchek takes the commissioner's office, Michael takes Omar's shotgun, and Dukie takes Bubbles's needle.

Burns broke -30- with Simon around the arithmetic of replacement — Valchek for Daniels, Michael for Omar, Dukie for Bubbles, Fletcher for Haynes — so that the finale resolves nothing and staffs everything.

Simon's half of the Middle Ground story is the political machinery around the killing: Colvin's zones already condemned, Avon's stash handed to the police by his own partner, and Stringer walking into a meeting he has been set up for.

Pelecanos took the teleplay as well as a share of the story, and the rooftop scene between Avon Barksdale and Stringer Bell — two men spending a last night together, each having already sold the other — is the writing the Emmy nomination was for.
Simon broke Clarifications with Lehane, the two having settled on an unceremonious death for the character the audience most expected to be given one.
Lehane shares the story with Simon; his part is the corner-shop geography — a counter, a display of cigarettes, a child small enough to go unregarded — which is what makes the ending land as it does.
Clark Johnson shot the pilot with no expressive lighting and no camera move a documentary crew could not have managed, a grammar the production then held to for six years and eight further directors.

Clark Johnson directed The Pager, in which the Barksdale crew starts defeating the surveillance aimed at it; the episode drew close to three million viewers, among the higher figures the series ever managed.
Bianchi directed the episode that shares the series' title, shooting the wiretap room itself as the drama — headphones, logbooks, and detectives waiting for a phone that mostly does not ring.

Colesberry had shaped the series' visual method since the pilot as its executive producer — the available light, the static camera, the refusal to tell an audience how to feel — and directed only once, on the second season finale. He died six months after it aired, aged 57, from complications of cardiac surgery, and the third season's closing dedication is to him.
Ed Bianchi directed Time After Time, staging the Franklin Terrace demolition and the crowd watching it — the shot the third season is remembered by.
Dan Attias directed Straight and True, covering both Avon Barksdale's release party and the police operation to push the trade into Bunny Colvin's designated blocks.
Joe Chappelle directed Middle Ground, staging both the rooftop conversation between the Barksdale principals and the ambush that ends the episode.
Ernest Dickerson directed Final Grades, at 78 minutes the longest fourth-season episode, cutting between the opening of the vacant houses and four boys arriving at four different endings.
Anthony Hemingway directed Clarifications, staging the shop killing so plainly that its suddenness is the whole point — no music, no build, a child and a counter.
Clark Johnson directed -30-, having also directed the pilot; by then he was playing the Sun city editor on screen as well.
Final Grades carries an on-screen dedication to Robert F. Colesberry, the executive producer who had died two years before it aired.
-30- closes with a dedication to Robert F. Colesberry, four years after his death and at the end of the series he had helped shape.
Dead Soldiers writes out Detective Ray Cole, the character Robert F. Colesberry played, and gives him a wake in the homicide unit; it is the production's on-screen farewell to Colesberry himself.

Pelecanos wrote seven episodes across all five seasons and produced the third. Simon habitually gave him the penultimate hour of a season — the position where the year's major death occurs — including the killings of a teenage lookout, a union official, a drug organisation's second in command and a young enforcer.

Price, a novelist whose book Clockers covers similar ground — a drug crew and the detectives working it — wrote five episodes between the third and fifth seasons. Reviewers had spent two years comparing The Wire to Clockers before Simon and Pelecanos approached him at a reading and recruited him.

Lehane's three scripts are spread one per season from the third on — Dead Soldiers, Refugees and Clarifications — and between them they contain the homicide unit's wake for Ray Cole and the corner-shop killing of Omar Little, so the novelist brought in for plot got handed two of the series' most elegiac hours.
Rafael Alvarez wrote three episodes of The Wire across its first three seasons and brought first-hand knowledge of the Baltimore waterfront to the second.

Zorzi covered Maryland state politics for the Baltimore Sun before joining the writing staff in the third season. He wrote two episodes and supplied the reporting behind the show's City Hall material, and appears on screen in the final season as a Sun reporter under his own name.
Joy Lusco Kecken wrote three episodes across the first three seasons, among them The Hunt, which handles the department's total mobilisation after an officer is shot.

Mills wrote two episodes, in the fourth and fifth seasons. He and Simon had been student journalists together and had written for Homicide: Life on the Street more than a decade earlier; Mills died of a brain aneurysm in New Orleans on 30 March 2010, aged 48, while the first season of Simon's next series was filming — twelve days before it went to air.
Eric Overmyer joined The Wire for its fourth season as writer and producer before co-creating Treme with David Simon.
Kia Corthron, a playwright by trade, wrote Know Your Place — the episode in which Prez recognises the school's test drilling as the same instrument as a clearance rate.

Chris Collins joined The Wire in 2004 as script coordinator, became a staff writer for the fourth season and story editor for the fifth, where he took his one teleplay credit — the clearest case of the show promoting a writer from inside rather than recruiting a novelist from outside. He went on to write and executive-produce Sons of Anarchy, and to work on The Sopranos and The Man in the High Castle.

David H. Melnick and Shamit Choksey are credited on one episode of The Wire and on nothing else in television — a single contribution to a series whose writers' room was otherwise built from novelists, journalists and a former detective.
George Pelecanos served as a producer on The Wire's third season as well as writing for it.

Burns took a producer credit from the fourth season, the year drawn most directly from his own life: after twenty years as a police detective he taught seventh grade in a Baltimore middle school, and that season follows four thirteen-year-old boys through a school year that decides what each of them becomes.

Pelecanos is a Washington crime novelist whom Simon recruited to The Wire's writing staff after reading his books. He became the writer Simon trusted with the penultimate episode of every season — the hour where each year's central death falls — and the two later co-created two further HBO series, The Deuce and We Own This City.
David Simon and David Mills met as student journalists, wrote together on Homicide, shared an Emmy for The Corner, and were working together again on Treme when Mills died in 2010.
George Pelecanos, with David Simon, recruited Richard Price to The Wire, and the two novelists later wrote together again on The Deuce.

Dennis Lehane and George Pelecanos were two of the three crime novelists on The Wire's staff and, with Richard Price, David Simon and Ed Burns, co-signed a 2008 letter in Time declaring they would refuse to convict in a drug case if called for jury duty.
Dennis Lehane and Richard Price were both recruited to The Wire as established crime novelists and both signed the writers' 2008 protest letter against American drug laws.
David Simon wrote Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets after taking leave from the Baltimore Sun to spend a year with the city's homicide detectives; it was published in 1991.
Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets is a first-hand account of one year inside the Baltimore Police homicide unit.
The Mystery Writers of America gave Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets the 1992 Edgar Award for Best Fact Crime.
David Simon's book Homicide was developed by Paul Attanasio into the NBC drama Homicide: Life on the Street, which ran from 1993 to 1999.

After leaving the Baltimore Sun, Simon joined Homicide: Life on the Street, the NBC police drama adapted from his own book about a year spent observing Baltimore's homicide detectives. It was his first sustained television work, and where he learned the craft he later used to run a series himself.

Mills and Simon had been student journalists together before either wrote for television; Mills came to Homicide from the Washington Post and went on to Emmy-nominated work on NYPD Blue and to ER, which is why Simon could hand him half of The Corner years later.
Eric Overmyer wrote and produced on Homicide: Life on the Street, one of several Simon collaborators who came out of that NBC series.
Clark Johnson starred as Detective Meldrick Lewis on Homicide: Life on the Street before directing the pilot and finale of The Wire.
Homicide: Life on the Street was set and largely shot in Baltimore, establishing the city as viable ground for a continuing drama.
Homicide: Life on the Street taught David Simon how television is made and carried many of the same real Baltimore cases and detectives that would later resurface, reshaped, in The Wire.
David Simon co-wrote The Corner with Ed Burns, the pair spending a year on and around a West Baltimore drug corner; it was published in 1997.
Ed Burns co-wrote The Corner with David Simon, his first book and the beginning of their writing partnership.
The Corner is reported entirely at the junction of West Fayette and North Monroe Streets in West Baltimore.
The 1997 book by David Simon and Ed Burns was adapted into HBO's six-part miniseries The Corner in 2000.
Fran Boyd is one of the real people whose year David Simon and Ed Burns chronicled in The Corner, and the figure at the centre of the book's account of getting clean.
David Simon co-wrote all six parts of The Corner with David Mills, adapting the book he had written with Ed Burns.
David Mills was an executive producer as well as co-writer on The Corner, and shared in its Emmy for Outstanding Miniseries in that capacity.
Charles S. Dutton directed all six parts of The Corner, having initially wanted nothing to do with the project, and won an Emmy for it.
Robert F. Colesberry was an executive producer on The Corner, his first project with David Simon and the start of the team that made The Wire.
Nina Kostroff Noble produced The Corner, her first project with David Simon and the one that established the Baltimore-based production model she has run for him ever since.
David Mills took an executive producer credit on The Corner alongside Robert Colesberry and David Simon, and shared in the 2000 Emmy for Outstanding Miniseries in that capacity.
The Corner was Blown Deadline's first television production, shot in West Baltimore with a largely local cast and crew, and the template for how every Simon series has been made since.
HBO broadcast The Corner over six weeks in spring 2000; its success gave David Simon the standing to pitch The Wire to the same network.

The miniseries was filmed in the neighbourhood the book reports on, using the real names of the people whose year it dramatises — a choice that made the production answerable to the residents while it was shooting there.

The Corner was a six-part HBO miniseries Simon and Burns made in 2000 from their book about a year in the life of a drug-ridden West Baltimore street corner, using the real names of the people involved. It proved to HBO that Baltimore material could sustain a series, and much of its cast moved directly to The Wire — several of them into roles opposite the ones they had just played.
The Corner took three Emmys from four nominations in 2000, a result that gave David Simon the standing at HBO to pitch a five-season series about the same city.
David Simon shared The Corner's 2000 Emmy for Outstanding Writing for a Miniseries or Movie with David Mills.
David Mills shared The Corner's 2000 writing Emmy with David Simon, and shared in its Outstanding Miniseries win as an executive producer.
Charles S. Dutton won the 2000 Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Miniseries, Movie or Special for The Corner.
Rafael Alvarez compiled The Wire: Truth Be Told, the series companion volume, gathering essays from the show's writers and the real cases behind particular scenes.
The Wire: Truth Be Told is the official companion to the series, documenting all sixty episodes and the reporting underneath them.

Simon contributed essays to The Wire: Truth Be Told, the official companion book compiled by Rafael Alvarez, one of the show's own writers — a volume of episode notes, cast interviews and staff essays published while the series was still running.
Zorzi's contribution to the companion volume covers the political reporting behind the show's City Hall, the beat he had worked at the Sun before writing for it.
David Simon covered crime for the Baltimore Sun from 1983, leaving in the mid-1990s for television; the paper's decline later became the material of the show's last season.
William F. Zorzi was a political reporter at the Baltimore Sun alongside David Simon before joining The Wire.
Rafael Alvarez was a Baltimore Sun colleague of David Simon before joining The Wire's writing staff.
Ed Burns served some twenty years in the Baltimore Police Department, in homicide and then on long-term narcotics wiretap cases, before leaving to teach.
Jay Landsman was a sergeant in the Baltimore Police homicide unit that David Simon spent a year observing.
Edward T. Norris was commissioner of the Baltimore Police Department from 2000 to 2002, shortly before The Wire began filming in the city.
The Baltimore Police Department is the city agency at the centre of The Wire's account of how Baltimore's institutions actually work.
The Baltimore Sun is the city's daily paper and, in the fifth season, the last of the Baltimore institutions the series examines.
The Gun Trace Task Force was a plainclothes squad of the Baltimore Police Department, and its exposure as a robbery crew is the department scandal that followed The Wire into reality.
The Baltimore Sun employed David Simon on the crime beat, the job that produced both of his books and, indirectly, everything that followed from them.
The Baltimore Police Department employed Ed Burns for around two decades, and its resistance to the long cases he wanted to build is the frustration The Wire dramatises.
Detective Ed Burns built the long wiretap case that led to Melvin Williams's arrest in the mid-1980s; years later the two met again as friends when Williams was cast on The Wire.
David Simon covered Melvin Williams for the Baltimore Sun and, after Williams's conviction, wrote a five-part series on the anatomy of his drug empire.
Melvin Williams's West Baltimore heroin operation, and the patient wiretap investigation that dismantled it, are the acknowledged model for the Barksdale case that drives the first season.
Melvin Williams, a former kingpin turned ordained minister, played the Deacon on The Wire, a community elder steering ex-offenders toward second chances.
Donnie Andrews turned himself in for murder to Detective Ed Burns; years later Burns and David Simon campaigned for his parole, and Andrews then consulted on The Wire.

Donnie Andrews, a Baltimore stick-up man who robbed only dealers, was the primary real-world source for Omar Little; David Simon has named Shorty Boyd, Ferdinand Harvin and Anthony Hollie as further models, and particular scenes, including dealers dropping a stash out of a window rather than face him, came straight from Andrews's own life.
Donnie Andrews appeared in The Wire's fifth season as a character named Donnie, an associate of Omar Little's, having spent years advising the writers.
Donnie Andrews and Fran Boyd were introduced while he was in prison and she was coming off heroin; they married in 2007, with David Simon as best man.
Fran Boyd, the central figure of The Corner, worked on The Wire as a loop group supervisor and was among the crew named on the show's sound editing nomination.
Sergeant Jay Landsman is among the most prominent real detectives in David Simon's Homicide, and his voice carried from the book into the fictional sergeant of the same name on The Wire.
The real Jay Landsman appeared on The Wire not as himself but as Lieutenant Dennis Mello, while an actor played the sergeant who bears his name.
Former commissioner Edward T. Norris played a Baltimore homicide detective under his own name across the run of The Wire.
Ed Burns's years teaching in a Baltimore middle school after leaving the police are the direct source of the fourth season's classroom material.
David Simon's years at the Baltimore Sun, and his disillusionment with its management and prize-chasing, supply the newsroom of the fifth season.
The Baltimore Sun's buyouts and shrinking staff are the model for the fictional Sun of season five, where fewer reporters are told to produce more.

Zorzi appears on screen in the fifth season as a Baltimore Sun reporter called William Zorzi, sitting in a fictionalised version of the newsroom he had actually worked in, writing about a city he had actually covered.
Tom Waits recorded the original of his own song for the 1987 album Franks Wild Years, and that recording — the gravel-voiced version, not a cover — is the one used to open the second season.
Way Down in the Hole was The Wire's title theme across all five seasons, a different recording each time; David Simon chose it for what he called its sense of ubiquitous drudgery.

Blake Leyh wrote The Fall as the fixed element in a title sequence that changed every year: the opening song was re-recorded by a different artist each season, and his closing instrumental was the one piece of music that never moved.
The Fall closed all sixty episodes, so that a series which changed its title song every season and its subject every year ended each hour on exactly the same piece of music.
The Blind Boys of Alabama's gospel recording opened all thirteen episodes of season one, and their full version plays out the closing moments of the series.

Season two is the only year that uses Waits's own recording rather than a cover, and it is the season set among longshoremen — the version with the least gospel in it laid over the least redeemable of the five stories.

The Neville Brothers' looser, brass-inflected recording of the title song opened season three — the year that begins with the demolition of the high-rise public housing blocks where most of the drug trade had been conducted, scattering it into streets the police have never mapped.

DoMaJe — Ivan Ashford, Markel Steele, Cameron Brown, Tariq Al-Sabir and Avery Bargasse — recorded the only arrangement commissioned rather than licensed, five Baltimore teenagers singing over a season about four Baltimore thirteen-year-olds.
Steve Earle's version opened the fifth and final season, in which he also appeared on screen as the recovery sponsor Walon.

The Blind Boys of Alabama, formed in 1939 by schoolchildren in Talladega, Alabama, and originally called the Happy Land Jubilee Singers, gave the song its gospel reading for season one — and it returns to close the series.
Tom Waits's own recording of the song, from Franks Wild Years, is the version used to open season two — the only year of the five to use the original rather than a cover.
The Neville Brothers brought New Orleans brass to the song for season three, the year that opens on the Franklin Terrace towers coming down.
DoMaJe's version was recorded specially for the series by five Baltimore teenagers, the only arrangement of the theme commissioned rather than licensed.
Steve Earle recorded the final season's version, the only one of the five performers who also appears on screen — as Walon, the recovery sponsor who keeps turning up for Bubbles.
Steve Earle played Walon, a recovering addict who sponsors Bubbles through Narcotics Anonymous, as well as recording the fifth season theme.
As music supervisor, Blake Leyh worked with David Simon on selecting Way Down in the Hole and on commissioning a fresh recording of it for each season.
The Wire received a Peabody Award in 2004, one of the few institutional honours it collected while on air; Robert F. Colesberry was recognised posthumously among its producers.
Middle Ground was nominated for Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series in 2005 and lost to House — the first of only two Emmy nominations the series ever received, both for writing.
George Pelecanos was nominated for the 2005 writing Emmy for Middle Ground, on which he had the teleplay and shared story credit.
David Simon shared the 2005 writing Emmy nomination for Middle Ground with George Pelecanos on their joint story credit.
-30- was nominated in the same category in 2008 and lost to Mad Men, leaving the series nought for two, with no acting, directing or outstanding-series nomination in five years.

Simon's second and last Emmy nomination, for -30-, lost to Mad Men; the 2005 nomination for Middle Ground had lost to House, so the series finished nought for two in the only category it was ever nominated in.
Ed Burns shared the 2008 writing Emmy nomination for -30- with David Simon on their joint story credit; it was Burns's only Emmy nomination for the series.
The Writers Guild of America gave its 2008 award for Television: Dramatic Series to The Wire for its fourth season.
Simon accepted the 2008 Writers Guild award for the fourth season as showrunner and the writer of its premiere and finale teleplays.
Burns's name on the 2008 Guild award marks the series' only competitive writing win, for the season built on the schools — a year that drew no acting or outstanding-series nomination at all.
Pelecanos was named on the 2008 award having written That's Got His Own, the penultimate hour in which Randy Wagstaff's foster home burns.
Price's work in the awarded season was Corner Boys and Home Rooms, the two hours that set a former policeman's classroom against the trade waiting outside it.
Lehane's contribution to the awarded season was Refugees, one of three scripts he wrote across the last three years of the series, each in a different season.
Mills wrote Soft Eyes for the fourth season, two years before his death during Treme's production.
Overmyer wrote both Margin of Error and Misgivings in the awarded season, the election hour and the hour Randy's placement comes apart.
Zorzi wrote Unto Others, bringing to the season's City Hall material the political reporting he had done at the Baltimore Sun.
Corthron is named on the 2008 award as one of the fourth season's credited writers — a playwright from western Maryland who wrote for the series once and never again.
The Writers Guild nominated The Wire again in 2009, for its fifth and final season, without a second win.
Simon wrote the fifth season's premiere and its finale, and the nomination did not convert as the previous year's had.
Burns wrote Transitions and The Dickensian Aspect for the nominated season, including the episode that took the series' only Directors Guild award.
Pelecanos wrote Late Editions, his last penultimate episode for the series, in which Michael Lee kills Snoop.
Price wrote for the fifth season having been recruited to the staff after two seasons of reviewers comparing the series to his novel Clockers.

Lehane is one of eight writers named on the 2009 nomination, having written one episode in each of the last three seasons — a rhythm Simon used with all three of the novelists he recruited from outside Baltimore.
Mills wrote React Quotes for the final season; he died two years later while working on Treme.
Zorzi wrote Unconfirmed Reports, taking the fabricating-reporter material from the newsroom he had himself worked in.
Collins is named on the 2009 nomination as one of the fifth season's eight credited writers, the only one whose entire connection to the series is that single season.
The Directors Guild's 2009 dramatic series award went to Transitions, with Nina Kostroff Noble named as unit production manager on the directorial team.
Nina Kostroff Noble was named among the recipients of the 2009 Directors Guild award for Transitions, in her capacity as unit production manager.
The Television Critics Association gave The Wire its Heritage Award in 2008, the show's only win from ten TCA nominations.
The American Film Institute named The Wire one of the ten outstanding television programmes of the year three times, in 2003, 2006 and 2008.
The Wire received sixteen NAACP Image Award nominations across its run, in drama series and acting categories, and won none of them.

The episode that won is the fourth-season premiere: four thirteen-year-olds intercut through the last fortnight of a summer holiday, with nothing but the cutting to hold the four strands together and no narration explaining who anyone is.
David Simon ran Generation Kill as showrunner and co-writer, adapting Evan Wright's embedded reporting into seven parts and shooting it in southern Africa for the Iraqi terrain.
Ed Burns co-wrote Generation Kill with David Simon and Evan Wright, adapting Wright's embedded reporting from Iraq.
HBO broadcast Generation Kill as a seven-part miniseries in 2008, the network's first project with David Simon and Ed Burns after The Wire had finished.
Blown Deadline made Generation Kill with Company Pictures, taking the company outside Baltimore for the first time and shooting the invasion of Iraq in Namibia, Mozambique and South Africa.
David Simon co-created Treme and ran it for four seasons, moving his institutional method from Baltimore to post-Katrina New Orleans.
Eric Overmyer co-created Treme with David Simon, bringing his own long familiarity with New Orleans to it after writing for The Wire.
HBO carried Treme for four seasons from 2010 to 2013, a series about musicians in post-Katrina New Orleans with far less plot than The Wire and a comparable indifference to ratings.
Blown Deadline Productions made Treme for HBO, moving the company's Baltimore production model to New Orleans for four seasons.
David Simon co-wrote Show Me a Hero, adapting Lisa Belkin's account of the Yonkers public housing fight.
William F. Zorzi co-wrote Show Me a Hero with David Simon, their first project together after The Wire and their years at the Baltimore Sun.
HBO broadcast Show Me a Hero over three nights in August 2015, a six-part account of a federal desegregation order and the Yonkers council that refused to comply with it.
Blown Deadline made Show Me a Hero with Paul Haggis directing, shooting in Yonkers itself to reconstruct a housing dispute that had happened there twenty-five years earlier.
David Simon co-created The Deuce, applying the same institutional approach to the New York sex trade of the 1970s and 1980s.
George Pelecanos co-created The Deuce with David Simon, the first series on which the two took joint creator credit after a decade of Pelecanos writing for him.
HBO carried The Deuce for three seasons from 2017 to 2019, following the legalisation and industrialisation of pornography in New York across roughly fifteen years.
Blown Deadline made The Deuce, applying the institutional method to an industry rather than a city and tracking how money reorganises a street over three separate periods.
David Simon co-created and co-wrote The Plot Against America, adapting Philip Roth's novel about a Lindbergh presidency into six parts centred on a single Newark family.

Burns adapted Philip Roth's novel with Simon — the only project of theirs not built from reporting either man had done himself, and the first in which they worked from someone else's imagined America rather than a city they knew.
HBO broadcast The Plot Against America across six weeks in spring 2020, the first Simon project not drawn from journalism or his own reporting.
Blown Deadline Productions made The Plot Against America for HBO with Annapurna Television and RK Films.

Simon returned to Baltimore policing with a real scandal instead of a fictional one, adapting Justin Fenton's reporting on the Gun Trace Task Force with Reinaldo Marcus Green directing, and casting so many Wire alumni that the series doubles as a reunion.
Pelecanos co-created We Own This City with Simon — their second joint creator credit after The Deuce, and the project that brought both men back to Baltimore twenty years after The Wire began.
HBO broadcast We Own This City over six weeks in spring 2022, returning to Baltimore policing with a real scandal rather than a fictional organisation at its centre.

Blown Deadline made We Own This City with Spartan Productions twenty-two years after it started shooting The Wire in the same city — the same company, the same production base, and a police department that had by then produced the real corruption case the series dramatises.
Evan Wright's book Generation Kill was adapted by David Simon, Ed Burns and Wright himself into the HBO miniseries of the same name.
Justin Fenton's book We Own This City was adapted by David Simon and George Pelecanos into the 2022 HBO limited series.
The Gun Trace Task Force prosecutions are the events Justin Fenton reported and then set out in the book We Own This City.
We Own This City is set and shot in Baltimore, dramatising the real corruption of the city's Gun Trace Task Force.

We Own This City is a 2022 HBO miniseries by the same creators about a real Baltimore police unit — the Gun Trace Task Force — whose officers were convicted in 2018 of robbing the citizens they policed. It uses the same city, production company and many of the same actors, and dramatises in fact what The Wire had argued in fiction the department would eventually produce.
Burns produced We Own This City, returning to the department he had served in for twenty years to dramatise a plainclothes squad that robbed the people it policed.
William F. Zorzi wrote for and co-executive produced We Own This City, again working the Baltimore beat alongside David Simon.
Richard Price wrote for The Deuce, reuniting with David Simon and George Pelecanos a decade after The Wire.
George Pelecanos wrote and produced on Treme, continuing with David Simon into New Orleans after having written at least one episode of every season of The Wire.
Mills was a writer and co-executive producer on Treme's first season and died of a brain aneurysm on 30 March 2010, before the season he was working on had finished airing its first episodes.
Nina Kostroff Noble produced Treme across its four seasons, relocating the production model she had built in Baltimore to New Orleans.
Nina Kostroff Noble produced We Own This City, bringing the same Baltimore production operation she had run on The Wire back to the city two decades on.
Nina Kostroff Noble executive produced Generation Kill, managing a location shoot across three African countries standing in for Iraq.

West plays McNulty in the first season as a detective whose competence is real and whose judgement is not: he is right that the murders are being ignored, and wrong about what going over his commanders' heads will cost the colleagues who get assigned to the case he forces into existence.
Exiled to the marine unit for season two, West's McNulty spends the season trying to force his way back onto a case by dredging up bodies nobody else wants.
Season three gives West's McNulty the Stringer Bell pursuit and the discovery, over the body, that the man he chased for three years had been trying to get out.
West's McNulty spends most of season four in uniform in the Western District, sober, domesticated and visibly better for it, which the season uses as its only quiet thread.
Season five has West's McNulty invent a serial killer to fund a case, the performance turning steadily from black comedy into something closer to breakdown.

Doman's Deputy Commissioner Rawls spends the first season trying to get the new investigative unit shut down before it produces murder victims his own homicide squad would then have to solve and be judged on — treating a colleague's success as a threat to his figures.

Season two has Doman's Deputy Commissioner Rawls treat thirteen women found dead in a shipping container primarily as an accounting problem: unsolved murders damage the share of killings his detectives officially close, so most of his effort goes into having another agency take the case.

Season three shows Doman's Deputy Commissioner Rawls running Comstat — the department's statistics meetings, where district commanders stand in front of colleagues and account for their crime figures. The humiliation is the point: the numbers, not the policing behind them, are what the meeting exists to correct.
Season four has Rawls manoeuvring for the commissioner's office as Burrell's position collapses, and discovering that a new mayor's promises are worth exactly what his predecessor's were.
Season five ends Doman's Rawls, in the closing montage, as superintendent of the Maryland State Police, having survived every administration he served.

Elba's Stringer Bell runs the organisation's daily business from behind a photocopy shop counter, keeping himself off telephones and out of the places where drugs change hands — which is why a year of police surveillance produces almost nothing that would stand up against him.
With Avon Barksdale in prison for season two, Elba's Stringer runs the organisation alone, trading territory for better product and having D'Angelo killed to protect it.
Season three takes Elba's Stringer to economics classes, development meetings and a state senator's fraud, and kills him on the site he thought was his way out.
Faison's Burrell spends season one pressing Cedric Daniels to close the case early, because a long investigation into a drug organisation is precisely what City Hall has not asked for.

Faison's Burrell spends season two as acting commissioner, and the deal he strikes with Major Valchek — a detail on the stevedores' union in exchange for Valchek's backing in the confirmation — is the transaction the entire season proceeds from.
Season three has Burrell managing a district commander who has suspended the drug war without telling him, and disowning it the moment it becomes public.
Season four has Burrell fighting to keep an office a new mayor has already promised elsewhere, and trading his files for terms.
Gilliard's D'Angelo carries season one's conscience, from the chess lesson to the cooperation deal his mother talks him out of.
Season two has Gilliard's D'Angelo refuse the family entirely from prison, which is what makes Stringer Bell decide he cannot be left alive.

Harris's Avon Barksdale spends the first season almost entirely unheard on the wiretap: a name the investigators can attach to nothing, glimpsed once on a boxing-match videotape, which is what makes finally identifying him the season's central achievement.
Season two puts Harris's Avon in prison, running the organisation's supply and its violence from a tier while his partner reshapes the business outside.
Released in season three, Harris's Avon chooses a war for corners over his partner's business case, and gives up Stringer Bell to settle a debt.
Lovejoy's Pearlman writes season one's wiretap affidavits and has to persuade a judge to sign extensions on a case producing very little the department wants.
Season two has Pearlman carrying the port case through a prosecutor's office with no appetite for a target that cannot be named.
Season three has Pearlman arguing for a novel wiretap on Stringer Bell's property companies, a case that dies with him.
Season four has Pearlman preparing charges on a run of bodies recovered from vacant houses with almost no forensic evidence attached to any of them.
Season five ends Pearlman on the bench, after five seasons spent telling detectives which of their evidence a court would actually accept.

Pierce's Bunk Moreland works season one from the homicide squad rather than the new unit, and it is his interrogation of a Barksdale enforcer — conducted almost entirely by patience and bluff, with a photocopier passed off as a lie detector in a neighbouring scene — that produces the season's murder conviction.
Season two has Bunk working the container deaths and being reminded that thirteen women with no names attached are a clearance problem before they are anything else.
Season three has Bunk shepherding a reluctant Omar Little through a murder trial and telling him plainly what his career has done to the neighbourhood.
Season four has Bunk chasing the gun that keeps reappearing in West Baltimore killings, and arriving at the vacant houses from the other direction.
Season five sets Bunk against his own partner, working real cases at his own pace and refusing any part of the invented ones.

Reddick's Lieutenant Daniels is handed the new unit as a safe pair of hands expected to close it quickly, and spends the season choosing instead to protect a slow investigation his superiors want abandoned — a choice he makes knowing they can end his career with what they know about money in his past.
Season two puts Reddick's Daniels in charge of a case he did not choose, built on a major's grudge, and shows him deciding that running it properly matters more than what it was created for.
Season three has Daniels running the Major Crimes Unit at its most effective, and being told repeatedly that effectiveness is not what was requested.
Season four has Daniels promoted into the command staff and discovering that the figures he is now responsible for cannot be produced honestly.
Season five makes Reddick's Daniels commissioner and then requires falsified figures of him, which he refuses, resigning into private practice.

Royo's Bubbles is how the investigators put names to faces: a heroin addict who knows every corner, he walks the neighbourhood placing distinctive hats on the dealers he recognises so that the surveillance team photographing them can tell who is who.

Season two sends Royo's Bubbles to the docks, working for the police outside the West Baltimore streets where his knowledge is worth something — and useful there precisely because nobody on the waterfront knows to be careful around him.

In the third season Royo's Bubbles sells from a shopping trolley inside the tolerated blocks and reports back to detectives that everything is available in one place and nobody is being chased — which is simultaneously the experiment's success and the reason it cannot be publicly defended.
Season four takes Royo's Bubbles to its lowest point, the poisoned capsule intended for his tormentor killing the boy he had taken in.
Season five gives Royo's Bubbles a year clean, a newspaper profile he does not want, and finally the stairs to his sister's dining table.
Sohn's Kima Greggs supplies season one's street knowledge and is shot on the buy the department insisted on, which turns the case into something nobody can shut down.

Season two puts Sohn's Detective Greggs on light duty behind a desk after the shooting that nearly killed her, taking the port smuggling case as paperwork she can do sitting down — and discovers she would rather be back doing dangerous work than safe at home with her partner and their expected child.

Season three returns Sohn's Detective Greggs to street work after the shooting that nearly killed her, investigating both West Baltimore drug organisations, while at home her partner and their newborn son get on with a life she has effectively opted out of.

Season four moves Sohn's Detective Greggs into the homicide squad, where she works the bodies recovered from the boarded-up houses, and shows her partner and the child they had planned together getting on with a life she is no longer part of.
Season five gives Sohn's Kima the decision that ends McNulty's career, reporting the fabricated murders to Cedric Daniels once she has worked out what they are.
Bauer's Frank Sobotka spends season two spending union money on lobbyists and taking smugglers' money to fund it, and dies having decided to tell the FBI everything.
Season two has Ben-Victor's Vondas conduct every negotiation the Greek's organisation makes, so that its head never has to be in a room with anyone.

Season two establishes Peters's Freamon as the investigation's methodical centre, and reveals why a detective of that ability was available for a throwaway unit: thirteen years and four months in the pawn shop section, a dead-end posting he was given for embarrassing a commander.
