Season three has Peters's Freamon chasing Stringer Bell's money through property companies, and arriving at the development site to find the case gone with the man.

In the fourth season Peters's Detective Freamon works out that a drug crew has been hiding its murder victims inside Baltimore's boarded-up empty houses, and obtains the authority to open them. Each body recovered is a new unsolved murder on the homicide squad's books, so solving the puzzle wrecks the department's statistics and makes him deeply unpopular for it.
Season five has Peters's Freamon join the fabricated-killer scheme in order to fund the wiretap that finally reaches Marlo Stanfield.
Season two has Ryan's Beadie Russell open a container of dead women and then be seconded into a homicide investigation she has no training for.

Gillen's Carcetti arrives as an ambitious councilman using police failures to build a public profile, and finds in the major's unauthorised arrest-free zone exactly the scandal his career needs — a reform he privately recognises as working and publicly destroys.
Season four has Gillen's Carcetti win the mayoralty and refuse the governor's school money, choosing his own future over the deficit he inherited.
Season five has Gillen's Carcetti govern toward Annapolis, demanding crime figures he knows cannot be produced honestly.
Season three ends True-Frost's Prez as a policeman, shooting a plainclothes officer in an alley and resigning before the department can decide what to do with him.
Season four gives True-Frost's Prez a mathematics classroom and the discovery that the school is managing the same numbers the department was.

Wisdom plays Major Colvin as a man conducting an experiment he knows will end his career, telling a room of residents he cannot promise them anything will improve, and accepting the demotion delivered on his last working day without argument.
Season four puts Wisdom's Colvin in a school programme for the most disruptive children and ends with him taking one of them home.

Season three gives Gilliam's Carver the job of moving dealers into the arrest-free blocks, and the dressing-down from his major — asked to name a single person on the streets he has policed for years, and unable to — that changes how he works for the rest of the series.
Season four has Carver promise Randy Wagstaff a protection the department cannot deliver, and drive the boy to a group home himself.
Season five has Carver, now a sergeant, write up an officer for assaulting a schoolteacher rather than smooth it over, which is the measure of the distance he has travelled.
Season three has Lombardozzi's Herc lose a surveillance camera he had signed for, an incident the department pursues with more energy than most of its homicides.
Season four is where Herc loses a surveillance camera, invents an informant to cover it, and gives up the name that destroys Randy Wagstaff's foster placement.
Season five has Herc out of the department and working for Maurice Levy, where his loose talk hands the defence the illegal wiretap.
Season three has Williams's Bodie holding corners through the war with Marlo Stanfield and taking instruction from a Barksdale organisation that is coming apart.
Season four ends with Williams's Bodie refusing to leave the corner he built, and being shot on it for having been seen talking to a detective.
Season three has Omar shot at by Brother Mouzone, allied with him against the man who lied to them both, and finally throwing both their guns into the Inner Harbour.

In the fourth season Williams's Omar Little robs an entire wholesale drug shipment belonging to the dealers' co-operative, and is then framed for a murder he did not commit — a shopkeeper is beaten into swearing a false statement — and jailed on it.
Season five has Williams's Omar jump from a balcony, break a leg, and hunt Marlo Stanfield on a crutch before being shot by a child in a corner shop.
Season three has Robinson's Sydnor working undercover on the corners and taking the paper training from Lester Freamon that shapes the rest of his career.
Season four has Sydnor working the Stanfield case under Lester Freamon's direction while the unit is being actively dismantled around them.
Season five ends Sydnor in a judge's chambers complaining about his own command, taking up exactly the position McNulty occupied in the first episode.
Season four introduces Cathey's Norman Wilson running Carcetti's campaign and then telling the winner exactly what he has agreed to.
Season five has Norman Wilson watching the mayor he elected govern entirely toward Annapolis, and saying so to his face.
Season four has Coleman's Cutty running the gym as one of the few institutions in the neighbourhood that asks nothing of a boy before letting him in.
Hector's Marlo spends season four having his rivals sealed into vacant houses and demonstrating, in a corner shop, that his name is the only currency he cares about.
Season five takes Hector's Marlo to the Greek's connection, to Proposition Joe's death, to an indictment and then out of it, and finally back to a corner he no longer needs.
Season four has Turman's Royce concealing the school deficit through the primary and losing anyway to a challenger he never took seriously.
Season five gives Akinnagbe's Chris Partlow the confession that keeps Michael Lee out of the indictment, and a life sentence taken without visible complaint.
Season five has Steintorf transmit the mayor's demand for lower crime figures to a commissioner who resigns rather than meet it.
Season five leaves Crawford's Dukie in a scrapyard with an arabber and a needle, the series' bleakest and most quietly staged ending.
Season five takes Wilds's Michael from Chris Partlow's protection to killing Snoop and sending his brother away, ending as the city's next stick-up man.

In the final season Kostroff's Maurice Levy — the lawyer who has represented every major drug organisation in the series — exposes that the police wiretap was obtained illegally. That single fact collapses the state's case and returns the city's biggest dealer to liberty in exchange for his permanent retirement from the trade.

Paress plays the newsroom's junior reporter as someone who simply keeps working: filing the night calls, taking the cuts to her copy without protest, and only breaking when asked to stay quiet about a colleague she knows is inventing his sources.
Season five gives Whitlock's Clay Davis a state trial and a witness-stand performance that persuades a jury he was the victim of his own generosity.
Season five has McCarthy's Templeton invent a source, a quote and finally a serial killer's phone call, and collect a Pulitzer for the sequence.
Season five has Johnson's Gus Haynes ask the one question nobody above him wants asked, and be moved to the copy desk for asking it.
Felicia Pearson played Snoop on The Wire from the third season through the fifth, a fictionalised version of herself and one of the Stanfield organisation's two principal killers.
Robert F. Chew played Proposition Joe across all five seasons of The Wire, one of the very few drug-trade figures present from the first season to the last.
Pablo Schreiber played Nick Sobotka on The Wire, chiefly through the second season and returning briefly in the fifth.
James Ransone played Ziggy Sobotka through The Wire's second season, the union treasurer's son and the docks' standing joke.

Maestro Harrell played Randy Wagstaff across the fourth and fifth seasons, the boy whose small corridor business and eagerness to be useful to adults end with him in a group home learning not to be either.
Julito McCullum played Namond Brice across the fourth and fifth seasons, performing the swagger his mother demands of him until a separate classroom and a retired major make it unnecessary.

Jordan's Wallace is the boy who wakes and feeds a flat of younger children before school, and whose absence from the corner produces the question the season is remembered by; the part ends in the twelfth episode and was Jordan's first substantial screen role.
Delaney Williams played Sergeant Jay Landsman across all five seasons, giving the homicide unit its running commentary and, at the end, McNulty's mock eulogy over a pool table.

Michael Potts played Brother Mouzone across the second and third seasons: a New York enforcer hired to protect drug-selling territory, who reads intently between acts of violence, speaks with elaborate courtesy, and is shot on the false word of the man who hired him.
Anwan Glover played Slim Charles from the third season onward, hired muscle who outlives every organisation he works for and delivers the series' last named killing.
Hassan Johnson played Wee-Bey Brice on The Wire, from the first season through his character's life sentence and beyond.

Clifford Smith, performing as Method Man, played Cheese Wagstaff across all five seasons: a drug dealer working for his uncle whose disloyalty escalates from betraying his own crew to giving up the man who raised him in the business.
Tray Chaney played Poot Carr on The Wire from the first season, the last of the original corner crew left alive and out of prison.
Felicia Pearson's Snoop becomes a central figure in season four, the season in which the Stanfield organisation's vacant houses fill up.
Robert F. Chew's Proposition Joe is killed in season five, once Marlo Stanfield has taken his connection to the Greek.
Pablo Schreiber's Nick Sobotka is one of season two's two young leads, a capable stevedore with no legitimate work to be had.
James Ransone's Ziggy Sobotka is season two's other young lead, and his shooting of a smuggler's associate is the season's turning point.
Michael B. Jordan's Wallace is killed at the end of season one, the death that fixes the show's moral terms.

Harrell's Randy Wagstaff runs a sweet business from his school locker in season four and unknowingly passes on the message that sets up Lex's murder; by the season's end Carver is driving him to a group home.

McCullum's Namond Brice spends season four performing for the classroom until he is selected out of it into Colvin's separate room, where without an audience he turns out to be a different child entirely.
Potts's Brother Mouzone returns to Baltimore in season three hunting the man who shot him, takes Dante to find him, and instead makes common cause with Omar Little against Stringer Bell.
Clarke Peters played the addict Fat Curt in The Corner, two years before taking the near-opposite role of Detective Freamon on The Wire.
Lance Reddick appeared in The Corner two years before being cast as Cedric Daniels, one of the Baltimore-shot miniseries' actors that David Simon carried directly into The Wire.
Corey Parker Robinson appeared in The Corner before playing Detective Sydnor, part of the company The Corner assembled and The Wire then drew on.
Robert F. Chew appeared in The Corner two years before playing Proposition Joe, one of a large group of Baltimore actors the earlier miniseries brought into David Simon's company.
Delaney Williams appeared in The Corner before playing Sergeant Landsman, and later returned for We Own This City, making three Baltimore productions with David Simon.
Reg E. Cathey played Scalio in The Corner before returning to David Simon's Baltimore as Norman Wilson.
Clarke Peters was part of Treme's starring ensemble, one of several Wire actors David Simon took to New Orleans.
Wendell Pierce starred in Treme as a New Orleans trombonist, a lead role after five seasons as Bunk Moreland.
James Ransone was cast in Generation Kill as a Marine corporal, David Simon and Ed Burns bringing him back after his season two work as Ziggy Sobotka.
Gbenga Akinnagbe appeared in The Deuce, one of several Wire actors David Simon and George Pelecanos carried over to their New York series.
Lawrence Gilliard Jr. appeared in The Deuce more than a decade after playing D'Angelo Barksdale, one of the Wire alumni its ensemble was partly built from.
Michael Kostroff was in the starring cast of The Plot Against America, having played Maurice Levy on The Wire.
Jamie Hector returned to a Simon Baltimore series in We Own This City, this time as a police detective rather than a kingpin.

Lombardozzi was recalled for We Own This City alongside Delaney Williams, Tray Chaney, Jermaine Crawford and Anwan Glover, an ensemble assembled substantially from the earlier show's Baltimore company.
Delaney Williams appeared in We Own This City, his third Simon Baltimore production after The Corner and The Wire.
Jermaine Crawford appeared in We Own This City, having played Dukie as a teenager on The Wire.
Anwan Glover appeared in We Own This City, one of a large group of Wire actors recalled for a series about the police scandal that followed the world they had played in.
Tray Chaney appeared in We Own This City, returning to a Simon production in Baltimore some fourteen years after first playing Poot Carr.
Evan Wright wrote Generation Kill from his own embedded reporting with a Marine reconnaissance battalion during the invasion of Iraq.
Evan Wright co-wrote the HBO adaptation of Generation Kill with David Simon and Ed Burns, working on the scripts drawn from his own book.
Alexa L. Fogel's casting of The Wire's first season was nominated for an Artios award by the Casting Society of America in 2003.
The Casting Society of America nominated The Wire's first season for an Artios award in 2003, the show's earliest industry recognition of any kind.
Sonja Sohn's Kima Greggs is shot at the end of The Cost, the wounding that turns a quiet wiretap case into a departmental emergency.
Andre Royo's Bubbles sets up the undercover buy in The Cost that ends with Kima Greggs shot, and carries the guilt of it for the rest of the season.
Simon's teleplay for All Prologue gives D'Angelo Barksdale the book-group argument about Gatsby — that a man cannot outrun what he was — twenty minutes before he is killed for having tried.
Lawrence Gilliard Jr.'s D'Angelo Barksdale is strangled in the prison library in All Prologue, his last appearance in the series.
Joy Lusco Kecken wrote The Hunt for season one, the episode dealing with the aftermath of Kima Greggs's shooting.

Lusco wrote Back Burners, her last script for the series, covering the West Baltimore war between the established Barksdale organisation and the younger Stanfield crew taking its corners — and the moment the newer boss quietly stops holding corners at all and becomes a wholesaler instead.

Melnick and Choksey's episode arrives at the point in the first season where the wiretap has stalled and the case can afford to stop for a day — which is what lets the hour show the drug organisations as neighbourhood institutions with fixtures and rivalries of their own, rather than as a target the police are working.
Joe Chappelle produced on The Wire alongside directing for it, one of the small group of directors who stayed with the show across its whole run.
Ernest Dickerson directed for season four, including its finale, bringing a cinematographer's eye to the season's classroom and corner material.

Anthony Hemingway worked as a first assistant director on the first season — on One Arrest, Game Day, The Hunt and Sentencing — before directing episodes himself in the fourth and fifth seasons, so the production promoted him from its own crew rather than hiring him in.

Amy Ryan played Beadie Russell across The Wire, central to the second season and returning in the fourth and fifth as the person McNulty is trying, and failing, to stay steady for.
Chad L. Coleman played Cutty Wise on The Wire from the third season to the last, following the character from a prison release to a boxing gym.
Glynn Turman played Clarence Royce, appearing first at a tower demolition staged as reform and last as a lobbyist's introduction after losing the primary.
Neal Huff played Michael Steintorf on The Wire, the mayor's chief of staff, appearing from the fourth season as Carcetti's administration takes shape.
Tom McCarthy's Scott Templeton collects a Pulitzer in -30- for work he invented, one of the finale's flatter and more damning notes.
Michelle Paress played Alma Gutierrez on The Wire's fifth season, the reporter who does the work and is exiled to a suburban bureau for backing her editor.
Tristan Wilds's Michael Lee is one of the four boys season four follows, and the one the Stanfield organisation takes.

Robert F. Colesberry was recognised posthumously among the recipients of The Wire's Peabody Award in May 2004, three months after his death.

The American Film Institute's 2003 citation went to the second season — the year the series left the drug corners for the docks, following stevedores whose work is disappearing. It was the season contemporary audiences liked least, and the institute listed it anyway.
The AFI cited The Wire again for 2006, the school season, in the year the series drew its widest critical acclaim and still no Emmy nomination outside writing.

The institute's 2008 citation was the third and last time it listed The Wire, and the only one of the three to name a season whose reviews were mixed — the newspaper year divided critics as none of the others had.

Michael K. Williams was nominated for an NAACP Image Award as outstanding supporting actor in a drama series for his work as Omar Little, one of the sixteen Image nominations the show accumulated without a win.

This is the only craft award the fourth season received. It took the Writers Guild prize the same year and no Emmy nomination outside writing, so the editors' guild and the writers' guild between them account for the whole of its industry recognition.
The Wire is, by its creators' own account, an argument against the drug war conducted in the form of a police series; every season returns to the same conclusion from a different institution.

The Wire treats institutional self-preservation, rather than any individual villainy, as the force that determines outcomes; David Simon has called the show a study of how institutions consume the people inside them.
The Wire measures every character against the code they claim to follow, and the erosion of that code across five seasons is one of its through-lines.

The Wire is set in a majority-black city and carried by a predominantly black cast at a time when American television rarely attempted either, and it makes race and class the determinants of who is policed and whose death is investigated.
The Wire was consciously written as tragedy with institutions in the role of the gods, a structure its writers cited explicitly to explain why reform never holds.

The series shows the same trick in four institutions in turn: police reclassifying serious crimes as lesser ones to improve the proportion of cases they close; schools drilling children for the one test they are measured on; a newspaper chasing prizes rather than reporting; and politicians promising figures they know cannot be met. In each, managing the measurement replaces doing the work.
Every reformer in The Wire succeeds and is destroyed for it, a pattern the series repeats deliberately enough to constitute its answer to the question of whether the system can be fixed from within.
Season one is built around the mechanics of a wiretap, from pager clones and payphone pen registers to the affidavit a judge has to be persuaded to sign.

The first season lays out the unwritten rules the drug trade runs on, through characters who keep them: what a soldier owes the organisation that employs him, what happens to anyone who talks to police, and why a robber who only ever robs dealers can walk unarmed through neighbourhoods that would otherwise give him up.
Season two moves the argument to the docks, where the disappearance of industrial work leaves a union with nothing to sell but access to the port.
Season three tests reform directly: a district major suspends drug enforcement in three blocks, violent crime falls, and the experiment is destroyed the moment it is spoken about aloud.
Season three puts the drug war's futility on screen as policy rather than argument, by showing what happens in a district that stops fighting it.
Season four sets a school system measured on test scores against a corner economy that offers the same children money and standing, and follows four boys through the contest.

The fourth season sets a school system and a police department side by side doing the same thing: the school suspends its curriculum for weeks to drill children on the single standardised test it is judged by, exactly as commanders massage the proportion of murders recorded as solved. A former policeman turned teacher recognises the practice on sight.
Season five adds the newspaper as the last institution examined, and finds it too diminished by buyouts and prize-hunting to notice what is happening in its own city.

Season five completes the pattern with a fabricated serial killer and a fabricated news story, the police department and the newspaper each manufacturing the numbers and narratives their managers reward.
The Hamsterdam episode is where the reform experiment starts visibly working, which is the point from which its destruction becomes inevitable.
Middle Ground turns on two men who have each broken the code they were raised on, spending a last night on a rooftop pretending otherwise.
Final Grades closes the school year by showing which system got each of the four boys, and the answer is the corner in three cases out of four.

The finale's structure is the theme stated as form. Rather than resolving anything, it casts each vacated role — commissioner, kingpin, robber, addict, editor — and the effect is that the machine is shown to be indifferent to who is standing in any particular place in it.

The hour's argument is that an institution's memory is shorter than any individual's career in it: each removal here is arranged by someone who benefits, each vacancy is filled within days, and nothing about how the place works is altered by the change of occupant.
The Baltimore Police Department's real statistical culture, which David Simon reported on for years and Ed Burns worked inside, is the source of the show's account of managed crime figures.
The Baltimore Sun's buyouts, out-of-town management and prize-hunting under new ownership are what David Simon drew on for the show's account of a failing newsroom.
Baltimore's loss of its industrial and shipping employment across the late twentieth century is the real economic history behind the show's account of what fills the gap.
Ed Burns's years building wiretap cases against Baltimore drug organisations supplied the procedural detail — the pagers, the payphones, the affidavits — that gives the series its title.

The Wire's critical standing is largely a retrospective phenomenon: modest notices and a small audience while it aired, and near-universal placement among the greatest television series in the years after it ended.
The Wire's audience was small throughout and shrank across the run, which is the context for every renewal decision HBO made about it.
University courses built on The Wire began appearing while the series was still recent, treating it as a text on cities, poverty and institutions.
The Time essay was published days after The Wire's finale and made explicit the political argument the series had spent five seasons dramatising.
Barack Obama's repeated public praise for The Wire, as candidate and as president, did more than any review to fix its standing outside television criticism.
The 2015 White House conversation used The Wire as the shared reference point for a discussion of drug policy, seven years after the series had finished.
Jonathan Abrams's oral history exists because of the interest The Wire accumulated after it ended, and is now the standard behind-the-scenes source on it.
Within The Wire's critical reputation, season four is the season most often singled out as the peak, and the one most cited in arguments for the series as the finest American television drama.
Viewership for The Wire fell again during season five, reported at the time by the Baltimore Sun, so the series ended with the smallest audience it had ever had.
The box-set and streaming audience for The Wire is the direct answer to its low broadcast ratings: the viewers who did not watch it weekly found it later, in the form its structure had always suited.
The Wire's reputation as one of the greatest series ever made was built by the box-set and streaming audience rather than the broadcast one, which is why the acclaim postdates the show by years.
University courses on The Wire typically take race, class and urban poverty as their subject, using the series as a case text rather than as drama.
Sociology and law courses on The Wire use it chiefly as a study of how institutions behave, which is the reading its writers have always endorsed.
The Time essay states the series' drug-war argument as direct political advocacy, calling for jury nullification in non-violent drug prosecutions.

Simon drafted the March 2008 Time essay in which the series' writers pledged to vote to acquit in any drug case they were empanelled on, the argument the show had been making in fiction for five years put as a direct call to jurors.
Burns signed the jury-nullification essay having spent twenty years making the drug arrests it asks jurors to refuse to convict on.
Pelecanos signed the 2008 essay, one of the three crime novelists on the staff to put their names to it.
Price added his name to the Time essay, extending to policy the position his fiction had taken since Clockers.
Lehane signed the essay alongside Simon, Burns, Pelecanos and Price — the five writers stating that a juror's refusal to convict was a legitimate answer to the drug war.
Barack Obama took part in the 2015 White House conversation with David Simon, describing The Wire as one of the greatest pieces of art of recent decades.
David Simon took part in the 2015 White House conversation with President Obama, arguing there that what drugs do not destroy the war on drugs does.
George Pelecanos gave interviews for Jonathan Abrams's oral history, including the account of how Donnie Andrews served as the model for Omar Little in the writers' room.
Wendell Pierce gave interviews for Jonathan Abrams's oral history, describing what the material demanded of the cast.

Holland's third-season episode is Moral Midgetry, in which Prez cracks Bodie's mobile and Stringer Bell finally admits to Avon that he had D'Angelo killed.
For season four Holland directed Corner Boys, the hour in which Colvin's separate classroom asks the boys how a corner works.

For season two Van Patten directed Stray Rounds, which opens on a child killed indoors by a bullet from a corner dispute and ends with a federal agent protecting the Greek.
Van Patten's three episodes fall one per season across the first three years, the last of them in season three.

Brad Anderson's only first-season credit is The Cost; he returned five years later to direct A New Day in season four.
Brad Anderson directed in season four, returning to the show four years after his first-season work as the series moved into the school system.
Seith Mann directed in season four, having come up through the production's own crew rather than arriving from outside it.
Seith Mann directed in season five, one of the directors the production had trained up from its own crew rather than hired in.

Uta Briesewitz was director of photography on The Wire's early seasons and set the visual rule the show kept throughout: no expressive lighting, no camera movement that a documentary crew could not have managed.

Briesewitz shot the whole first season as director of photography, establishing a look built on natural light and long static takes — a deliberate refusal of the visual grammar that tells an audience how to feel about what it is seeing.
Vincent Peranio was production designer on The Wire, using long familiarity with Baltimore to choose and dress the courtyards, row houses, bars and vacants the series is built out of.
Vincent Peranio has spent his career designing films shot in Baltimore, and brought that accumulated knowledge of the city's fabric to The Wire.
Chappelle opened the final season having also directed Middle Ground four years earlier, so the same hand staged both Stringer Bell's death and the budget meeting that sets the last season's terms.

Dickerson directed Misgivings, whose closing sequence — a foster home set alight because the boy inside was seen talking to police — is shot from across the road, at the distance a neighbour would have watched it from rather than from inside the burning house.

The Hunt shows season one what the department is capable of when it wants to be: every resource in the city deployed within hours, and the implicit comparison with every other victim left unstated.
Sentencing closes season one on the arithmetic of a plea: a kingpin serving seven years, a nephew taking twenty, and a detail broken up for having done what it was asked to do.
Ebb Tide reorients the series in season two, opening on the water rather than a corner and introducing an entire second economy the first season never mentioned.

Hard Cases is season two's assembly episode, reconstituting the investigative unit out of officers the department has once again decided it can spare, and setting them a case — thirteen dead women in a shipping container — that no squad in the city wants to own.
Duck and Cover marks season two's low point for McNulty personally, and the point at which Frank Sobotka's arrangement with the Greeks has clearly stopped being something he controls.

Margin of Error delivers season four's election, and ends on a new mayor alone with the size of what he has actually taken on.
Unto Others is where season four's obligations start arriving: the mayor-elect's debts, and the point at which Randy Wagstaff's usefulness to the police becomes dangerous to him.
Know Your Place shows each of season four's boys the ceiling above him, and is the episode after which none of their trajectories is really open any more.
Misgivings is where season four's consequences reach Randy Wagstaff's foster home, the word snitch having travelled faster than any protection the police could offer.
A New Day shows season four's separate classroom working and the school system deciding, on budget and testing grounds, that working is not a sufficient reason to continue it.

React Quotes is where season five's invented killer acquires a telephone, and the newspaper supplies a reporter willing to say it rang for him.
The Dickensian Aspect takes its title from the instruction handed down season five's newsroom, and sets that instruction against the reporting that would actually explain the city.
Took gives season five its courtroom set piece, Clay Davis testifying about his own generosity and a jury choosing to believe every word of it.

Simon's Sentencing teleplay closes the first season on a courtroom where everyone gets what the system can deliver and nobody gets what the case was for.
David Simon wrote the teleplay of Ebb Tide, opening the second season on the water and introducing the port that will carry it.
Lusco's Hard Cases teleplay is where the container dead acquire nationalities, effects and a route, and stop being a number the department is arguing over.
George Pelecanos wrote the teleplay of Duck and Cover, following McNulty's drinking and the union's position to their respective conclusions.
Ed Burns wrote the teleplay of Storm Warnings, bringing the docks case and the Barksdale organisation's prison business to a head at once.

Richard Price wrote the teleplay of Moral Midgetry, containing Stringer Bell's admission to Avon Barksdale about D'Angelo.

David Mills wrote the teleplay of Soft Eyes, which gives the fourth season its instruction about how to look at a room.

Lehane's teleplay for Refugees follows the four boys through the opening weeks of the school year while Bubbles enrols Sherrod by posing as his uncle — two sets of adults trying to get children into classrooms, from opposite ends of the city.

Zorzi's teleplay for Unto Others runs the mayor's first weeks against a prisoner's, both men working out what the institution they have entered will actually let them do.
Kia Corthron wrote the teleplay of Know Your Place, her only script for the series, in which each of the four boys is shown his ceiling.
Overmyer's Misgivings teleplay closes on a firebombed house and a boy who told the truth to a police officer, and it is the episode after which nothing in the fourth season can be undone.
Burns's A New Day teleplay puts Colvin's separate classroom at the point where it starts working, and shows the system deciding that is not a sufficient reason to pay for it.
Mills wrote React Quotes, whose title is newsroom jargon for the quotes gathered in reaction to someone else's story — which is precisely what the episode's reporter manufactures.
Ed Burns wrote the teleplay of The Dickensian Aspect, whose title is the managing editor's instruction to find a human angle instead of a story.
Richard Price wrote the teleplay of Took, built around Clay Davis's testimony and a jury that decides to believe it.

Burns broke Misgivings with Overmyer; his half is Clay Davis calling on Burrell to be reassured that the commissioner's race still protects the job.
Overmyer broke Misgivings with Ed Burns, whose own years teaching supplied the machinery by which a boy's usefulness to the police destroys his placement.
Simon broke the final season premiere with Burns around a single instruction issued twice in one hour, to two institutions that both comply.
Ed Burns shares the story credit on More with Less with David Simon, opening the final season on a department and a newspaper each told to produce more from less.
Michael K. Williams's Omar Little first appears in The Buys, walking a corner that empties ahead of him.

Gillen plays Carcetti's victory night as an anticlimax: the room empties, the noise stops, and the mayor-elect sits down with the size of the job.
Sonja Sohn's Kima Greggs is the wounded officer whose shooting drives the department's response throughout The Hunt.

Burns broke The Cost with Simon: an undercover buy arranged through a club owner the organisation has already beaten once, and a detective shot in a car because the detail was pushed into speed it had not earned.

Simon and Burns's story turns a slow wiretap investigation into an emergency by having a police officer shot. The point is what follows: the only kind of crisis the command staff understands is one involving its own, and it responds by destroying the case that caused it.
Marlyne Barrett played Nerese Campbell, the council president who trades her influence with the ministers for a written understanding about the mayoralty and collects on it.

In season five Campbell converts that leverage into the mayoralty, taking the office Carcetti vacates for Annapolis and installing Stanislaus Valchek as commissioner.
Michael Willis played Andy Krawczyk, the developer who takes drug money into downtown projects without inquiry and is standing on the site when Stringer Bell is shot.
Willis's Andy Krawczyk takes Stringer Bell's money into his downtown developments in season three and is standing on the half-built site when Stringer is shot there.
Krawczyk reappears in season five still developing, the waterfront project running on undisturbed while every institution around it is in trouble.

Nicholls-King's Cheryl is at home with Kima Greggs in season one urging her toward law school and away from street work, and at the hospital after the undercover buy goes wrong.

In season two Nicholls-King's Cheryl and her partner, Detective Greggs, have a son by donor insemination. Greggs's decision to go back to dangerous street police work rather than into the household they had planned is the argument the relationship does not survive.
Frederick Strother played State Delegate Odell Watkins, the veteran legislator whose endorsement Carcetti needs and whose withdrawal of it costs the mayor his base.
Strother's Odell Watkins spends season three as the delegate whose blessing Clarence Royce still has, and whose patience with the administration is beginning to run out.
In season four Watkins breaks with Royce over a broken funding promise and a rigged ticket, sits out the primary, and then endorses Carcetti — the swing that decides it.
Christopher Mann played Councilman Tony Gray, encouraged into a mayoral run with no path to victory by a friend who needed the vote split.
Mann's Tony Gray is Carcetti's council colleague in season three, pressing police failures in hearings alongside the man who is quietly measuring him for a purpose.
In season four Gray runs for mayor at Carcetti's encouragement and splits the black vote three ways, which is the arithmetic that puts Carcetti in office and ends Gray's career.
Benjamin Busch played Officer Anthony Colicchio, whose appetite for confrontation the Western District tolerates until he assaults a schoolteacher in front of witnesses.

Busch's Officer Colicchio polices the arrest-free blocks and supplies their nickname, sneering that his major has built an Amsterdam in West Baltimore — which is how an unauthorised police experiment acquires the name everyone in the city then uses for it.
In season four Colicchio drags a substitute teacher out of a car in front of witnesses, and Carver writes him up rather than smooth it over.
Brian Anthony Wilson played Detective Vernon Holley, who rises to sergeant and carries the homicide unit's real caseload while its overtime funds a murder nobody committed.
Wilson's Vernon Holley works homicide through season four as the vacant-house bodies begin to surface and the squad's clearance arithmetic starts to break.

In the final season Wilson's Detective Holley reluctantly helps a colleague reopen Omar Little's murder and breaks down the false statement that had framed Omar for an earlier killing — accepting that reversing a case already recorded as solved will damage his own solved-case figures.
Michael Salconi played Detective Michael Santangelo, offered a choice between informing on McNulty and losing his place in homicide, and losing it anyway.
Salconi's Michael Santangelo is pressed by Rawls in season one to inform on McNulty's movements in exchange for keeping his place in homicide, and is transferred out regardless.
Santangelo reappears in season four back in uniform in the Western District, one of the officers whose careers the first season's politics quietly ended.
Benjamin Busch, a former Marine Corps infantry officer, worked behind the camera on The Wire as well as appearing in it, taking second unit directing work on the production.
Clement Virgo directed Old Cases and Cleaning Up, giving him both Freamon's account of his thirteen years in the pawn shop unit and the killing of Wallace.

Middle Ground is the series' clearest piece of tragic construction: two men who have each already destroyed the other spend a last night together on a rooftop, and the audience knows before either of them does.
Season two is built as the tragedy of Frank Sobotka, a man destroyed by the one thing he is unambiguously trying to do well, which is to keep work on the docks for the next generation.
Dennis Lehane, like the other novelists on the staff, has discussed The Wire's construction as tragedy rather than crime drama, with the institutions functioning as the implacable force overhead.
Attias directed Transitions, cutting between three removals — a commissioner levered out, a supplier shot in his own kitchen, and a retired robber pulled back across the water.
Dan Attias received the 2009 Directors Guild award for dramatic series direction for Transitions, in which a commissioner, a kingpin and a newsroom veteran are all cleared out inside an hour.
Karen L. Thorson produced across the run and took a credit on this episode, one of the fourth season's late hours shot largely on location in the vacant blocks.
Peter Medak directed The Buys, staging the courtyard chess lesson in which a crew chief explains an organisation to two teenagers by way of a board.
Peter Medak directed The Buys, the episode that introduces Omar Little and the low-rise courtyard the season is played out in.
Know Your Place is where Prez names the mechanism outright, recognising the school's test-preparation fortnight as the same operation he watched commanders run on crime figures.
Corner Boys contains Namond Brice's charge of hypocrisy — that the corner does what the city does and is called animal for it — which is the season's thesis spoken by one of its subjects.
More with Less takes its title from the instruction issued to the Sun newsroom, and sets it against the identical instruction being issued across town to the police department.
The series is named for the wiretap, and returns across five seasons to the gap between what the police can hear and what a court will let them use.
Slapstick removes Prez from the police department two episodes before the season ends, which is what makes the fourth season's schoolteacher possible.
David Simon wrote the teleplay of Slapstick, in which a career the series had spent three seasons rehabilitating is ended by a single shot fired in the dark.

Pelecanos broke Slapstick with Simon around the moment the season stops being about an experiment and becomes about its cost: an alley, a misheard call, and the end of a man's usefulness to the only institution that had him.
Simon wrote the Slapstick teleplay from the story he broke with Pelecanos: the hour that takes Prez out of the department for good and so makes the fourth season's schoolteacher possible.
Zakrzewski directed Slapstick, staging the shooting so quickly and with so little light that the audience is as uncertain as the man who fires.
J. D. Williams plays Bodie's last stand on the corner he had held since he was fifteen, shouting at men who will not come out from behind cars.
Gbenga Akinnagbe's Chris Partlow tortures and kills Butchie in Not for Attribution, on Marlo Stanfield's instruction that the death be conspicuous enough to reach Puerto Rico.
In -30-, Akinnagbe's Chris Partlow confesses to the killings outright so that Michael Lee is left out of the indictment, and takes a life sentence served alongside Wee-Bey Brice.
Felicia Pearson opens the fourth season in a hardware shop discussing the merits of the .27 calibre load with an assistant who has no idea what she wants it for.
Felicia Pearson plays Snoop's last scene in Late Editions as a woman who understands the moment before it happens and asks only how her hair looks.
Chris Bauer's Frank Sobotka is introduced in Ebb Tide arguing for the canal and the grain pier, before the season shows what he is paying for that campaign with.
Amy Ryan's Beadie Russell finds the container with the broken customs seal in Ebb Tide, and the thirteen bodies inside it start the season.
Robert Wisdom's Colvin watches the free zones acquire their nickname and their momentum in Hamsterdam, and realises the experiment is working faster than he can defend it.

The finale ends Wisdom's Major Colvin: the three blocks where he had suspended drug arrests are bulldozed, his pension is reduced, and thirty years of service are settled by a demotion delivered on the day he retires.
True-Frost plays Prez in the seconds after the shot as a man who already knows, before anyone tells him, that this one cannot be survived in uniform.
In Home Rooms, True-Frost's Prez takes his first classroom and finds that the room cannot be commanded the way a corner could.
Chad L. Coleman's Cutty is introduced in Time After Time as a prisoner about to be paroled after fourteen years, talking to Wee-Bey Brice about a city he has not seen since.
Glynn Turman's Royce first appears in Time After Time presiding over the demolition of the Franklin Terrace towers, staged as a demonstration of urban reform.
React Quotes is Turman's last appearance as Royce, by then out of office and making introductions for other people's business.
In -30-, Michael Kostroff's Levy trades Chris Partlow's life sentence and Monk's twenty years for Marlo Stanfield walking out of the courthouse entirely.
Neal Huff's Steintorf sits in the budget meeting in More with Less asking the police commanders where else the department can be trimmed.
Tom McCarthy's Templeton begins inventing in Unconfirmed Reports, at the point where the newsroom's thinning staff and his own ambition meet.
McCarthy plays Templeton in the hour where the invention stops being opportunistic and becomes method — a reporter deciding it is easier to supply the story than to find it.
Michelle Paress's Alma Gutierrez is moved to a suburban bureau in -30- for having backed her city editor against the paper's prize-winning fabricator.
Tristan Wilds's Michael Lee shoots Snoop in Late Editions, having worked out from her own instruction that she was sent for him.
Jermaine Crawford's Dukie is last seen in -30- in a scrapyard with an arabber, taking his first shot, the series' quietest and bleakest ending.
Maestro Harrell's Randy Wagstaff sees his foster placement start to come apart in Misgivings, as the word snitch reaches the house.
Julito McCullum's Namond Brice is taken into Bunny Colvin's suburban home in Final Grades, with his imprisoned father's consent.
Michael B. Jordan's Wallace is shot in Cleaning Up by the two friends he grew up beside, in the flat where he had been waking younger children for school.
Michael Potts's Brother Mouzone corners Stringer Bell with Omar Little in Middle Ground, having come back to Baltimore for the man who set him up.
Anwan Glover's Slim Charles is introduced in Time After Time as Stringer Bell's new chief enforcer, sceptical from the outset about running a drug organisation without territory.
Hassan Johnson's Wee-Bey agrees in Final Grades to meet Bunny Colvin, and then overrules his own wife to give his son away.
Tray Chaney plays Poot in Final Grades as the one who goes back to work the next morning, which is the part of Bodie's death the episode is actually about.

Clifford Smith's Cheese Wagstaff is shot mid-sentence at the final meeting of Baltimore's drug wholesalers' association — moments after arguing that loyalty is bad business, and immediately after it emerges he informed on his own uncle, the man who founded it.
Ransone plays Ziggy in Backwash as a man who has run out of ways to be taken seriously, and finds one behind a warehouse counter.
Old Cases is where season one stops being a procedural about a wiretap and starts being about the people assigned to it, giving Freamon his history and the homicide pair their most quoted scene.
David Simon wrote the teleplay of Old Cases, including the wordless crime-scene reconstruction that has become the series' most anthologised sequence.

Simon broke Old Cases with Burns around a piece of police craft rather than a plot turn — a detective explaining how a career gets spent, and what a man can build inside a bureaucracy that has forgotten he is there.

Burns supplied the procedural half of Old Cases: how a shooting years cold is reconstructed from the physical evidence alone, and why a detective who can do that has been left in a pawn-shop office for thirteen years.
Clement Virgo directed Old Cases, staging the crime-scene sequence in which two detectives work an entire reconstruction without saying anything else at all.
Clarke Peters's Freamon explains in Old Cases exactly what a police officer assigned to the pawn shop unit does, and how long he did it: thirteen years, and four months.
Joe Chappelle directed One Arrest, in which a wiretap produces its first bodies and the squad discovers that arresting people is the fastest way to lose the line.

The episode's proposition is that the trade has civic institutions of its own. An annual East–West basketball match empties the corners for a day, the crews field teams and recruit ringers, and everyone present — including the police who cannot find anyone to arrest — understands it as a fixture that outranks business.
Amy Ryan's Beadie Russell works with Freamon and McNulty in Hard Cases to put a name to one of the dead women from the container, which is the first real investigative work anyone has asked of her.
The title of Hard Cases refers in part to the fourteen open homicides sitting on Pierce's Bunk Moreland, a caseload the squad has no intention of helping him clear.
Duck and Cover takes Dominic West's McNulty through a drinking binge of some magnitude and out the other side into the marine unit, sober enough for Bunk to argue him back onto a case.
James Ransone's Ziggy is talked into fighting Maui by fellow stevedores in Duck and Cover, another humiliation absorbed in the hope it will read as respect.

Potts's Brother Mouzone is installed in the high-rise public housing blocks by the head of the Barksdale organisation, to keep a robber who has been raiding them away from the most profitable drug-selling ground in West Baltimore.
Robert Wisdom plays the moment Colvin stops running buy-and-busts as an administrative announcement delivered to a roll-call room that does not understand what it has just been told.
Wood Harris's Avon Barksdale comes home in Homecoming to a West Baltimore that has been taken while he was inside, and chooses territory over his partner's argument for product.
Elba plays Stringer Bell admitting to Avon Barksdale what he did to D'Angelo, and the performance is built on how little he expects it to cost him.
True-Frost plays the moment Prez stops being a liability and becomes the reason the case works, reading a network off a handset nobody else could make sense of.
True-Frost's Prez is given the advice that names the episode in Soft Eyes — look at the room the way you would look at a crime scene, and it will show you what is in it.
Andre Royo plays Bubbles enrolling Sherrod by claiming to be his uncle, and the performance is built on how practised the lie is.
Anthony Hemingway directed Unto Others, staging the prison-tier stabbing in full view of a landing of men, which is the entire purpose of it.

Williams plays Omar Little's weeks in prison as a man behaving exactly as he does outside it — attacked on a landing, he stabs his assailant in front of everyone present, which is the whole purpose of doing it that way.

Asked in A New Day what the homicide unit would want from a new mayor, Clarke Peters's Freamon asks for proactive investigation and time to prepare cases, while the room around him votes for a pay rise.
Aidan Gillen's Carcetti meets what he calls his first bowl of shit in A New Day, the phrase coming from an anecdote a former mayor had told him about the job.
West plays McNulty in React Quotes discovering that his invention has acquired a second author, and being unable to object to it.

Collateral Damage starts the season's two engines at once: thirteen bodies nobody wants on their books, and a police unit created purely because a major wants revenge on a union official over a church window.
Simon's teleplay for Collateral Damage puts a deputy commissioner in front of a whiteboard doing arithmetic on thirteen dead women, and a major trading a union detail for a confirmation vote.

Burns's half of this story is the police mechanics of avoidance — the specific procedural moves by which a command staff makes a case belong to somebody else, and the arithmetic that motivates each one.

Valchek trades his backing for Burrell's confirmation against a detail on the stevedores' union — the bargain Simon and Burns put at the centre of Collateral Damage, and the reason the second season's investigation exists at all.

Bianchi stages the container scene as a slow official process — a medical examiner working through thirteen bodies in sequence, filmed without music or reaction shots, so the horror registers as administrative volume rather than as a discovery.
John Doman's Rawls does the arithmetic aloud in Collateral Damage — 51.6 per cent down to 39.4 — which is the clearest statement the series makes of what a body actually means to a commander.
Chris Bauer's Frank Sobotka learns in Collateral Damage what was in the container he waved through, and starts trying to find out who put it there.
The Blind Boys of Alabama's gospel reading, which opened all thirteen first-season episodes and played out the last minutes of the series, leads the compilation's run of five title themes.
Tom Waits's own recording, used for season two, sits on the compilation alongside the four covers of his song.
The Neville Brothers' brass-inflected third-season version is among the five title recordings gathered on the compilation, the only release that puts all of them side by side.
DoMaJe's fourth-season recording, made specially for the show by five Baltimore teenagers, appears on the compilation.
Steve Earle's fifth-season recording closes the compilation's sequence of title themes, from the performer who also appeared on screen across the run as Bubbles's recovery sponsor.
Blake Leyh, who supervised the series' music and wrote its closing theme, assembled the compilation from what had been used on screen.
Blake Leyh's closing instrumental is included on the compilation, the one piece of music that had run under all sixty episodes unchanged.
Clement Virgo directed Cleaning Up as well as Old Cases, so the same director handled both Freamon's account of his exile and the killing of Wallace.
Vincent Peranio designed The Buys among the first season's episodes, dressing the low-rise courtyard that most of the season is played out in.
Peranio was still production designer at the fourth season finale, by which point his vacant row houses had become the show's central image.
Uta Briesewitz shot The Buys to the rule she had set for the series: available light, no move a documentary crew could not make, and nothing that tells the audience what to feel about a corner.

Dutton and Simon are both Baltimore men who came to the city's story from opposite ends — Simon reporting on it, Dutton having served time for manslaughter before training as an actor. Their work together on The Corner is what convinced HBO that Simon could carry a Baltimore series of his own.
Peter Medak was one of the rotating directors the first season used after Clark Johnson's pilot, taking The Buys.
Seith Mann came up inside the production rather than being brought in, and directed across the final two seasons.
Justin Fenton wrote We Own This City out of his own courtroom and street reporting on the Gun Trace Task Force prosecutions.
Justin Fenton covered the Gun Trace Task Force case for the Baltimore Sun as it went through federal court, which is the reporting the book and then the series were built from.
Justin Fenton worked the crime beat at the Baltimore Sun a generation after David Simon held the same job, and produced the story Simon would come back to Baltimore to adapt.
Alexa L. Fogel cast the fourth season's four boys, drawing on the same practice of hiring Baltimore locals and non-professionals that had filled out the show since the pilot.
Paul Ben-Victor played Vondas across the series, a character who survives every investigation aimed at him and is still supplying the city after the Greek has gone.

In the final season Clifford Smith's Cheese Wagstaff informs on his own uncle, the wholesaler who raised him in the business, and is shot dead at the dealers' co-operative's last meeting immediately after arguing that loyalty has no place in business.

Edward T. Norris, a real former Baltimore police commissioner, appears as a fictional homicide detective in Final Grades — in the squad room where the bodies recovered from boarded-up empty houses are being added to the wall chart of open murder cases.
Evan Wright worked with David Simon and Ed Burns on the scripts adapting his own embedded reporting, an arrangement Simon had not used before or since with a source author.
Ed Burns and Evan Wright co-wrote the Generation Kill adaptation, Burns bringing the institutional reading and Wright the reporting he had done inside the battalion.
Ebb Tide opens the second season on men waiting at a hiring hall for shifts that are not there, which is the economic fact the rest of the season proceeds from.

Bad Dreams ends the union's attempt to buy its own future back: Frank Sobotka's lobbying money is gone, the grain pier is not reopening, and he walks under the interstate to talk to the federal investigators.

Season four follows four black thirteen-year-olds through a school system that is measured on their test scores and a street economy that pays them, and declines to treat either as a matter of individual choice.
The Corner had already put a year in the life of a black West Baltimore family on American television, using their real names, before The Wire fictionalised the same ground.
HBO's box sets and later its streaming service delivered the audience the broadcasts never found, so the network's back catalogue did more for The Wire's standing than its scheduling ever did.
Pablo Schreiber's Nick Sobotka is taken into federal custody at the end of Port in a Storm, the only one of the three Sobotkas who comes out of the season alive and free.
Evan Wright's book is his own embedded reporting for Rolling Stone, written from inside a Marine reconnaissance battalion during the 2003 invasion rather than assembled afterwards.
Holland directed Corner Boys, and the classroom sequence — adults asking rather than telling, for the first time in the season — is staged as an experiment that visibly works.
Brad Anderson directed A New Day, cutting between a mayor's first working morning and a homicide unit being asked, for once, what it actually wants.
Robert F. Chew's Proposition Joe first appears in Game Day, running the East Side team's side of the annual match and the betting around it, three seasons before he becomes the city's supply.
Transitions is Chew's last appearance as Proposition Joe, shot in his own house by Chris Partlow after Marlo Stanfield has taken the connection Joe spent years protecting.

By this episode Potts's Brother Mouzone has become a problem for the man who hired him: the enforcer is doing exactly the job he was brought from New York to do, and the organisation's second in command wants him gone without anyone knowing why.
Brother Mouzone is shot by Omar Little at the end of season two on Stringer Bell's false information, the wound that brings him back to Baltimore a year later.
Potts's Mouzone appears once more in Mission Accomplished, settling accounts and returning to New York with the debt for his shooting paid.

Cheese Wagstaff sits at the drug wholesalers' table in this episode while Marlo Stanfield moves against Cheese's own uncle for control of the supply, and says nothing — the first visible sign of where his loyalties will land.
Cheese is present for the aftermath of Proposition Joe's killing in Transitions, having supplied Marlo Stanfield with what he needed to reach him.

Cheese Wagstaff appears as the drug wholesalers' association reorganises itself around Marlo Stanfield, the younger boss who has taken the supply connection that the association's founder — Cheese's uncle — had built it on.
Cheese Wagstaff is among those taken in the Late Editions sweep, and gets out again — the one member of the co-operative for whom the arrests change nothing at all.
Calvin Ford, who runs boxing at Baltimore's Upton Boxing Center after a life in the drug trade, is the trainer the character of Cutty Wise was drawn from.
Calvin Ford coaches at the Upton Boxing Center in Baltimore, where he has trained fighters out of the same neighbourhoods the series is set in.

Attias directed Duck and Cover, following a detective through a night of drinking that ends in a wrecked car, and shooting his subsequent exile to the harbour patrol as the punishment the department had been waiting to hand him.

Mančevski directed Game Day, staging an annual basketball match between rival drug organisations at which the police finally get a look at the man they have spent half a season unable to identify, and a robber's attempt on him afterwards fails.
Steve Shill directed The Hunt, the aftermath of Kima Greggs's shooting, in which Rawls clears every agency but homicide off the scene and then tells McNulty he did nothing to get a police shot.

Shill directed the episode in which an undercover drug buy — police purchasing narcotics then arresting the seller on the spot — is staged as entirely routine right up to the moment the officer making it is shot in the face.
Leslie Libman directed Homecoming, staging Avon Barksdale's release as a party in a house he no longer controls the streets around.
Ed Bianchi directed Ebb Tide, opening season two on McNulty exiled to the marine unit and Beadie Russell finding a container that has been sitting too long.
Elodie Keene directed Hard Cases, in which the container dead stop being a clearance-rate problem and start being thirteen individual people with belongings.
Steve Shill directed All Prologue, staging the prison library killing that follows the book-group scene by twenty minutes and is made to look like a suicide.
Thomas J. Wright directed Backwash, in which a cloned union computer becomes evidence and the season's second killing happens off a private humiliation rather than any plan.
Rob Bailey directed Storm Warnings, the second season's most watched hour at nearly three and a half million viewers.
Ernest Dickerson directed Bad Dreams, and the long silent approach under the interstate — a man walking toward people he has known for years — is the season's last sustained image.
Rob Bailey directed Dead Soldiers, and the wake at the bar — the body in dress blues, the singing, the drinking around it — is staged as a ritual the squad has plainly performed before.
Joe Chappelle directed Boys of Summer, opening the season on four boys with a fortnight of freedom left and cutting between them as the school year closes in.

Holland shoots the confession in a single unbroken take with no music and no cutting to reaction, so that the admission has to carry itself — a decision that makes the scene play as two men talking rather than as a revelation being delivered to an audience.

Chappelle stages the season's turning point from outside: the fire shot from across the street at a neighbour's distance, and the boy who caused it by telling the truth to a police officer shown afterwards in a corridor, being processed.
Christine Moore directed Soft Eyes, which takes its title from the advice given to Prez about reading a classroom and contains Norris's discovery that the body he has caught is a state's witness.
Seith Mann directed Home Rooms, in which a former policeman discovers that a classroom cannot be secured, only negotiated with.

Jim McKay directed Refugees, one of very few hours of the series containing almost no police work — following four thirteen-year-olds into a school year that will sort each of them toward a different future.

Zakrzewski directed the hour in which a dealer released from prison finds West Baltimore under new management, and a former policeman turned teacher recognises his school's weeks of test drilling as the same manipulation of figures he used to watch police commanders perform.

This second episode assembles the police unit the whole season runs on — each squad contributing the officer it would most like to be rid of — and in the same hour has the one witness who told the truth at the drug organisation's murder trial shot dead in the open, days after the acquittal.
Lessons is where the case first runs into a politician it cannot touch, four seasons before Clay Davis is tried and acquitted.
Hot Shots starts the Sobotkas' own criminal enterprise, separate from Frank's arrangement and considerably less careful.
Undertow marks the point where Ziggy's attempts to be taken seriously start costing him things he cannot replace.
Stray Rounds contains the federal betrayal that lets the Greek's organisation survive the season, buried inside an episode about a child killed by a bullet meant for nobody.

Back Burners falls at the point in the third season where the war over territory starts to look obsolete to everyone except the men fighting it, and where a bar owner supplies the epigraph the hour is built on: conscience do cost.
Reformation sets up the alliance between Omar Little and Brother Mouzone that kills Stringer Bell an episode later.
Alliances is the episode the fourth season's group of children is most often identified from, and the last time they are all in the same frame.

Simon's teleplay for the second episode shows how the police unit at the centre of the series is actually assembled: no commander will surrender a good officer to a case he does not want brought, so each sends the person he would most like to lose, and the resulting squad is expected to fail.

Burns shares this story with Simon and supplied its institutional detail — the horse-trading between commanders over which bodies each unit will accept, and the assumption on all sides that a unit built this way is meant to produce nothing.

Johnson directed three of the series' hinge hours — the pilot, this second episode, and the finale — bookending five years of television, and returned in the fifth season as an actor, playing the city editor who tries to stop a reporter inventing his stories.

Simon's teleplay has the investigators seize a courier carrying a state senator's campaign cash and be ordered to hand it straight back — the case's first collision with money it is not permitted to touch — and gives the robber Omar Little the series' most quoted line, that a man who comes at the king had best not miss.

Burns supplied what happens inside a unit when an arrest it made legitimately is ordered undone from above: how fast officers learn which names not to type into a warrant, and what that teaches them about the work.
Elodie Keene directed Hot Shots as well as Hard Cases, both early second-season episodes turning on what the Sobotkas are prepared to move through the port.

Simon's teleplay for Stray Rounds sets the two halves of the season against each other in a single hour — a killing in a residential street that no organisation claims, and a federal office quietly deciding which organisation it will not pursue.

Van Patten stages the shooting entirely from indoors: the camera stays with a family in a front room, the shots come from outside the frame, and the audience learns what has happened at the same moment and in the same way the family does.
Lusco's teleplay opens on Butchie's epigraph — conscience do cost — and closes on a dealer who has worked out that holding corners is the expensive way to sell drugs.
Van Patten directed Back Burners, staging Avon Barksdale's tour of his own corners as a survey of ground that has quietly stopped being worth holding.
Burns's Reformation teleplay opens on two young dealers finding a body they were not meant to find, and closes with a man being made to give up an address.
Christine Moore directed Reformation, in which Brother Mouzone returns to Baltimore and takes Dante, and Soft Eyes two seasons later — her only two episodes of the series.
Ed Burns wrote the teleplay of Alliances, drawing on his own years teaching for the material about the boys outside the classroom.

Gloria Muzio directed Lessons, staging the scene in which a detective takes his own young sons to a market and has them follow a drug organisation's second in command through the stalls to read his car number plate.
Steve Shill directed Undertow, staging the loss of Ziggy Sobotka's Camaro to men who will not be argued with as the humiliation from which the rest of his season follows.
Burns's Undertow teleplay follows a man discovering that the people paying him will not meet him, and a boy discovering that the people he wants to impress will simply take his car.
Simon's Hot Shots teleplay sends two detectives to Philadelphia to interview a ship's crew, the unglamorous canvass that putting names to thirteen bodies actually requires.

Dickerson shoots the community meeting as a single wide room of faces, holding on the residents rather than cutting to the major who is telling them he cannot promise them anything — so the scene belongs to the people being told, not the man doing the telling.

Pelecanos's teleplay is where the experiment acquires its name: a police major has quietly stopped arresting anyone selling drugs in three abandoned blocks, and a patrolman sneers that his commander has built an Amsterdam in West Baltimore. The corner dealers mangle it into Hamsterdam, and the name sticks city-wide.

Platt directed Alliances, in which a heroin addict who informs for the police finds the teenage boy living with him selling drugs on a corner instead of attending school, and is beaten in public by the boy's customer for interrupting the sale.
Ernest Dickerson directed Unconfirmed Reports, cutting between a detective staging a corpse and an addict following a stranger through a recovery meeting.
Holland directed React Quotes, cutting between a detective inventing a caller and a reporter inventing the call — two fabrications built in the same hour without either man knowing of the other.
Seith Mann directed The Dickensian Aspect, following an injured Omar Little through a city where every crew is looking for him and none of them finds him.
Joe Chappelle directed Late Editions, staging the vacant-lot killing in which a boy who was recruited at thirteen shoots the woman who recruited him.
Simon broke Ebb Tide with Ed Burns around a single image: a can left too long on the pier with thirteen women dead inside it, and a detective exiled to the marine unit who cannot leave it alone.

Burns shares the Ebb Tide story with Simon; the season's premise — that the port's paperwork is where the crime actually lives — is the kind of institutional detail he had spent two decades working around.

Simon broke Hot Shots with Burns; its other half is the Sobotkas' own enterprise starting up — a container of digital cameras stolen and sold on, entirely separate from the arrangement Frank thinks he controls.
Burns co-broke Hot Shots; its title is police slang for a deliberately poisoned package, the trade's own way of removing a witness.
Simon broke Hard Cases with Joy Lusco around Bunk Moreland's fourteen open files, and the arithmetic that makes a name-less body worth less than a clearance.
Lusco broke Hard Cases with Simon; her half is Beadie Russell being seconded to a homicide investigation several ranks above anything she has done.
Simon broke Undertow with Burns on the metaphor of its title: Frank Sobotka's per-container fee is tripled and he is still refused the meeting he wants.
Burns wrote Undertow's teleplay from the story he broke with Simon, in which Ziggy Sobotka loses his Camaro to East Side dealers and Nick cannot buy it back.
Simon and Rafael Alvarez broke Backwash around the union computer: Bunk and Beadie Russell bring Landsman what a cloned terminal can show about vanished containers.
Alvarez, a former Sun reporter who had worked the waterfront beat, shares the Backwash story and wrote its teleplay — the episode in which Ziggy Sobotka shoots George Glekas.

Simon broke Storm Warnings with Burns at the point where two separate investigations — one into smuggling through the port, one into a West Baltimore drug war — turn out to be the same case, with the police still weeks behind understanding it.

Burns's half of this story is the port case closing on people who have already been warned — the specific frustration of building something for months against a target with better information than you have.
Simon broke Bad Dreams with Pelecanos around a man who has already decided to inform and spends the day doing ordinary union business anyway.
Pelecanos broke Bad Dreams with Simon; their structure puts the federal approach, the union's collapse and the Greek's decision on the same afternoon.

Simon broke this episode with Pelecanos around a police major who has privately concluded that thirty years of drug arrests changed nothing, and has quietly stopped making them in three abandoned blocks of his district — an unauthorised experiment his superiors have not yet discovered.

Pelecanos wrote Hamsterdam from the story he broke with Simon; the free zones take their name from Officer Colicchio comparing them to Amsterdam's drug laws — the same officer who calls them moral midgetry — which is how policy gets named on a corner.
Simon and Burns broke Straight and True around Cutty Wise's first weeks out, in which the organisation expects him back and the city offers him lawn work.
Burns wrote the Straight and True teleplay from their joint story, following Colvin's zones from an idea into an operation his own officers have to run.
Simon broke Homecoming with Rafael Alvarez around two men coming back to work they no longer fit: Avon Barksdale out of prison, and Cutty Wise out of a landscaping crew.

Alvarez, who had reported on Baltimore's waterfront for the Sun before writing for the series, shares this story with Simon and wrote its teleplay — bringing to it the working detail of a city where the honest routes out of poverty have already closed.
Simon broke Back Burners with Joy Lusco; his half is Avon Barksdale's tour of corners under police pressure, conducted as though the ground still meant what it once did.
Lusco shares the Back Burners story with Simon; her half is Marlo Stanfield, retail closed and wholesaling instead, doing what Stringer Bell had argued for and Avon refused.
Simon broke Reformation with Burns; the episode's function is assembly — putting Omar Little and Brother Mouzone in the same room a fortnight before Stringer Bell is killed.
Burns wrote Reformation from their joint story, the episode that assembles the alliance which kills Stringer Bell one hour later.
Burns broke Know Your Place with Kia Corthron; the episode's other half is Poot Carr's release into a West Baltimore where the Barksdale organisation no longer exists.

Corthron shares the story credit with Burns; the material about a test-preparation fortnight standing in for education came from Burns's own classroom years, and she built the boys' four separate ceilings around it.
Burns broke Home Rooms with Richard Price, drawing on his own years teaching for Prez's first days in front of a class he cannot command.
Price broke Home Rooms with Burns, the second of the school season's opening hours, in which the classroom's rules turn out to be nothing like the corner's.
Burns broke Soft Eyes with David Mills, drawing the classroom material from his own years teaching after twenty in the department, and Mills taking the newsroom and homicide threads.
Mills wrote Soft Eyes from his story with Burns; Detective Norris works what turns out to be the murder of a state's witness while Prez scrapes gum off desks.
Burns broke Refugees with Lehane; the school-year material is drawn directly from his own years teaching in Baltimore classrooms.
Lehane broke Refugees with Burns, the middle of his three scripts — one per season from the third on — and the one that puts a research grant in front of Bunny Colvin.
Burns broke Margin of Error with Overmyer around a primary decided by a split black vote, and the arithmetic Carcetti had counted on from the beginning.
Overmyer wrote Margin of Error from his story with Burns; Sydnor and Herc watch Marlo Stanfield meet his lieutenants while the city votes.
Simon broke Unconfirmed Reports with Zorzi, whose Sun years supplied the newsroom half — a buy-out list circulating while a reporter works out what he can get away with.
Zorzi brought to this story the thing he had actually lived: what a newsroom feels like when the people who know the city are being bought out, and the ones left cannot check what they are printing.
Simon and David Mills broke React Quotes around two inventions feeding each other: McNulty gives his imaginary killer a telephone, and a reporter supplies the calls.
Mills broke React Quotes with Simon; his own years in newsrooms supplied the mechanics of how an unverifiable claim gets into print once an editor above the city desk wants it there.
The phrase in the title came from Simon's own editor at the Sun, and he broke the episode with Burns around what a newsroom does when asked for a narrative it has not reported.
Burns's half of The Dickensian Aspect is the police side: Bunk working the vacant-house files by the book while an injured Omar Little moves around a city hunting for him.
Simon handed Pelecanos the penultimate episode for the last time in Late Editions, keeping to the pattern established with Cleaning Up five years earlier.
Pelecanos broke Late Editions with Simon — the last of his penultimate episodes, and the one that finally puts handcuffs on the organisation the series has spent two seasons failing to reach.
Simon broke All Due Respect with Price; the hour turns on a district commander deciding that what he has been ordered to do has never once worked.
Price broke All Due Respect with Simon, his first work on the series, introducing the Stanfield organisation as a crew that does not negotiate and cannot be reasoned with.
Burns broke Corner Boys with Richard Price, using Colvin's separate classroom to ask the boys how a corner actually works and getting a more sophisticated answer than the curriculum contains.
Price broke Corner Boys with Burns, drawing on the years Burns spent teaching for a scene in which the adults stop instructing and start listening.
Simon and Burns broke Alliances around the last time the six neighbourhood boys are shown together, before the season separates them for good.
Burns wrote Alliances from their joint story; it is the last episode to show all six neighbourhood boys — the four principals with Donut and Kenard — in one group.
Scott Kecken co-directed Not for Attribution, the pair having previously made We Are Arabbers, a documentary about Baltimore's horse-drawn produce vendors.
Joy Lusco Kecken had written for the first three seasons and returned to the last as a director; Not for Attribution is the only episode she directed, shared with her husband.
Dominic West directed Took while starring in it, the episode in which McNulty phones Templeton as the invented killer and Clay Davis talks a jury round in open court.
Simon broke Not for Attribution with Chris Collins around a newsroom thinning itself by buy-outs while a reporter manufactures the quote that decides a police commissioner's succession.
Collins shares the Not for Attribution story with Simon, his first credit after coming up as a staff writer on the fourth season.
Collins's teleplay for Not for Attribution has Butchie killed in his own bar and a newsroom offered buy-outs in the same hour, two institutions losing the people who held them together.
Simon broke Took with Richard Price around two performances of invention in one hour: McNulty's voice-modulated call to a reporter, and Clay Davis testifying his way to an acquittal.
Price broke Took with Simon and wrote it; Simon's note on the courtroom material was that a real prosecutor would have objected far more often than Bond does.

Simon broke this early episode with Burns around a buy-and-bust — police buying drugs undercover then immediately arresting the seller — which nets a low-level dealer, teaches the investigators nothing they did not know, and costs them a week of surveillance.
