Burns co-broke this episode around the argument he lost repeatedly as a real detective: whether to keep making quick street arrests that look like progress, or spend months building a case against the people actually running the organisation. The department always wants the arrests.

Simon and Burns broke One Arrest around the cost of appearing to succeed: making arrests off the wiretap tells the drug organisation exactly how closely it is being listened to, so the visible win destroys the invisible one.
Burns co-broke One Arrest, in which Rawls gives Santangelo the choice between clearing a case by the day's end and informing on McNulty.
Simon and Burns broke Game Day as the season's one deliberate pause — an episode in which the investigation stops for a day and the trade's own calendar takes over.

Burns co-broke Game Day, in which a detective redirects two junior officers away from watching street corners and onto the drug organisation's money instead — bank records, property deeds, front companies — which is the investigative method the rest of the series runs on.
Simon and Burns broke The Hunt around what a department does when one of its own is shot: city-wide raids, dope on the table, and a case worth less at the end than at the beginning.
Burns co-broke The Hunt, in which Bubbles unwittingly implicates himself in the shooting of the detective he informs for.
Simon broke Cleaning Up with Burns; the arithmetic in it is Stringer Bell's — a boy who has spoken to police is a cost, and the cheapest way to settle it is to send his own friends.
Burns co-broke Cleaning Up, in which Stringer Bell collects the crew's pagers, replaces them with phones, and rules that business is henceforth discussed face to face.
Simon and Burns broke the first season finale so that everyone in the organisation who could be reached takes a plea, and the man the case was built against takes seven years.

Burns shares the Sentencing story with Simon; the arithmetic that ends the season — a soldier accepting a list of murders so the organisation survives — is the outcome he watched real cases reach for twenty years.
Simon broke Duck and Cover with Pelecanos around McNulty's collapse: a failed reconciliation, a drunken crash, and a request to be let back onto murders.
Pelecanos broke Duck and Cover with Simon and wrote it; the episode was the second most watched programme on American premium cable in its debut week.

Simon broke Dead Soldiers with Lehane; its title refers both to the empty drug vials littering the streets and to the people killed in it, as a war between rival dealers empties corners that the police have not yet noticed are changing hands.
Lehane broke Dead Soldiers with Simon and wrote it; the eulogy he gives Jay Landsman is the closest the series comes to stating what it thinks of the men who do this work.
Simon broke Moral Midgetry with Price; his half is the Western District command discovering that it can no longer claim not to know what Colvin is running.
Price broke Moral Midgetry with Simon; the title is Officer Colicchio's verdict on the tolerated zones, delivered while he polices them.
Simon broke Boys of Summer with Burns; its structure is four separate summers running in parallel that the first day of term will end simultaneously.

Burns co-broke the fourth season's opening from the side he knew: what a Baltimore classroom is like in the weeks before the children arrive, and how little of what happens there is decided by the teacher.
Burns broke Unto Others with Zorzi; his half is the bounty Marlo Stanfield has placed reaching inside a prison, and what a man does when he learns of it.
Zorzi shares the Unto Others story with Burns; the City Hall material — a new mayor discovering what he has inherited — comes from the beat Zorzi covered at the Sun.
Simon and Burns broke A New Day around a new mayor meeting what a predecessor had called his first bowl of shit, and a homicide unit asked what it wants and answering: a pay rise.
Burns broke A New Day with Simon and wrote its teleplay; the classroom material comes from his own years teaching in Baltimore schools after twenty years as a police detective.
Burns broke the episode with Pelecanos; his half is Prez failing to keep Dukie Weems out of a high school that will do none of what Tilghman did for him.
Pelecanos shares the That's Got His Own story with Burns; the fire at Randy Wagstaff's foster home is the season's irreversible act, and it happens to the boy who had least to do with any of it.

Simon and Burns broke Transitions around what an institution does when it replaces someone: each of the hour's departures is arranged by people who benefit, and each vacancy is filled within days by a figure the audience already distrusts.
Burns broke Transitions with Simon and wrote its teleplay; it took the series' only Directors Guild award, for Dan Attias.
Simon is one of four writers credited jointly on All Prologue, the only episode of sixty without the usual story-and-teleplay split.
Burns shares the four-way credit with Simon, Joy Kecken and Rafael Alvarez; the prison book-group scene in which D'Angelo reads Gatsby against his own life is the episode's centre.
Joy Kecken shares the four-way writing credit on All Prologue, one of two episodes she is credited on before returning to the series as a director.
Rafael Alvarez shares the All Prologue credit; a former Sun waterfront reporter, he wrote or co-wrote three of the docks season's episodes.

Simon broke Stray Rounds with Burns around a bullet that goes through a wall and kills a child indoors — a death that belongs to nobody in the trade and is investigated as though it belonged to everybody.

Burns co-broke Stray Rounds; his contribution is what a wiretap sounds like when the target has been warned — coded calls, meetings moved without notice, and investigators listening to people who know they are listening.

David Simon and George Pelecanos approached Richard Price at a Washington reading and recruited him to the writing staff; he wrote five episodes between 2004 and 2008 after two seasons of reviewers comparing the show to his novel Clockers.

Rafael Alvarez knew David Simon from the Baltimore Sun and joined the writing staff with something none of the other novelists had: years of working knowledge of the waterfront, its unions and its paperwork.
William F. Zorzi covered Maryland politics at the Baltimore Sun alongside David Simon, and supplied the City Hall material of the later seasons from that beat.

Overmyer, a playwright who had worked with Simon years earlier on the NBC police series Homicide: Life on the Street, wrote two episodes of The Wire's fourth season and then co-created Treme with Simon — a drama about musicians in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina.
Nina Kostroff Noble is David Simon's producing partner at Blown Deadline Productions, the company through which every Simon television project since The Corner has been made.

Blown Deadline Productions is Simon's own company and the vehicle through which The Wire and every project he has made since has been produced — almost all of them for HBO, and almost all of them run with the same producing partner and much of the same Baltimore crew.
Michael K. Williams met Felicia Pearson in a Baltimore club and brought her to the production, which cast her as a version of herself under her own name.

The federal prosecution of the Gun Trace Task Force is the subject We Own This City dramatises, a real Baltimore plainclothes unit robbing the people it policed twenty years after The Wire fictionalised the department.
Denise Francine Boyd is one of the central figures whose year The Corner reports and dramatises, under her own name; she came out of addiction afterwards to work as a counsellor in the city.

Delaney Williams plays a sergeant carrying the name and manner of the real Baltimore homicide detective Jay Landsman, whom Simon had written about in Homicide and who appears on the series himself as a different officer.

Kate Sanford edited across all five seasons of The Wire, the only cutter to work on every year of it, and the editing is where the show's refusal to guide an audience actually happens — scenes held past the point another drama would cut, and no reaction shot inserted to tell the viewer what to feel.

Sanford had cut episodes for four years before this one, and what the guild recognised was restraint: no reaction shots inserted to explain the boys to the audience, and scenes allowed to run past the point another drama would have cut away.
The American Cinema Editors gave their 2007 award for best edited one-hour series to Kate Sanford for Boys of Summer — one of very few individual industry awards anyone on The Wire received.
Sanford followed David Simon to Treme, his New Orleans series, and won a second American Cinema Editors award for its episode Do You Know What It Means.

Peroni came to television having spent her career on features, and cut for The Wire in the years when its method was still being set — one of several people the production drew from film rather than from episodic TV, which is part of why it does not look or move like the drama around it.

Peroni had cut episodes of the first two seasons, bringing the sensibility she built across eight films with Robert Altman — long takes, overlapping talk, no simplifying a scene for the viewer. She died in August 2004, aged 51, weeks before the third season went to air, and the production dedicated Back Burners to her memory.
Thom Zimny edited episodes of the first three seasons, including the hour that shares the series' title, in which the wiretap finally goes live after six episodes of legal groundwork.

Eagle Egilsson shot seven episodes of the third season — the year that opens on the demolition of the high-rise housing blocks and runs an unauthorised police experiment through three abandoned streets.

Russell Lee Fine photographed eighteen episodes between 2006 and 2008, more than any other cinematographer on the series, which makes the look of the school season and the final newspaper season substantially his.

The 2014 high-definition rescan of The Wire reopened a question the series had never had to answer: what shape it was meant to be. Recomposing sixty episodes from 4:3 to 16:9 meant cropping frames its directors had approved, and the argument set the preferences of the people who made it against the screens people now watch it on.

The framing at issue in the remaster is the one Uta Briesewitz set in the first season and the later cinematographers maintained: available light, a static or slow camera, and a composition that does not tell the viewer where to look.

The remaster is a direct consequence of the delayed audience: a series whose viewers mostly arrived years after broadcast, on laptops and widescreen televisions, was reshaped to fit the screens they were using rather than the ones it was made for.

Reputation is what made the rescan worth doing — HBO went back to 8,000 reels of negative for a series that had never drawn an audience while it aired, because by 2014 it was being called one of the best ever made and had an indefinite commercial life ahead of it.

Two actors from the fifth season's newsroom storyline met again on Spotlight: Tom McCarthy, who played the Baltimore Sun reporter who invents his sources, directed the film, and cast Neal Huff — the mayor's chief of staff in The Wire — as one of the abuse survivors whose account the Boston Globe's reporters actually verify.

sg_baltimore.title: The Wire: The World of Baltimore

the_detail.name: The Major Crimes Unit
the_detail.desc: The special investigative unit at the centre of the series, created under protest after a judge telephones the deputy commissioner. Because no commander wants to lose good officers to it, each unit sends the people it would rather be rid of — which is how it acquires a detective exiled for thirteen years to the pawn shop unit and another banned from street duty. It is repeatedly disbanded, reconstituted, and handed to commanders instructed to dismantle it, and rebuilt whenever the department has no other answer.

barksdale_org.name: The Barksdale Organisation
barksdale_org.desc: The West Baltimore drug organisation the first three seasons are built around, run by Avon Barksdale and his business partner Stringer Bell. Its wealth rests on holding two kinds of ground: the high-rise public housing towers, where selling is most profitable, and a low-rise courtyard of flats used for the people and business it wants out of sight. It is destroyed less by police than by the argument between its two leaders over whether a drug operation should behave like an army or a company.

stanfield_org.name: The Stanfield Organisation
stanfield_org.desc: The drug crew that takes West Baltimore from the older Barksdale organisation in the fourth and fifth seasons. Its distinguishing practice is concealment: victims are wrapped in plastic, sealed inside boarded-up empty houses with quicklime and the boards nailed back, so that the killings never enter the city's murder statistics and the police have no bodies to investigate. When detectives finally open the houses, every recovery becomes a new unsolved murder on their own record.

new_day_coop.name: The New Day Co-Operative
new_day_coop.desc: The drug co-operative founded on Proposition Joe's arrangement with Stringer Bell, in which the city's crews share a single high-grade supply and settle disputes by discussion rather than shooting. Marlo Stanfield joins it, takes its connection and destroys it.

greek_organisation.name: The Greek's Organisation
greek_organisation.desc: The importing network at the Port of Baltimore, which never sells on a street corner: it brings heroin in by container and wholesales it to the crews who do. What defeats every attempt to prosecute it is structural — no principal handles goods or money, business is conducted through intermediaries in public places, and personnel are replaced rather than defended. When the second season's investigation finally closes, it has charged dock workers and nobody above them.

local_1514.name: IBS Local 1514
local_1514.desc: The stevedores' union branch at the Port of Baltimore, whose members hold cards but cannot get enough shifts because too few ships call. Its predicament is the second season's subject: a union with no work to distribute, spending money it does not have on political influence, and dissolved by the end after re-electing a dead man as treasurer in defiance of federal warnings.

omar_crew.name: Omar Little's Crew
omar_crew.desc: The small, changing group of robbers Omar Little assembles to hold up drug crews. They work to a rule he sets and enforces — nobody outside the drug trade is ever harmed — which is what lets them operate in neighbourhoods that would otherwise give them up. Its members are steadily killed or driven out by the cost of robbing organisations that can afford to hunt them.

jimmy_mcnulty.name: Jimmy McNulty
jimmy_mcnulty.desc: A Baltimore homicide detective who, in the first episode, goes over his commanders' heads to complain privately to a judge that the department is not investigating a drug organisation's murders. The judge's phone call forces the police to create the special unit the series follows. McNulty is a gifted investigator, a heavy drinker and incapable of obeying an order he disagrees with; by the final season he has invented a fictional serial killer preying on homeless men, purely to unlock the overtime and wiretap money his real case is denied, and is quietly forced out when it is discovered.

bunk_moreland.name: Bunk Moreland
bunk_moreland.desc: A Baltimore homicide detective who works cases slowly and by the book, drinks heavily, and is both the closest friend and the most consistent critic of Jimmy McNulty, the detective whose insubordination drives the series. When McNulty invents a serial killer to unlock funding, Bunk refuses on principle to have anything to do with it.

lester_freamon.name: Lester Freamon
lester_freamon.desc: A detective who spent thirteen years and four months exiled to the pawn shop unit — a dead-end posting given to officers who have annoyed a commander — and who turns out, once returned to real work, to be the best investigator in the department. His method is to follow money and paperwork rather than make arrests, and it produces both the case against the Barksdale drug organisation and, years later, the discovery of murder victims sealed inside boarded-up empty houses.

kima_greggs.name: Kima Greggs
kima_greggs.desc: A narcotics detective assigned to the original special unit, shot and badly wounded in the first season during an undercover drug buy that had been rushed by pressure from above. She returns to the work rather than take a desk, later transfers to homicide, and is the officer who eventually reports McNulty's invented serial killer to their commander — the one person in the unit who will not let the fraud stand.

cedric_daniels.name: Cedric Daniels
cedric_daniels.desc: The lieutenant put in charge of the special investigative unit because his superiors expect him to produce a quick, shallow case and close it. Instead he protects his detectives' slow, methodical work for five years. He is vulnerable throughout because of unexplained money in his own past, which City Hall holds over him; promoted to police commissioner at the end, he resigns within months rather than falsify the city's crime statistics as the mayor requires.

rhonda_pearlman.name: Rhonda Pearlman
rhonda_pearlman.desc: The assistant state's attorney attached to the police investigation — the lawyer who must persuade a judge that there is enough evidence to authorise each wiretap, and who then has to make the resulting case survive a courtroom. She is also, for much of the series, in a relationship with the detective whose conduct most often threatens the cases she is defending; she is made a judge at the end.

ellis_carver.name: Ellis Carver
ellis_carver.desc: A police officer who comes up in the narcotics squad as a corner-clearing brawler, is loaned to the first special investigative unit, and is then sent to the Western District. There a major asks him to name one person living on the streets he has patrolled for years, and he cannot — the moment that changes how he works. He rises to sergeant and then lieutenant, and eventually reports a fellow officer for assaulting a teacher, knowing his own squad will call him a rat for it.

herc_hauk.name: Thomas Herc Hauk
herc_hauk.desc: A police officer whose instinct is always force and shortcuts, in a series about patient investigation. He loses a surveillance camera worth thousands of dollars, then invents an informant to justify a warrant; between them those two failures collapse the case against the city's biggest drug organisation. He leaves the police and goes to work for the defence lawyer who represents it.

prez.name: Roland Prez Pryzbylewski
prez.desc: A patrolman so dangerous with a weapon that his own commanders keep him off patrol duty — he blinds a boy in a stop and later kills a plainclothes colleague by mistake in a dark alley. Between those two acts he turns out to have an unexpected gift for reading codes, phone records and paper trails, and becomes the reason the wiretap works. After the shooting he resigns and becomes a middle-school mathematics teacher, where he recognises the school's manipulation of test scores as the same thing he watched police commanders do with crime figures.

leander_sydnor.name: Leander Sydnor
leander_sydnor.desc: A young detective brought into the special investigative unit for undercover work and trained in financial investigation by Lester Freamon, the unit's most methodical officer. The series' closing sequence casts him in the role his mentor and Jimmy McNulty had occupied — the detective going over his commanders' heads to a judge, so that the cycle restarts.

william_rawls.name: William Rawls
william_rawls.desc: A homicide commander and later deputy police commissioner, for whom the only measure that exists is the clearance rate — the proportion of murders officially closed. He runs Comstat, the department's statistics meetings, as public humiliations of the commanders whose numbers have slipped, and treats each new body primarily as a question of whose figures it will damage. He ends the series promoted to head the Maryland State Police, his reward for helping conceal a detective's fabricated serial killer rather than expose it.

ervin_burrell.name: Ervin Burrell
ervin_burrell.desc: The Baltimore police commissioner, whose hold on the job depends entirely on delivering acceptable crime figures to City Hall and who therefore obstructs any investigation likely to take years or embarrass a politician. When a new mayor needs someone to blame for figures that will not fall, Burrell is removed by a negotiated deal — a quiet exit in exchange for keeping what he knows to himself.

jay_landsman.name: Jay Landsman
jay_landsman.desc: The homicide sergeant who runs the squad's caseboard, on which open murders are written in red and closed ones in black. His decisions are governed by that board: he opposes opening the boarded-up houses where a drug crew has hidden its victims, because every body recovered is another red name he cannot turn black.

bunny_colvin.name: Bunny Colvin
bunny_colvin.desc: The police major commanding Baltimore's Western District, who after thirty years concludes that drug arrests have never once changed anything on his streets. Facing retirement, he quietly herds the whole trade into three abandoned blocks and instructs his officers not to make arrests there — an unauthorised experiment the corner boys nickname Hamsterdam. Violent crime in his district falls sharply; when it becomes public he is demoted on the day he retires. He later joins a university project working with the most disruptive schoolchildren.

beadie_russell.name: Beadie Russell
beadie_russell.desc: A port authority officer whose ordinary work is checking seals on shipping containers, and who opens one with a broken seal to find thirteen dead women inside. Untrained in murder investigation and several ranks below everyone she then works with, she proves better at the patient documentary side of it than the detectives do, and later becomes Jimmy McNulty's partner.

stan_valchek.name: Stanislaus Valchek
stan_valchek.desc: Commander of the Southeastern police district, whose feud with a union treasurer over a rival stained-glass window donated to their parish church is what causes the entire second-season investigation: he demands a detail be assigned to the union purely out of spite. He ends the series appointed police commissioner.

maurice_levy.name: Maurice Levy
maurice_levy.desc: Defence attorney and the drug trade's institutional memory, moving from the Barksdale organisation to the Stanfield one without a break. He employs Herc after the department is finished with him, and it is Herc's loose talk that lets Levy expose the illegal wiretap, dissolve the case, and trade Chris Partlow's life sentence and Monk's twenty years for Marlo Stanfield walking free.

judge_phelan.name: Judge Daniel Phelan
judge_phelan.desc: Circuit court judge who takes McNulty's off-the-record complaint about the Gant killing and telephones the deputy commissioner over the heads of everyone concerned, which is the single act that creates the detail. He signs its wiretap orders and extensions afterwards, and is candid that a case in the papers does his own re-election no harm at all.

ray_cole.name: Ray Cole
ray_cole.desc: Homicide detective of no great distinction and considerable decency, played by the show's own executive producer Robert Colesberry. He is written out with a wake at the squad's bar in season three, and the cases Landsman credits him with in the eulogy — a Mississippi extradition, an after-hours triple, the Fayette Street drug wars — are Colesberry's own producing credits.

avon_barksdale.name: Avon Barksdale
avon_barksdale.desc: The head of a West Baltimore drug organisation, who thinks of himself as a soldier rather than a businessman: what he wants is to hold territory and be respected on it, not to maximise profit. That instinct divides him from his own second in command, who would rather abandon the street corners and launder the money into property, and the two men end by arranging each other's destruction.

stringer_bell.name: Stringer Bell
stringer_bell.desc: Second in command of the Barksdale drug organisation, who tries to run it as a legitimate business: he takes economics classes at a community college, holds meetings by formal committee rules, and moves drug profits into property development. He is defeated in both directions at once — the developers he pays take his money and deliver nothing, and his own partner, who values territory and reputation over profit, eventually has him killed.

dangelo_barksdale.name: D'Angelo Barksdale
dangelo_barksdale.desc: Nephew of the drug kingpin Avon Barksdale, demoted to a low-rise housing courtyard after beating a murder charge too publicly. Unlike the men around him he cannot stop registering what the work costs other people, which makes him useless to the organisation and then a danger to it. Sentenced to twenty years, he begins to consider cooperating with police; Stringer Bell has him strangled in prison and the death arranged to look like suicide.

brianna_barksdale.name: Brianna Barksdale
brianna_barksdale.desc: Sister of the drug kingpin Avon Barksdale and mother of D'Angelo, the nephew who runs a low-rise corner for the family. She handles the organisation's money and its family discipline — including persuading her own son to refuse a police cooperation deal and accept twenty years instead, a decision she is left to live with after he is killed in prison.

wee_bey_brice.name: Wee-Bey Brice
wee_bey_brice.desc: The Barksdale organisation's most prolific killer, who accepts a life sentence and confesses to a string of murders — including several he did not commit — so that the men above him survive. Years later, from prison, he overrules his own wife and gives their son away to a retired police officer, to keep the boy out of the trade.

de_londa_brice.name: De'Londa Brice
de_londa_brice.desc: Wife of the imprisoned enforcer Wee-Bey Brice and mother of Namond, one of the four schoolboys at the centre of the fourth season. She expects the drug organisation to keep paying her while her husband serves life, and pushes her plainly unsuited son toward selling drugs to replace that income — until Wee-Bey overrules her from prison and gives the boy away to a retired police officer.

bodie_broadus.name: Bodie Broadus
bodie_broadus.desc: A corner dealer who appears in the first episode as teenage muscle and rises over five years to run a corner of his own. He believes the drug trade has rules and keeps them even when nobody else does — which is why, when a newer and more ruthless organisation takes over West Baltimore, he refuses to work on its terms and is shot on his own corner, the last soldier of a gang that no longer exists.

poot_carr.name: Poot Carr
poot_carr.desc: A low-rise corner dealer present from the first episode, who takes part in the killing of his closest friend on orders from above and is visibly diminished by it. He serves fifteen months in prison, returns to the corners under new management, and is last seen working in a shoe shop — the only member of the original crew to leave the drug trade alive and free.

wallace.name: Wallace
wallace.desc: A sixteen-year-old lookout for a West Baltimore drug crew, who lives in an abandoned flat and wakes and feeds a group of younger children there each morning before school. When he identifies a rival in a police surveillance photograph, the man is tortured to death, and Wallace — unable to live with his part in it — asks to leave the corner. Asking is treated as a threat: the crew's second in command, Stringer Bell, orders his death, and it is carried out by Bodie and Poot, the two boys he grew up beside.

slim_charles.name: Slim Charles
slim_charles.desc: An enforcer hired during a West Baltimore drug war who outlives every organisation that employs him, moving from the Barksdales to the city-wide dealers' co-operative. Consistently the most level-headed man in any room, he fires the last significant shot of the series and observes immediately afterwards that it was for nothing.

marlo_stanfield.name: Marlo Stanfield
marlo_stanfield.desc: A young drug boss who displaces the established Barksdale organisation in West Baltimore by refusing every convention the trade had run on — no truces, no negotiation, no tolerance of insult. What he wants is not money but that his name should frighten people, which is why an insult costs a life and a robbery of his card game becomes a season-long hunt. He walks free at the end when the case collapses, on condition he leave the trade permanently.

chris_partlow.name: Chris Partlow
chris_partlow.desc: Chief enforcer for the Stanfield drug organisation, a calm and methodical killer who developed the practice of sealing victims inside Baltimore's thousands of boarded-up empty row houses with quicklime, so that the deaths never appear in the city's murder figures at all. He departs from that method exactly once — beating a man to death by hand for personal reasons — and it is the forensic evidence from that scene that convicts him.

snoop.name: Snoop
snoop.desc: A young soldier for the Stanfield drug organisation, recruited and trained by its chief enforcer, who kills without visible emotion and buys the nail gun used to seal murder victims inside boarded-up empty houses. She is shot by Michael Lee, a teenager she had helped bring into the organisation, when he works out that she has been sent to kill him.

monk_metcalf.name: Monk Metcalf
monk_metcalf.desc: Stanfield lieutenant trusted with the organisation's money and its telephones, and therefore its weak point: Marlo Stanfield will not carry a traceable handset, so it is Monk's line the Major Crimes Unit finally gets up on, and Monk's twenty-year plea that Maurice Levy negotiates at the end.

o_dog.name: O-Dog
o_dog.desc: Stanfield soldier of no standing until the ambush on Bodie Broadus's corner stalls — Bodie having driven Chris Partlow and Snoop behind parked cars — and O-Dog walks up the pavement behind him and fires the two shots that finish it.

omar_little.name: Omar Little
omar_little.desc: A robber who makes his living holding up drug crews rather than dealing, working to a personal code that nobody outside the trade is ever harmed. He carries a shotgun, wears a long coat, whistles as he walks, refuses to swear and is openly gay — a combination that makes him the most feared and most quoted figure in the series. He is killed in a corner shop by a child with a handgun, and the murder is barely investigated.

brandon.name: Brandon Wright
brandon.desc: Omar Little's boyfriend and a member of the small crew that robs drug organisations with him. Caught by the Barksdale organisation after one such robbery, he is tortured for Omar's whereabouts, gives up nothing, and his mutilated body is left displayed in the low-rise courtyard where the crew's youngest members will have to walk past it.

renaldo.name: Renaldo
renaldo.desc: Omar Little's partner in the later seasons, who robs with him, drives for him, and retires with him to Puerto Rico. His refusal to return to Baltimore when Omar goes back to avenge a friend's killing leaves Omar working alone, wounded and unsupported through the weeks before he is shot dead in a corner shop.

brother_mouzone.name: Brother Mouzone
brother_mouzone.desc: A fastidious, bow-tied enforcer brought down from New York to protect the Barksdale organisation's high-rise territory, who reads intently between acts of violence and speaks with formal politeness. Stringer Bell arranges for him to be shot by falsely telling Omar Little that Mouzone was responsible for the death of Omar's partner; when both men work out who lied to them, they join forces to kill Stringer.

butchie.name: Butchie
butchie.desc: A blind bar owner in East Baltimore who acts as banker and adviser to the robber Omar Little, holding his money and passing his messages while Omar is away. Marlo Stanfield, the drug boss Omar has been robbing, has Butchie tortured and killed purely as bait, knowing it is the one thing certain to bring Omar back to the city.

kenard.name: Kenard
kenard.desc: A child from the West Baltimore corners, first seen playing at being Omar Little in an alley game with other boys. Years later, unimpressed by the limping, ageing man the legend has become, he follows Omar into a corner shop and shoots him dead — the most feared figure in the city killed by someone too young for anyone in the trade to have considered him a risk.

proposition_joe.name: Proposition Joe
proposition_joe.desc: The East Baltimore drug wholesaler who treats the business as wholesaling rather than war, and whose private line to the importers bringing heroin through the port makes him the source every crew in the city depends on. His fatal mistake is teaching his methods to Marlo Stanfield, who takes the connection for himself and has Joe shot in his own kitchen.

cheese_wagstaff.name: Cheese Wagstaff
cheese_wagstaff.desc: A drug dealer working for his uncle, the East Baltimore boss Proposition Joe, whose disloyalty escalates across the series from betraying his own crew to giving up his uncle's whereabouts to a rival. He is shot mid-sentence at the drug co-operative's final meeting, immediately after arguing that sentiment has no place in business.

frank_sobotka.name: Frank Sobotka
frank_sobotka.desc: Secretary-treasurer of a stevedores' union local whose members hold cards for work that no longer exists, because too few ships call at the port to fill the shifts. His answer is political: sell the smugglers safe passage for their containers and spend the money on lobbyists in Annapolis who might reopen the grain pier and dredge the canal. He takes nothing for himself, which is the distinction the season turns on — and it does not save him or the union, which is dissolved after his death.

nick_sobotka.name: Nick Sobotka
nick_sobotka.desc: The union treasurer's nephew, who has a card and cannot get enough shifts off it to keep a flat, and who collects the smuggled container serial numbers from Vondas at the diner. He moves stolen cameras and then drugs, enters witness protection when the case collapses, and reappears in the final season at the dedication of the port memorial his uncle never lived to see.

ziggy_sobotka.name: Ziggy Sobotka
ziggy_sobotka.desc: The union treasurer's son, a checker for Local 1514 whose bids for respect run from lighting a cigarette with a hundred-dollar bill in a bar full of men who have no work to parading a pet duck he feeds whisky until it dies. Cheated once too often by George Glekas, he shoots him dead behind the warehouse counter and ends the series in prison.

the_greek.name: The Greek
the_greek.desc: The unnamed head of the operation smuggling contraband through the Port of Baltimore, who is protected twice over: an FBI agent values him as a source on terrorism and repays him with warnings, and he conducts no business himself, so that police photographing his meetings never establish which man at the table he is. He walks out of the second season untouched, and is still supplying the city at the end of the series.

vondas.name: Vondas
vondas.desc: Spiros Vondopoulos, underboss of a smuggling operation that runs well beyond Baltimore, who does all of its talking so that the man at the top need never appear. He runs his business from a booth in a waterfront diner, hands Nick Sobotka the serial numbers of the containers to lose from the port computer, and is still supplying the city when the series ends.

sergei_malatov.name: Sergei Malatov
sergei_malatov.desc: Enforcer in the Greek's organisation who collects and enforces, is identified off the port wiretap and taken in the sweep, and is one of the few people connected to the Greek that the case ever manages to charge. He gives up nobody above him.

tommy_carcetti.name: Tommy Carcetti
tommy_carcetti.desc: A white city councilman who wins the mayoralty of a majority-black Baltimore by encouraging a second black candidate to run and split the vote against the incumbent. He inherits a school-system deficit his predecessor had concealed, and then refuses the state governor's offer to cover it, because accepting money from a rival party's governor would damage his own planned run for that office. He becomes governor in the closing montage; the schools never get the money.

clarence_royce.name: Clarence Royce
clarence_royce.desc: Mayor of Baltimore, first seen presiding over the demolition of the Franklin Terrace towers as a demonstration of reform, and last seen in the fifth season making introductions for a lobbyist. He conceals the scale of the school system's deficit through the primary, loses to a challenger he never took seriously, and is the figure Carcetti inherits every unsolved problem from.

clay_davis.name: Clay Davis
clay_davis.desc: A Maryland state senator who takes money from property developers, drug dealers and his own constituents' campaign funds alike — including several hundred thousand dollars from Stringer Bell for political favours he never intends to deliver. Prosecuted in state court by a state's attorney chasing the publicity, he talks the jury round entirely and leaves the courthouse to applause, more untouchable than when he entered it.

norman_wilson.name: Norman Wilson
norman_wilson.desc: Tommy Carcetti's campaign manager and then senior adviser, a newspaperman before he was an operative. He is the aide sent to leak the Daniels story to the papers, and the one who tells Carcetti that leaving the governor's school money on the table is a decision about Annapolis rather than about Baltimore. Steintorf displaces him as the mayor's closest counsel in the final season.

odell_watkins.name: Odell Watkins
odell_watkins.desc: Veteran black state delegate and political king-maker who delivered his constituency for Clarence Royce until Royce ignored their joint witness-protection proposal and was found to be running Marla Daniels's opponent in her weak districts. He confronts Royce, sits out the primary, and then endorses Tommy Carcetti — the swing that decides it. His first counsel to the new mayor is that Ervin Burrell cannot simply be sacked in a majority-black city.

michael_steintorf.name: Michael Steintorf
michael_steintorf.desc: Tommy Carcetti's chief of staff, who displaces Norman Wilson as the mayor's primary adviser and exists to carry the instructions nobody wants written down — the demand for lower crime figures that Cedric Daniels resigns over, and the offer to Rawls of the state police superintendency in exchange for burying McNulty's fabrication.

michael_lee.name: Michael Lee
michael_lee.desc: The most capable and most guarded of four thirteen-year-olds the fourth season follows. He will not discuss his home with any adult who offers help, because the household contains the man who abused him and is now turning toward his younger brother. He takes a drug crew's protection on the condition that man is dealt with, and the debt binds him to the organisation for the rest of the series.

randy_wagstaff.name: Randy Wagstaff
randy_wagstaff.desc: Foster child who runs a sweet business from his school locker and, without understanding it, passes on the message that sets up Lex's murder. Confiding that to a teacher and then to Carver marks him as a snitch, his foster home is burned, and Carver drives him to a group home himself and cannot speak afterwards. Bunk finds him there in the fifth season, bigger, harder, and finished with talking to police.

namond_brice.name: Namond Brice
namond_brice.desc: The loud, soft-centred son of an imprisoned drug enforcer, and the boy among the fourth season's four schoolchildren least equipped for the life his mother expects him to take up. Moved into a separate classroom for the most disruptive pupils, he turns out — without an audience to perform for — to be articulate and observant. He is the only one of the four to get out, adopted by a retired police major.

dukie_weems.name: Dukie Weems
dukie_weems.desc: The gentlest and most academically able of the four boys whose thirteenth year the fourth season follows, from a household that sells his clothes for drug money; his teachers wash and feed him at school. Promoted into a high school by a system counting test scores rather than readiness, and able to hold neither school nor street work, he is last seen injecting heroin in a scrapyard.

cutty_wise.name: Cutty Wise
cutty_wise.desc: Dennis Wise, a legendary soldier finishing a fourteen-year sentence when Avon Barksdale reaches the same prison, whose nickname comes from the Jessup penitentiary known as the Cut. He goes out once for the organisation on release, cannot pull the trigger, tells Avon the game is not in him any more, and opens a boxing gym instead.

david_parenti.name: David Parenti
david_parenti.desc: A university researcher whose grant funds a separate classroom for a school's most disruptive thirteen-year-olds. He is steered toward a just-retired police major on the grounds that an academic studying children from the drug corners needs someone who has actually worked those streets, and the project survives only while it does not disturb the school's test averages.

gus_haynes.name: Gus Haynes
gus_haynes.desc: City editor of the Baltimore Sun: a reporter's editor who checks facts, knows the city and its people, and recognises invented quotes when he reads them. For insisting that a star reporter's sourcing be verified he is overruled by the executives above him and demoted to the copy desk.

scott_templeton.name: Scott Templeton
scott_templeton.desc: A Baltimore Sun reporter who invents sources, quotes and eventually telephone calls from a serial killer who does not exist. What makes him possible is that nobody above the city desk asks him to prove any of it; he is promoted, given a Pulitzer, and never caught, while the two colleagues who challenge him are moved off the story.

alma_gutierrez.name: Alma Gutierrez
alma_gutierrez.desc: A junior reporter at the Baltimore Sun who does the unglamorous work — night calls, door-knocks, checking things — while a colleague invents his quotes and wins a Pulitzer for them. She backs her city editor when he tries to stop it, and is transferred to a suburban bureau for having done so.

thomas_klebanow.name: Thomas Klebanow
thomas_klebanow.desc: Managing editor of the Baltimore Sun and the executive who handles the newsroom day to day for its out-of-town owners. He is the one who tells his city editor to stay collegial and cut back on the profanity, who overrules the doubts raised about a star reporter's sourcing, and who signs off on the buy-outs removing the paper's most experienced staff.

james_whiting.name: James C. Whiting III
james_whiting.desc: Executive editor of the Baltimore Sun, brought in from outside the city, whose enthusiasm for an ambitious prize-winning narrative about Baltimore outruns any appetite for checking whether it is true. He asks his newsroom for a Dickensian aspect — a human angle on poverty — rather than for reporting, and promotes the reporter who supplies it by invention.

bubbles.name: Bubbles
bubbles.desc: A heroin addict who survives by scavenging scrap metal and by informing for the police, whose knowledge of every corner in West Baltimore makes him more useful to detectives than most of their own equipment. He tries to save a teenage boy living with him and accidentally causes his death, which is what finally stops him using. He is one of the very few characters the series allows a hopeful ending.

johnny_weeks.name: Johnny Weeks
johnny_weeks.desc: Bubbles's closest friend and partner in petty theft, beaten nearly to death in the first episode for passing counterfeit money to a drug crew, and told in hospital afterwards that he is HIV positive. He refuses every attempt to get him clean, disapproves of Bubbles informing for the police, and dies of an overdose in an abandoned house inside the three blocks where police have stopped making arrests.

sherrod.name: Sherrod
sherrod.desc: Homeless teenager who last attended school regularly in the fifth grade at Steuart Hill and lives with Bubbles in a vacant room without electricity. Bubbles enrols him at Tilghman by posing as his uncle; Sherrod attends once, goes back to working a corner, and dies after drinking from a capsule Bubbles had doctored for the addict who had been robbing them both.

walon.name: Walon
walon.desc: A recovering heroin addict who sponsors others through Narcotics Anonymous — tattooed, plain-spoken, and one of very few people in the series offering help that is not conditional on something in return. He keeps turning up for Bubbles, the addict informant, across the years it takes him to stop using. Played by the singer-songwriter Steve Earle, himself in long-term recovery.

the_deacon.name: The Deacon
the_deacon.desc: Church elder and neighbourhood fixer who finds Cutty Wise work and then the money and paperwork for his gym, steers David Parenti's research grant toward Bunny Colvin, and tells Colvin, having walked through Hamsterdam, that he has built a great village of pain and left it unattended — the one verdict on the experiment Colvin takes seriously.

the_pit.name: The Pit
the_pit.desc: A low-rise housing courtyard in West Baltimore where the Barksdale drug organisation places whoever it has no better use for — a demoted nephew, two teenagers and a boy who sleeps in an abandoned flat. Much of the first season is spent here, at ground level, watching how a corner actually operates hour by hour.

franklin_terrace.name: The Franklin Terrace Towers
franklin_terrace.desc: The high-rise public housing towers that are the Barksdale organisation's most valuable territory and the reason most of its violence happens. Mayor Royce demolishes the 221 block at the opening of the third season as a demonstration of reform, which removes the ground the organisation stood on and scatters its trade into streets the police have never mapped.

hamsterdam.name: Hamsterdam
hamsterdam.desc: The nickname corner dealers give three abandoned blocks of the Western District where a police major quietly stops making arrests, in an unauthorised attempt to concentrate the drug trade away from residential streets. The name comes from an officer sneering that it is like Amsterdam. Violent crime in the district falls by fourteen per cent; the experiment is destroyed the moment City Hall learns of it, and the major's career with it.

port_of_baltimore.name: The Port of Baltimore
port_of_baltimore.desc: The city's working waterfront, with too few ships calling for the men on the union rolls and containers that can be lost from the computer for a fee. It is where Beadie Russell opens a can with a broken customs seal and finds thirteen dead women inside, and where Frank Sobotka spends the local's money lobbying to get the canal dredged and the grain pier reopened.

tilghman_middle.name: Edward J. Tilghman Middle School
tilghman_middle.desc: The West Baltimore middle school where the fourth season's four thirteen-year-olds are enrolled, and where a former police officer teaches mathematics. It is run on its standardised test results, to the point of suspending normal teaching for weeks of drilling, and its staff spend as much energy managing which children appear in the figures as teaching them.

sun_newsroom.name: The Baltimore Sun newsroom
sun_newsroom.desc: The fictionalised city desk of the Baltimore Sun, run down by successive buyouts while its executive editor asks for a sustained narrative with a Dickensian aspect and its managing editor asks the staff to do more with less. It is the room in which a reporter's invented quotes go unchecked because the people above the city desk want the story more than they want it verified.

cutty_gym.name: The Ricardo Hendrix Boxing Gym
cutty_gym.desc: A boxing gym opened in a derelict building by a former drug enforcer just out of a fourteen-year prison sentence, funded by a church elder who finds him the money and the paperwork. It is one of very few places in the series offering the neighbourhood's boys anything at all, and it can hold only some of them.

orlandos.name: Orlando's
orlandos.desc: The strip club the Barksdale organisation uses to hold and launder its money, and the first place the police investigation finds a paper trail into the organisation's finances rather than its street sales. A dancer who works there becomes the investigators' source inside it.

homicide_unit.name: The Homicide Unit
homicide_unit.desc: The Baltimore Police homicide squad, run on a board listing open murder cases in red and closed ones in black. Its governing measure is the clearance rate — the percentage moved from red to black — which shapes every decision the squad makes, including its resistance to opening cases likely to add names it cannot close.

states_attorney.name: The State's Attorney's Office
states_attorney.desc: The city prosecutor's office, whose judgement about which cases can actually be won shapes what the police are permitted to build — a wiretap is worth authorising only if the resulting case will stand up. It also takes the Clay Davis prosecution away from federal prosecutors and loses it in state court.

fbi_baltimore.name: The FBI
fbi_baltimore.desc: The Bureau's Baltimore presence, useful to the city police for surveillance equipment and financial analysis but unwilling to spend serious resources on a municipal drug case now that its priorities are terrorism and political corruption. When it does offer real help, the offer arrives attached to a corruption investigation into City Hall that the police cannot accept.

city_council.name: The Baltimore City Council
city_council.desc: Baltimore's elected city council, where Tommy Carcetti sits before running for mayor and over which Nerese Campbell presides as president. In a majority-black city with a white minority holding significant power, the council is where the racial and factional arithmetic of every appointment and budget is done in public — which is why a white councilman needs a second black candidate in the race before he can win.

school_system.name: The Baltimore City School System
school_system.desc: Baltimore's public schools, carrying a structural deficit the Royce administration concealed through the mayoral primary and Tommy Carcetti then refused the governor's money to close, because taking it would have cost him his own run for Annapolis. The year inside the buildings is organised around the standardised test, which Prez recognises on sight as the same operation he watched commanders run on crime figures.

narcotics_anonymous.name: Narcotics Anonymous
narcotics_anonymous.desc: The recovery fellowship whose meetings run through the series in church basements — and, notably in a show about institutions that fail people, the one institution shown working roughly as intended. It has no budget, no statistics to protect and nobody's career riding on it, which is the series' implicit explanation for why.

charles_marimow.name: Charles Marimow
charles_marimow.desc: A lieutenant installed over the special investigative unit as a favour to City Hall, with the understood purpose of ending its work. He dismantles the wiretap case, drives out the detectives who built it, and treats long-term investigation as insubordination — the department's standard method for closing an inquiry without appearing to close it.

ray_foerster.name: Raymond Foerster
ray_foerster.desc: The colonel commanding the criminal investigation division, one of very few senior officers who protects real casework from the pressure to produce quick statistics. He dies of cancer while still in post, and the squad lays him out in dress blues on the pool table at their bar.

michael_santangelo.name: Michael Santangelo
michael_santangelo.desc: A homicide detective pressured by his commanders into reporting on a colleague's movements in exchange for keeping his place in the squad, and transferred out regardless. Out of desperation on a case he cannot close, he consults a psychic — a scene the series uses to show how little the department's methods have to offer a detective without luck.

kenneth_dozerman.name: Kenneth Dozerman
kenneth_dozerman.desc: A young officer shot in the face during a buy-and-bust — police buying drugs undercover and arresting the seller on the spot — and whose service weapon is taken at the scene. The lost gun matters institutionally as much as the wound: a police weapon on the street is a scandal, so a senior detective spends weeks chasing it.

anthony_colicchio.name: Anthony Colicchio
anthony_colicchio.desc: An officer in the Western District drug squad who gives the arrest-free blocks the name that sticks, by sneering that his commander has built an Amsterdam. His appetite for confrontation escalates until he drags a substitute teacher out of a car in front of witnesses and is written up for it by his own sergeant.

michael_crutchfield.name: Michael Crutchfield
michael_crutchfield.desc: A homicide detective who catches several of the murders the series turns on, including Omar Little's, and works each at the pace the squad's only real measure rewards — the share of killings officially recorded as solved. A case unlikely to close quickly gets the effort that implies.

dennis_mello.name: Dennis Mello
dennis_mello.desc: The Western District lieutenant who is Bunny Colvin's administrative second, and one of the few officers let in on what his commander is actually doing — running an unauthorised arrest-free zone and concealing it from headquarters. He handles the daily business of it and keeps it off the paperwork.

vernon_holley.name: Vernon Holley
vernon_holley.desc: A Baltimore homicide detective, later a sergeant, remembered in the squad for having beaten a police informant during an interrogation after wrongly taking him for a shooter — then claiming the man attacked him first. He is also, late in the series, the detective who agrees to help reopen a murder already recorded as solved, knowing it will damage his own figures.

ilene_nathan.name: Ilene Nathan
ilene_nathan.desc: Assistant State's Attorney who tries the Barksdale organisation's murder cases, and who wins the Bird Hilton conviction by putting a self-declared robber of drug dealers on the stand in an ascot and trusting the jury to take him at his word.

rupert_bond.name: Rupert Bond
rupert_bond.desc: The State's Attorney who takes the prosecution of state senator Clay Davis out of federal hands and into state court, for the profile the case will bring him. He loses it: Davis testifies in his own defence, casts himself as a man redistributing money to the poor, and is acquitted to applause.

bird_hilton.name: Marquis Bird Hilton
bird_hilton.desc: Marquis Bird Hilton does the Barksdale organisation's witness work, shooting William Gant on a public street in daylight days after Gant testified. Omar Little identifies him from the stand, in an ascot, and the conviction is the one clean result the first season's case produces.

stinkum.name: Stinkum
stinkum.desc: Anton Stinkum Artis is being promoted to run a corner of his own as a reward for expanding the organisation's territory, and takes part in the killing of Brandon Wright along the way. Omar Little shoots him in an alley on the night he is due to collect the promotion.

savino_bratton.name: Savino Bratton
savino_bratton.desc: A Barksdale organisation soldier who drove the car for a killing, accepted three years in prison rather than name anyone above him, and came out to find the organisation gone and only the newer, more violent Stanfield crew still hiring — the fate of a man whose loyalty outlives the thing he was loyal to.

little_man.name: Little Man
little_man.desc: Wintell Little Man Royce is the soldier whose panic in Orlando Blocker's car puts a bullet in an undercover detective, and who is shot by Wee-Bey Brice within days because a crew that has hit a police officer cannot afford anyone who might talk.

fruit.name: Fruit
fruit.desc: A crew chief in the Stanfield drug organisation who runs corners around the Franklin Terrace high-rises and recruits sellers from the neighbourhood's schoolchildren. He is shot dead in a dispute with another dealer, one of the deaths that shows how little standing anyone below the top of that organisation actually has.

old_face_andre.name: Old Face Andre
old_face_andre.desc: A West Baltimore shopkeeper whose store launders money for the Stanfield drug organisation. Robbed by Omar Little, he is then used by the organisation's chief enforcer to frame Omar for a murder he did not commit — a woman shot dead inside Andre's own shop to make the story stand up — and is killed himself once the statement has served its purpose.

dante.name: Dante
dante.desc: Omar Little's partner in the second and third seasons, whose accidental shooting of Tosha Mitchell during a botched raid poisons the crew, and whose later capture by Brother Mouzone forces the meeting that ends Stringer Bell's life.

tosha_mitchell.name: Tosha Mitchell
tosha_mitchell.desc: Member of Omar Little's crew, killed by Dante's stray round during a daylight raid Omar had insisted on against her judgement. Her death splits the crew, drives Omar briefly out of Baltimore, and is the one occasion its rules fail to protect one of its own.

kimmy.name: Kimmy
kimmy.desc: A member of Omar Little's crew who robs drug organisations alongside him for years, and who was also Tosha Mitchell's partner — the two women having worked together before joining him. When Tosha is killed by a stray shot from their own side during a raid, Kimmy refuses to let it be smoothed over, settles the account herself, and then leaves on the plain ground that there are easier people in Baltimore to rob than the Barksdales.

horseface_pakusa.name: Thomas Horseface Pakusa
horseface_pakusa.desc: Thomas Pakusa, veteran stevedore who works the cranes and knows the port's paperwork well enough to lose a container from the computer, which is the service Frank Sobotka is actually selling. He escalates the feud with Major Valchek by walking into the Southeastern District car park, driving off with the police surveillance van, and having it photographed around the world.

george_glekas.name: George Double G Glekas
george_glekas.desc: The warehouse manager for the smuggling operation running goods through the Port of Baltimore, who handles stolen cargo coming off the docks and cheats the people bringing it to him. He underpays Ziggy Sobotka — the union treasurer's son, already a joke on the waterfront — once too often, and Ziggy shoots him dead behind his own counter.

nat_coxson.name: Nat Coxson
nat_coxson.desc: Stevedore and union officer in Local 1514, whose agreement Frank Sobotka needs to extend his own term because the local rotates its leadership between a white and a black officer each year. He asks Sobotka where the money in the envelope came from and does not get an answer, and after Sobotka's death is left carrying a campaign the local can no longer fund.

nerese_campbell.name: Nerese Campbell
nerese_campbell.desc: President of the Baltimore City Council, who brokers Ervin Burrell's quiet exit from the commissioner's office in exchange for his silence about Cedric Daniels's finances, and trades her influence with the ministers and the council for a promise of the mayoralty. She collects it when Carcetti leaves for Annapolis, and makes Stanislaus Valchek commissioner.

andy_krawczyk.name: Andy Krawczyk
andy_krawczyk.desc: A downtown property developer who takes money into his projects without asking where it came from — including several hundred thousand from a drug organisation's second in command, whose investment he pockets while delivering nothing. He prospers under every administration, and is standing on his own half-built site when that man is shot dead there.

theresa_dagostino.name: Theresa D'Agostino
theresa_dagostino.desc: A political consultant hired to run Tommy Carcetti's campaign for mayor, who treats the city as a set of numbers to be moved rather than a place, and briefly becomes the lover of the detective at the centre of the series. Her presence marks the point where the show's politics stop being local.

tony_gray.name: Tony Gray
tony_gray.desc: A black city councilman, friend and colleague of Tommy Carcetti, persuaded by Carcetti to run for mayor himself. The persuasion is a calculation: with two black candidates in the race the incumbent's vote splits three ways and a white councilman can win a majority-black city. Gray loses heavily and his political career ends with it.

grace_sampson.name: Grace Sampson
grace_sampson.desc: A teacher at the West Baltimore middle school where a former police officer takes a mathematics class in his first year out of the department. She explains to him what the school actually is — an institution measured on test results rather than on what its pupils learn — and what a teacher can and cannot change inside it.

marcia_donnelly.name: Marcia Donnelly
marcia_donnelly.desc: Assistant principal at the West Baltimore middle school the fourth season is set in, who runs the building with a realism that stops short of hope: she manages the test scores the system demands, knows exactly which children are beyond the school's reach, and keeps the place functioning on that basis.

donut.name: Donut
donut.desc: Neighbourhood boy too small to see over a steering wheel who steals cars for the pleasure of driving them, is arrested repeatedly by Carver and released every time because the system has no answer to a child that age. He drives past Bunny Colvin's suburban house at the end of the fourth season and exchanges a nod with Namond Brice, the last thread between Namond and the corner.

spider.name: Spider
spider.desc: Corner boy who becomes a regular at Cutty Wise's gym after befriending Justin and returns to the corner when Cutty sleeps with his mother. He deals with Sherrod, moves to Monk Metcalf's crew, works for Michael Lee on Bodie Broadus's old corner, and is running that corner himself by the final episode.

zenobia_dawson.name: Zenobia Dawson
zenobia_dawson.desc: Pupil at Tilghman moved out of the mainstream classroom into the separate room for the most disruptive children, where she objects during test practice to answering questions about asking a father for pocket money when she has neither, and gives the season its clearest statement of its argument: we got our thing, but it's just part of the big thing.

bug.name: Bug
bug.desc: Michael Lee's much younger half-brother, whose protection governs every decision Michael makes. Michael raises him rather than leave him with their addicted mother or the man returning to that household, accepts a drug crew's protection in exchange for having that man killed, and at the end puts Bug on a bus to relatives rather than keep him.

mike_fletcher.name: Mike Fletcher
mike_fletcher.desc: A Baltimore Sun reporter who does the work his colleague Scott Templeton only claims to do — spending weeks with a homeless veteran to produce the humane, reported story the paper's editors say they want. The paper prefers the invented version; in the closing sequence Templeton collects a Pulitzer and Fletcher takes over the city desk his own editor was removed from.

elena_mcnulty.name: Elena McNulty
elena_mcnulty.desc: Jimmy McNulty's estranged wife and the mother of his two sons, who fights him through the courts over custody and whose flat assessment of him to a lawyer is among the few outside verdicts on McNulty the series leaves unanswered.

marla_daniels.name: Marla Daniels
marla_daniels.desc: Cedric Daniels's wife, a lawyer who spends years pressing on him the advancement he refuses to chase and leaves the marriage over it. She then wins a city council seat and builds the political career herself, and it is her warning about the money in his past that shapes what Daniels is willing to accept from City Hall.

cheryl.name: Cheryl
cheryl.desc: The partner of Detective Kima Greggs, with whom she has a son by donor insemination. She wants the settled household the two had planned; Greggs, having been shot on duty, chooses to go back to dangerous street police work instead, and the family does not survive the choice.

shardene_innes.name: Shardene Innes
shardene_innes.desc: A dancer at the strip club the Barksdale organisation launders money through, and D'Angelo Barksdale's girlfriend, until detectives show her the body of a fellow dancer who died of an overdose at a crew party and was rolled in a carpet and dumped. She leaves him, works as the investigators' source inside the club — wearing a microphone, then mapping its floorplan so a camera can be hidden in the boss's office — and afterwards leaves that life entirely, enrolling in nursing school at the encouragement of the detective who recruited her, and living with him through the rest of the series.

donette.name: Donette
donette.desc: The mother of D'Angelo Barksdale's son, who takes up with his uncle's business partner Stringer Bell while D'Angelo is serving twenty years. Her account of D'Angelo's unhappiness in prison is what convinces Stringer that he may cooperate with police — and so, indirectly, what gets him killed.

jen_carcetti.name: Jen Carcetti
jen_carcetti.desc: Tommy Carcetti's wife, who works the mayoral campaign and its fundraising and understands earlier than her husband will admit that the mayoralty was only ever the step before Annapolis. She is the person to whom the private cost of his ambition is visible before it becomes visible to the city.

the_vacants.name: The Vacant Houses
the_vacants.desc: The thousands of boarded-up, abandoned row houses left across West Baltimore by decades of population loss. The Stanfield drug organisation uses them as a burial ground, wrapping victims in plastic, laying them inside and nailing the boards back with quicklime to speed decomposition — with the result that its killings never enter the city's murder statistics, because no body is ever found to be counted.

city_hall.name: Baltimore City Hall
city_hall.desc: The seat of the mayor and the council, where the school deficit is concealed through an election and then inherited, where a police commissioner is removed by a deal brokered with Nerese Campbell, and where Carcetti turns down the governor's money for the schools because accepting it would cost him the governor's job.

western_district.name: The Western District
western_district.desc: The police district covering most of West Baltimore's drug-selling streets, and the ground on which the series' best-known experiment is run: its commanding major, a year from retirement, quietly stops arresting anyone selling drugs in three abandoned blocks, to see whether concentrating the trade in one place reduces violence everywhere else. It does — and the experiment ends his career.

greek_diner.name: The Diner
greek_diner.desc: An unremarkable waterfront diner used as an office by the second in command of the port's smuggling operation. It is where a dock worker collects the numbers of the containers he is to lose from the computer, and where police surveillance photographs everyone at the table except the man they are actually looking for.

snot_boogie.name: Snot Boogie
snot_boogie.desc: The dead man in the series' opening scene, shot over a craps pot he had robbed every Friday for years. The witness's explanation that they let him play because this is America, said over the body, is the show's thesis delivered before anything else happens.

william_gant.name: William Gant
william_gant.desc: A working man who happened to witness a murder in the low-rise courtyard and did the thing the neighbourhood's whole code exists to prevent: he took the stand and told the truth about what he saw. D'Angelo Barksdale was acquitted anyway, after another witness recanted, and Gant was shot dead on a street corner days later. The department's initial position was that the killing had nothing to do with the trial — which is the refusal that sends a detective to a judge and brings the series' investigation into being.

orlando_blocker.name: Orlando Blocker
orlando_blocker.desc: The nominal owner of the strip club through which the Barksdale organisation launders its money — a figurehead whose name is on the licence because the real owners' cannot be. Caught trying to deal drugs on his own account, he agrees to work for the police, and is shot dead in a car during the undercover buy he arranges, alongside the detective sitting beside him.

fitzhugh.name: Terrance Fitz Fitzhugh
fitzhugh.desc: An FBI agent and Jimmy McNulty's drinking companion, who lends the city investigators federal equipment and expertise while explaining that the Bureau's resources have moved to terrorism. His own routine query about a Baltimore suspect reaches, without his knowing, the agent who is protecting that organisation — and so tips it off.

miss_anna.name: Miss Anna
miss_anna.desc: Randy Wagstaff's foster mother, who keeps a household with rules in it and pushes him to keep up his schoolwork. Ellis Carver returns the boy to her after questioning him and vouches for him; once the word snitch reaches the neighbourhood her house is firebombed, she is badly burned, and Randy goes to a group home.

josephine.name: Josephine
josephine.desc: Omar Little's grandmother, whom he escorts to church every Sunday morning — the one part of his life that has nothing to do with robbing drug crews, and the only family the series shows him keeping contact with. Barksdale soldiers open fire on the pair in the street; she is unhurt but loses her best hat, and the head of the organisation, angrier at the breach of custom than at the failure, makes the shooters pay for a new one.

sunday_truce.name: The Sunday Truce
sunday_truce.desc: The unwritten agreement between West Baltimore's drug organisations that no violence is done on a Sunday, observed by every crew in the city until Stringer Bell authorises a hit on Omar Little while he is walking his grandmother to church. Its breach is what ends Omar's decision to retire and restarts the war that kills Stringer.

devonne.name: Devonne
devonne.desc: Woman hired by Avon Barksdale to seduce Marlo Stanfield and draw him to a meeting where he can be killed. Marlo sleeps with her, grows suspicious, sends Chris Partlow to scout the second meeting, and afterwards shoots her himself — one of only two killings he carries out with his own hands.

louis_sobotka.name: Louis Sobotka
louis_sobotka.desc: Frank Sobotka's elder brother and Nick's father, a shipwright forced into early retirement who spends his days placing imaginary bets on horses in Delores's bar and refuses any part of the family's smuggling. When a warrant is issued for Nick, it is Louis who persuades him to turn himself in.

aimee.name: Aimee
aimee.desc: Nick Sobotka's partner and the mother of their daughter Ashley. Nick lives in his mother's basement and her overnight visits have to be concealed, which is the domestic version of the season's argument: without shifts on the docks there is no household to move into.

raylene_lee.name: Raylene Lee
raylene_lee.desc: Michael Lee's mother, an addict who sells the household's benefit money and welcomes back the man Michael will not have in the house. Michael takes over the raising of his half-brother Bug rather than leave him in her care, and refuses every adult who asks about his home.

devar_manigault.name: Devar Manigault
devar_manigault.desc: Raylene Lee's partner and Bug's father, who molested Michael Lee at around nine years old and, on returning from a prison term for an unrelated offence, began grooming his own son. Michael's acceptance of Chris Partlow's offer is conditional on Devar being dealt with; Chris beats him to death and leaves the DNA that eventually convicts him of the murder.

agent_koutris.name: Agent Koutris
agent_koutris.desc: An FBI agent based outside Baltimore who handles the head of the port smuggling ring as a registered informant on terrorism, and repays him with warnings. When a Baltimore agent queries one of the ring's members, Koutris seals the file and tells the organisation the police are closing in — which is why it walks away from the second season untouched.

links.details: Cedric Daniels commands the Major Crimes Unit from the moment it is grudgingly assembled, and spends five seasons protecting its work from the department above him.

McNulty is the reason the unit exists and the reason it keeps nearly being disbanded, and he treats every assignment within it as an argument to be won with his own commanders rather than with anyone on a corner.

Freamon arrives as the makeweight nobody wanted and within days is the person explaining to the rest of the unit that following the money is the case, a lesson the unit is still working from five seasons later.

Greggs supplies what the unit's slow paperwork cannot: people on the street who will talk to her. When she is shot during a rushed undercover drug buy, the unit loses both its best source of street information and, for months, its own sense that the case is worth what it costs.

Carver is sent to the new investigative unit from the narcotics squad with his partner, not because he is wanted but because his own commander is glad to lose him. He is later returned to the Western District, where a major asks him to name one person on the streets he has policed for years, and he cannot — the conversation that changes how he works for the rest of the series.
Herc's tenure in the unit is a sequence of shortcuts — a stolen camera, a fabricated informant, a leaked name — each of which costs the case more than it ever gained.

Prez, banned from street duty after blinding a boy and shooting a colleague, turns out to be the person who can read the Barksdale organisation's pager code, and the unit builds its first wiretap on his work.
Sydnor is borrowed from the auto squad for undercover work and stays because Lester Freamon teaches him the paper, and by the finale he has become the unit's next unmanageable investigator.

Pearlman writes the affidavits the unit's wiretaps stand on, and spends five seasons explaining to detectives which of their evidence a court will actually accept and which of it they obtained in a way she cannot defend.

Avon Barksdale holds the organisation together by force and family rather than paperwork, to the point that when Wee-Bey runs through the murders he is preparing to confess to, Avon cannot place several of them and has to be reminded who the victims were.

Stringer Bell runs the organisation's business by Robert's Rules of Order, with a minute-taker and a chair, so that co-op meetings dissolve into Shamrock telling a member the chair does not recognise his ass and Stringer closing with an instruction to adjourn theirs.

D'Angelo, the boss's nephew, is punished for beating a murder charge too publicly by being moved from the high-rise housing projects — the organisation's most profitable ground — down to a shabby low-rise courtyard with a smaller crew. His real problem is that he keeps noticing what the work costs the people around him, which makes him first useless to the organisation and then dangerous to it.
Brianna Barksdale keeps the organisation's books and its family discipline, and her most consequential act for it is persuading her own son to refuse a cooperation deal and take twenty years instead.
Wee-Bey does the organisation's killing, keeps tropical fish, and eventually accepts a life sentence covering a list of murders on the understanding that his family will be looked after.

Bodie starts as teenage muscle in a low-rise courtyard and works up to running a corner of his own. When the organisation collapses and a more ruthless crew takes the territory, he keeps working the same corner out of loyalty to an outfit that no longer exists, and refuses the new bosses' terms — which is what gets him killed on it.

Poot works the courtyard from the first season, takes part in Wallace's killing under protest, serves his time, and ends the series alive and out of the trade in a shoe shop, which no other original member manages.

Wallace spots the surveillance photograph that gets Brandon killed, cannot live with what follows, and asks to come off the corner, which within the organisation's logic is the same as asking to be killed.

Slim Charles is hired muscle rather than family, brought in when the Barksdales go to war with a rival crew. Being an employee rather than a relative is exactly why he survives the organisation's collapse — he has no blood loyalty to avenge and no claim to inherit — and he simply moves on to enforce for the dealers' co-operative.
Cutty comes back to the organisation after fourteen years inside expecting his old place, goes out on one job, cannot pull the trigger, and asks Avon Barksdale to let him leave, which Avon does.

Marlo Stanfield runs his organisation on phone discipline and silence — changing handsets every two weeks and refusing to discuss business on them — while shoplifting lollipops in front of a security guard purely to establish that nobody may stop him.

Chris Partlow devised the organisation's method of disposal and carries it out personally, and his one departure from professional detachment, beating a man to death rather than shooting him, is the murder that finally links him to a scene.

Snoop is Chris Partlow's creation, copying his methods exactly, and her hardware-shop conversation about a powder-actuated nail gun opens the fourth season as a statement of what the organisation now is.

Monk handles the organisation's money and its phones, and it is his line rather than Marlo Stanfield's that the police eventually get up on, because Marlo will not carry a telephone that can be traced.
O-Dog is a soldier of no standing until the night the ambush on Bodie Broadus's corner stalls and he walks up behind the man Chris Partlow and Snoop could not put down.

Michael is recruited out of the eighth grade and given a corner within a year, and is the only person the organisation takes in who then turns on it, killing Snoop and disappearing rather than accept the debt he owes Chris Partlow.

Proposition Joe chairs the co-operative with an agenda and minutes, treating the drug trade as a wholesaling business in which shooting is a failure of negotiation and everyone's margin improves if nobody is at war.

Stringer Bell's trade — his organisation's high-rise selling territory in exchange for a rival's better-quality heroin — is the arrangement the city-wide dealers' co-operative grows out of. His argument to his own partner is that the money matters more than the ground: better to share territory and sell superior product than lose men fighting over street corners.

Marlo joins the dealers' co-operative — an arrangement in which rival crews share one high-quality supply and settle disputes by discussion rather than shooting — without ever accepting its premise. He treats the shared supply as something to take rather than share, and dissolves the whole arrangement the moment he has the importers' contact himself.
