Cheese sits in the co-operative on his uncle's standing, and sells that standing to Marlo Stanfield for a share of the connection, which is what puts Proposition Joe in a chair with Chris Partlow behind him.

After the Barksdale organisation collapses, Slim Charles enforces for the city-wide association of drug wholesalers that shares a single supply — and it is he who shoots the man who betrayed its founder, at the association's last meeting.
The Greek heads the smuggling organisation working out of the Port of Baltimore, and takes care that almost nobody in the city knows his name.
Vondas does all of the organisation's talking, meeting Proposition Joe and the union in person so that the man who actually runs it never has to appear at a table.
Sergei collects, enforces and eventually takes the fall for the drugs off the docks, and his loyalty holds because the organisation looks after the families of the people it loses.

Vondas keeps Sergei at exactly one remove from the Greek, which is why Sergei can be arrested with the drugs off the docks and still have nothing to trade that would reach the man who employs them both.
Frank Sobotka is treasurer of IBS Local 1514 and, in practice, the man who decides what the local's money is spent on.
Nick has the union card his uncle arranged and cannot get enough shifts off it to keep a flat, which is the specific economic fact that pushes him into moving chemicals and then drugs.
Ziggy holds a place on the roster because of his father and is treated by the hall as a joke, which is the humiliation the whole of his season is an attempt to answer.

Omar Little recruits and leads a small, changing group of robbers who hold up drug crews rather than sell drugs themselves. The rule he sets — that no one outside the trade is ever harmed — is what allows him to operate in neighbourhoods that would otherwise turn him in, and it is the reputation that makes his name empty a corner.
Brandon robs with Omar Little and is caught after a raid on a Barksdale stash, tortured, and left displayed on a fence with his eyes taken out, which is what turns Omar from a robber into a witness.
Renaldo drives for Omar Little in the later seasons and goes with him to Puerto Rico, and it is his refusal to come back to Baltimore that leaves Omar working the Stanfield organisation alone.
The Franklin Terrace towers are the Barksdale organisation's most valuable territory, and holding them is what most of its violence is for.

The Pit is where the Barksdale organisation puts the people it cannot use elsewhere, which is why its crew is a demoted nephew, two teenagers and a boy who sleeps in an abandoned flat, and why it is the corner the detail can actually get close to.

The club is held in Orlando Blocker's name because he has no criminal record, an arrangement Avon Barksdale unwinds the moment Orlando is arrested, having his name struck off the liquor licence before the case even reaches a court.
The Greek's organisation moves its cargo through the Port of Baltimore, paying the union to make particular containers vanish from the computer.
After the Franklin Terrace towers are demolished and the Barksdale organisation collapses, the trade around the site passes to the Stanfield organisation.
IBS Local 1514 works the Port of Baltimore, and the shortage of ships calling there is the union's whole crisis.

The Pit is a shabby low-rise housing courtyard where the drug organisation puts the people it has no better use for. It is there that D'Angelo teaches two teenage dealers chess by explaining their own organisation through it — the king is never taken, the pawns are used up first, and nobody in between is ever promoted.

Bodie is a teenager selling drugs on the courtyard's ground level when the series begins, arguing constantly with his crew chief about whether any of the work means anything. By the time everyone above him has been killed or imprisoned he is running that ground himself — the only member of the original crew to rise rather than fall.
Poot Carr works the Pit couch with Bodie Broadus and Wallace through the first season, the three of them running a low-rise package under D'Angelo Barksdale.

Wallace works as a lookout in the low-rise courtyard and keeps a flat off it where he wakes and feeds a group of younger children for school each morning. That flat is where his own friends shoot him, on orders, after he asks to leave the drug trade.

The Franklin Terrace high-rises are public housing towers and the most profitable place to sell drugs in West Baltimore. Avon Barksdale cannot conceive of an organisation that does not rest on holding them, which is the argument he loses first to his business partner and then to the city, which demolishes the buildings.

Stringer runs the organisation's business from the club and the copy shop, keeping several removes between himself and any package, and it is there that he holds meetings by Robert's Rules with a minute-taker.

Colvin marks three blocks of derelict housing on a map, tells his shift commanders that thirty years of drug arrests have changed nothing, and personally walks dealers into those blocks with a promise that nobody selling there will be arrested. He does not tell his superiors, because he knows they would forbid it.

Carver is given the job of moving dealers off the residential streets into the three tolerated blocks, which means for the first time negotiating with people he has spent years simply arresting. It is the assignment that turns him from an officer who clears corners into one who learns the names of the people on them.

Bubbles, a heroin addict who sells scrap and informs for the police, sets up with a shopping trolley inside the three tolerated blocks and reports back to detectives that every drug in the city is available in one place and nobody is being chased. That is simultaneously the experiment working and the reason it cannot survive being made public.

Frank spends the union's money on lobbyists in Annapolis and Washington to get the canal dredged and the grain pier reopened, and takes the Greek's money because the local has nothing else left to sell.
Nick checks the board at the hall for shifts that are not there, which is the daily fact of the season and the reason he ends up moving product instead.
Ziggy's reputation on the docks is built on a duck, a hundred-dollar note lit as a cigarette lighter and a series of stunts, all of which are attempts to be taken seriously by men who never will.
Beadie's job is checking seals on containers, which is why she is the one who opens a can that has been sitting too long and finds thirteen dead women inside it.

Prez discovers that the year is organised around a standardised test, that his classroom can be run only once he stops trying to command it, and that the department he left and the school he joined are managing the same numbers.
Michael is the pupil Prez cannot reach, silent about his home and unwilling to accept help from any adult, and the one whose absence from the classroom is most visibly a decision the school lost.
Randy runs a sweet business from his locker, which Prez converts into a mathematics lesson, and it is at the school that his name first gets attached to the word snitch.
Namond performs for the classroom continuously, which is what gets him selected out of it and into the programme where, without an audience, he turns out to be a different child.
Dukie is washed and fed at the school by teachers who buy his clothes themselves, and is then socially promoted out of it into a high school that will do none of that.

Parenti's grant buys a separate classroom inside the school, and the study he intends to publish depends on a system that will let the room exist only as long as it does not affect the aggregate scores.
Gus edits from the middle of the room rather than an office, checks copy against what he knows of the city himself, and is the only person in the building who asks Templeton for a phone number.
Templeton files from an empty desk and an invented notebook, and his copy survives because the people above him want the story he is producing more than they want it verified.
Alma Gutierrez does the night calls and the door-knocks, rising early to buy the paper the morning her first front page runs.
Klebanow runs the room on successive buyouts while asking for more ambitious work from fewer people, and treats an editor's doubts about a reporter as a personnel problem rather than a factual one.
Whiting wants a sustained narrative about the city with a Dickensian aspect, and is uninterested in the reporting that would establish whether the narrative is true.
Cutty finds the derelict building, gets the money and the paperwork through the Deacon, and runs the gym on the principle that a boy who turns up is owed something whether or not he can fight.

Cutty Wise thought Michael Lee a natural boxer and pressed him to train; Michael, wary of adult men, rebuffed the offer, would not be driven home alone, and hinted to his friends that he suspected Cutty of worse. Cutty finally told him never to return after Michael beat Namond Brice at the gym for teasing Dukie Weems.
Namond arrives at the gym in expensive gear and is told by Cutty, without malice, that there is no fight in him, which is the first honest assessment anyone gives the boy.

Michael Lee brought Dukie Weems to the gym after Spider beat him on the corner. Cutty watched him work, saw no boxer in him, and told him at closing time that learning to fight would not keep bullies away — then asked him why he thought he had become the target.
Jimmy McNulty and Bunk Moreland are homicide partners and drinking companions; Bunk works cases patiently and is the one man whose disapproval McNulty actually registers.

Freamon and McNulty are the two detectives in the unit who will not let a case go. Freamon builds the slow paper trail — phone records, property deeds, bank accounts — while McNulty forces the department to fund it by any means available. When McNulty invents a serial killer to unlock resources, Freamon joins the fraud knowing precisely what it will cost them both.

Inseparable for four seasons and barely on speaking terms by the fifth. What divides them is that Carver starts learning the names of the people on his post and Herc never does — and it ends with Carver, now a sergeant, filing the report that gets Herc thrown off the force. Herc goes to work for the lawyer who defends the dealers they used to arrest together.

Greggs and McNulty are the two detectives on the original special unit who work sources rather than wait for paperwork. Between them they persuade Omar Little — a robber of drug crews with no stake in the case — to give evidence against a killer, which produces the investigation's only conviction. Years later, both in the homicide squad, it is Greggs who reports McNulty's invented serial killer to their commander.

Daniels is the lieutenant put in charge of the special unit that McNulty's complaint to a judge brought into being, which means he inherits both the case and the man who forced it. He spends five years alternately protecting McNulty's work from commanders who want it stopped, and protecting the unit from McNulty himself.
Cedric Daniels commands Kima Greggs: Daniels brought her from his own narcotics squad and treats her as the unit's steadiest hand.
Cedric Daniels commands Lester Freamon: Daniels was sent him as a makeweight and repeatedly shields his slow paper cases from commanders wanting quick arrests.

Cedric Daniels commands Ellis Carver from the first detail onward and promotes him as he improves, and it is under Daniels that Carver goes from clearing corners with Herc Hauk to running a Western District shift of his own.

Daniels signs for the surveillance camera Herc loses and absorbs the fallout when Herc's fabricated informant and leaked name collapse two separate cases, protection that runs out only when Herc leaves the department for a defence attorney.

Rawls commands the homicide squad in which Landsman is a sergeant, and both men measure everything by the proportion of murders officially recorded as solved. Landsman keeps the board of open cases in red and closed in black; Rawls decides whose career the red names damage.
Jay Landsman is McNulty's homicide sergeant, alternately protecting him and describing at length the trouble McNulty has caused the squad.

Landsman orders Bunk to find the service weapon taken from a shot officer and refuses to let it drop, which reduces a senior homicide detective to searching a police database for every man in West Baltimore nicknamed Peanut — the sort of errand that fills the time a murder case needs.

Landsman delivers the eulogy at Ray Cole's wake, and the cases he credits him with — a Mississippi extradition, an after-hours triple on Hudson Street, the Fayette Street drug wars — are the titles Robert Colesberry produced, so the speech eulogises the actor as much as the detective.

Bunk Moreland works Jay Landsman's homicide squad alongside Ray Cole, and is among the detectives at Cole's wake in Dead Soldiers — with McNulty, Freamon, Holley, Santangelo, Ilene Nathan and Ed Norris — after Cole drops dead exercising at a gym.
Ervin Burrell as commissioner has William Rawls as his deputy for operations; Rawls serves him loyally up to the point where Burrell's removal creates a vacancy.

The police commissioner installs Daniels over the new unit expecting a quick, shallow case that will close within weeks and embarrass nobody. When Daniels instead lets his detectives build a long investigation into the drug organisation's finances, Burrell spends years pressuring him to wrap it up.
William Rawls is Bunny Colvin's superior and the man who takes most pleasure in destroying him once the tolerated zones become public.
Ervin Burrell is forced out as commissioner and Cedric Daniels succeeds him, only to resign within months rather than falsify the figures City Hall requires.
After Cedric Daniels resigns as commissioner, Stanislaus Valchek is given the office, the department's most transactional operator inheriting the job Daniels gave up on principle.
Lester Freamon takes Prez, a patrolman nobody trusts with a weapon, and teaches him to read pager codes, phone records and paper trails, finding the one thing Prez is good at.
Lester Freamon trains Leander Sydnor in wiretap and financial investigation across several cases, and Sydnor has inherited his methods by the finale.
Bunny Colvin tells Ellis Carver that he has policed a neighbourhood for years without learning a single name in it; everything Carver becomes follows from that conversation.
Cedric Daniels and Rhonda Pearlman conduct a long relationship alongside their working one, she handling his unit's cases in court as his marriage ends.
Jimmy McNulty and Rhonda Pearlman had an affair in the first season, before she and Cedric Daniels became a couple.
Jimmy McNulty and Beadie Russell meet over the container deaths at the port and later live together; her steadiness is what briefly holds his drinking in check.

McNulty tells a circuit court judge privately, over drinks, that his department has no intention of investigating a string of drug-related murders. Judges do not run police departments, but they can embarrass them: Phelan telephones the deputy commissioner, and the special unit at the centre of the series is created overnight purely to make the complaint go away.

A wiretap requires a judge's signature, renewed every thirty days on fresh evidence that it is still producing. Judge Phelan signs the orders that let the police listen to the Barksdale organisation's phones, and it was his telephone call to the deputy commissioner — after McNulty complained to him privately — that forced the investigation into existence at all.
Rhonda Pearlman drafts the affidavits and carries the indictments against the Barksdale organisation, and negotiates the pleas that end the first season.
Rhonda Pearlman prepares the case against the Stanfield organisation and has to watch it collapse once the illegal wiretap behind it is exposed.
Rhonda Pearlman worked up the financial case against Clay Davis before the State's Attorney's office took it from federal hands and lost it at trial.

Stanislaus Valchek is Prez's father-in-law, and it is Valchek's standing in the department that keeps Prez in uniform after he blinds a boy in a stop and again after the alley shooting, until Prez removes himself.

Stanislaus Valchek's grudge against Frank Sobotka, over a rival stained-glass window donated to their parish, is what makes him demand a detail on the union and sets the entire port investigation going.
Maurice Levy hires Herc Hauk as an investigator after Herc leaves the police, and Herc's loose talk is how Levy learns the Stanfield wiretap was illegal.
Maurice Levy is the Barksdale organisation's attorney, handling its charges and its bail and structuring the companies its money moves through.
Maurice Levy transfers his services to Marlo Stanfield and finally gets the charges dismissed by exposing the illegal wiretap they rest on.
Maurice Levy acts for Cheese Wagstaff as he does for most of the city's trade, and it is Levy who handles the Stanfield defendants after the wiretap is exposed.
Jimmy McNulty identified Avon Barksdale as the man behind a string of unsolved murders and forced the case that becomes the first season.
Jimmy McNulty pursued Stringer Bell for three seasons and reached the development site minutes too late, learning only from the body that Stringer had been trying to go legitimate.

Lester Freamon pursues Marlo Stanfield for years, finds the bodies sealed into the vacant houses and finally breaks the organisation's clock-face messaging system, using a wiretap he has no lawful basis for.
Lester Freamon gets up on Monk Metcalf's phone, and it is that line, more than Marlo Stanfield's own, that produces the Stanfield organisation's arrests.
Lester Freamon followed drug money into Clay Davis's accounts and built the paper case against him, which the State's Attorney then took over and lost.
Kima Greggs worked the Barksdale organisation from the narcotics side and was shot during an undercover buy arranged against it.
Prez broke the Barksdale organisation's pager and payphone codes on the first wiretap, the contribution that saved his career and defined his second one.

Beadie Russell is a port police officer whose job before this is checking seals on containers. Her paperwork is what first connects cargo vanishing from the docks to the smuggling ring behind it, and she is seconded into a homicide investigation several ranks above anything she has done.
The Major Crimes Unit is turned onto the Greek's organisation for the second season, and gets close enough to arrest its enforcers and nobody above them.
Jimmy McNulty invented a serial killer preying on homeless men to generate the overtime and wiretap resources needed to pursue Marlo Stanfield, a fraud that ends his career.

Avon Barksdale and Stringer Bell built the organisation together from childhood, Avon holding the territory and Stringer running the money; each eventually decides the other has become the greater danger.

Avon Barksdale and Brianna Barksdale are brother and sister; she handles the organisation's money and its family discipline, and in the season three closing montage she attends his trial and walks out of the courtroom when he looks at her — after learning he let Stringer Bell have her son killed.
Brianna Barksdale is D'Angelo's mother, and it is she who persuades her son to withdraw his cooperation with the police and take a twenty-year sentence for the family.

Avon Barksdale is both D'Angelo's uncle and his employer. He demotes his nephew from the high-rise projects to a low-rise courtyard as punishment for having drawn attention by beating a murder charge in open court — a family matter and a business decision at once, which is how the whole organisation is run.
Avon Barksdale's killings are done by Wee-Bey Brice, who eventually takes a life sentence for a list of them on Avon's behalf.
Avon Barksdale hires Slim Charles as muscle for the war with Marlo Stanfield and keeps him on as his most reliable lieutenant.
Stringer Bell gives Bodie Broadus his orders once D'Angelo Barksdale is gone, including the order to kill Wallace.

D'Angelo runs the small crew Bodie sells for, and teaches him the trade partly through a chess lesson — the pawns are used up quickly, the king is never taken, and nobody in between gets promoted. Bodie takes the lesson literally and spends the next five years being the pawn who refuses to accept it.
D'Angelo Barksdale runs the courtyard crew that includes Wallace and treats the boy with an affection neither of them can afford.

D'Angelo runs the small crew in the low-rise courtyard that Poot sells for. Poot is the one who argues back most — about women, about the work, about whether any of it means anything — which is exactly why D'Angelo tolerates him.
Bodie Broadus and Poot Carr work corners together from the first season to the last night of Bodie's life, when Poot begs him to run.

Wallace was a sixteen-year-old lookout who had spoken to police and then asked to come off the corner. Stringer Bell's decision was that asking is itself the danger, and that the cheapest way to settle it was to send the two boys Wallace had grown up beside — which made the killing a lesson to the crew as much as a removal.

Bodie Broadus drew the weapon in the flat where all three had grown up and could not fire until Poot Carr shouted at him to do it; his one shot did not kill Wallace, and it was Poot who took the gun and finished it.

Poot Carr had tried to talk Bodie Broadus out of the job and then urged him to get on with it, and when Bodie's single shot left Wallace alive and pleading, Poot took the gun from him and fired the shots that killed him.
Stringer Bell had D'Angelo Barksdale strangled in prison and the death staged as suicide, deciding without telling Avon Barksdale that the young man was too likely to talk.
Stringer Bell betrayed Avon Barksdale twice over: he had Avon's nephew D'Angelo killed behind his back, and he handed Avon's weapons stash to Major Colvin to end a war Avon would not stop.
Avon Barksdale betrayed Stringer Bell by giving Brother Mouzone the address of the building where Stringer would be alone, knowing precisely what would follow.
Wee-Bey Brice and De'Londa Brice are married, and she spends his life sentence expecting the organisation to keep paying for it.
Wee-Bey Brice is Namond's father, serving life, and from the visiting room he overrules his wife and gives his son to Bunny Colvin, understanding that the boy is not built for the work.
De'Londa Brice is Namond's mother, and pushes her plainly unsuited son toward the corner to keep the organisation's payments coming.
De'Londa Brice fights Bunny Colvin's attempt to take Namond out of the life, and loses only because her imprisoned husband overrules her.

Cutty Wise comes out of a fourteen-year prison sentence expecting his old place as an enforcer, goes out on one job and finds he can no longer pull the trigger. Avon Barksdale, the boss he served, lets him leave without penalty — unusual in an organisation that kills people who know too much — and later hands him fifteen thousand dollars in cash for boxing equipment when Cutty asks for ten.
Stringer Bell paid Clay Davis to move his development projects through city government; Davis took the money for years and delivered nothing.
Clay Davis took hundreds of thousands from Stringer Bell in exchange for political favours he never had any intention of arranging, a swindle Stringer only recognises near the end of his life.
Marlo Stanfield's orders are carried out by Chris Partlow, who handles the organisation's killing and asks nothing about the reasons.
Marlo Stanfield employs Snoop as a soldier alongside Chris Partlow; it is she who buys the nail gun used to seal the vacant houses.
Monk Metcalf handles Marlo Stanfield's money and messages and is trusted with more of the organisation's business than anyone but Chris Partlow.
Chris Partlow recruited and trained Snoop, and she copies his methods exactly, down to the lime and the boarded windows.
Chris Partlow and Snoop hunt together across the fourth and fifth seasons, sharing the van, the nail gun and the vacant houses.
Chris Partlow takes Michael Lee under his protection, teaches him the work, and kills the man Michael cannot bring himself to name, a debt that binds the boy to the organisation.
Chris Partlow leads the ambush on Bodie Broadus's corner with Snoop and O-Dog, and it is O-Dog who is left to finish it.

Bodie had already driven Chris Partlow and Snoop behind parked cars and was still shouting at them to come on when O-Dog came up the pavement behind him, which is why the killing takes three people and still counts as Bodie winning the argument.
Marlo Stanfield ordered Bodie Broadus killed after Bodie was seen getting into a detective's car, and sent Chris Partlow and Snoop to do it.
Avon Barksdale and Marlo Stanfield fight a street war over West Baltimore, Avon defending an empire already in decline and Marlo taking it corner by corner.

The Stanfield crew take over everything the older Barksdale organisation had: the street corners where drugs are sold, the standing that stops rivals testing you, and finally the wholesale supply itself. They run it on terms the older outfit would not have recognised — no truces, no negotiation, and bodies hidden rather than left in the street as warnings.

Proposition Joe held the city's only direct line to the international suppliers who bring heroin in through the port. Once Marlo Stanfield has taken that connection for himself, Joe is no longer necessary and is instead a man who knows too much; Marlo has him shot in his own kitchen, and is present to tell him his mistake was teaching him.
Chris Partlow shot Proposition Joe in his own house on Marlo Stanfield's order, with Marlo present to explain that Joe's mistake had been to educate him.

Proposition Joe teaches Marlo Stanfield the things that keep a wholesaler out of prison: not to talk on telephones at all, and how to move money through offshore accounts rather than hold it. Marlo learns both thoroughly enough that the police spend two seasons unable to record him — and then uses what he has learned to reach Joe's own suppliers and remove him.

Proposition Joe brought Marlo Stanfield into the dealers' co-operative and taught him how the supply worked. Marlo went behind it directly to the importers for his own private line, then had Joe killed to make sure nobody could take it back — betraying both the man and the arrangement that had kept the city's crews from shooting at each other.
Marlo Stanfield ordered Butchie tortured and killed purely as bait, knowing it was the one thing certain to bring Omar Little back to Baltimore.
Chris Partlow and Snoop took Butchie in his own bar and worked on him at length before killing him, on Marlo Stanfield's instruction that the death be conspicuous enough to reach Puerto Rico.
Chris Partlow takes responsibility for Michael Lee inside the organisation and, when the Stanfield indictments come, confesses to the killings outright so that Michael is not charged with them.
The Greek was Proposition Joe's source of heroin for years, dealing with Joe alone and keeping the rest of Baltimore at several removes.

The co-operative runs entirely on Proposition Joe's private connection to the Greek: he buys the package and sells it on to the other crews, which is the arrangement that makes him worth killing once Marlo Stanfield has the contact.

Proposition Joe, the East Baltimore boss, had a far better grade of heroin than the Barksdale organisation; the Barksdales had the high-rise projects, the most lucrative selling ground in the city. Stringer Bell trades access to that ground for the better product — a deal his own partner opposes, and the origin of the city-wide co-operative in which rival crews later share one supply.
Proposition Joe supplied Marlo Stanfield through the New Day Co-Operative on the Greek's product, an arrangement Marlo accepted only until he could reach the source himself.
Vondas is the man Proposition Joe actually meets, the Greek's organisation handling every transaction through him rather than through its head.
The Greek directs his organisation through Vondas, who does the talking so that the Greek himself need never be identified.
Frank Sobotka lets the Greek's organisation move containers through the Port of Baltimore untouched, and takes its money for the union's lobbying campaign.
Nick Sobotka deals directly with the Greek's people to move stolen chemicals and then drugs, going considerably further into the arrangement than his uncle intended.
Omar Little robbed the Barksdale organisation repeatedly and testified against one of its shooters, making him its most persistent single problem.

Omar Little robs the Stanfield organisation twice over: first a private card game where its leaders are gambling, then an entire wholesale shipment belonging to the dealers' co-operative it buys from. Marlo Stanfield, who cares more about being disrespected than about the money, spends the rest of the series hunting him.
Omar Little and Brandon Wright were partners in the robberies and in private, and Brandon's tortured body left on a fence is what turns Omar into a witness against the Barksdale organisation.
Omar Little and Renaldo were partners in the later robberies and retired together to Puerto Rico before Omar came back to Baltimore alone.

Avon Barksdale put a standing bounty on the robbers who had been holding up his crews, which made Brandon Wright — the boyfriend and partner of the robber Omar Little — a target. Avon ordered the mutilated body displayed in the low-rise projects where the crew's youngest members would have to walk past it; the killing itself was ordered by Stringer Bell once a lookout reported Brandon's whereabouts.
Omar Little and Avon Barksdale are locked into a private war from the moment Avon has Brandon killed, and Omar's testimony puts one of Avon's shooters away.

Butchie holds Omar Little's money behind the bar, passes his messages, and is the man Omar calls from Puerto Rico; it is Butchie's killing on Marlo Stanfield's order that brings Omar back to Baltimore.
Omar Little came out of retirement in Puerto Rico the moment he learned Butchie had been tortured and killed, which is exactly what Marlo Stanfield had intended.
Stringer Bell told Omar Little that Brother Mouzone had been responsible for Brandon's death, sending Omar to shoot a guard Stringer had never wanted in the first place.
Omar Little shot Brother Mouzone on Stringer Bell's false information and later, once both men understood who had lied to them, joined him to kill Stringer.

Omar Little and Brother Mouzone had both been told lies by Stringer Bell — Omar that Mouzone killed his partner, Mouzone that Omar shot him — and when each worked out who had lied, they hunted him together. They cornered him in the half-finished development that was to have been his way out of the drug trade, and he died standing in it.
Brother Mouzone shared in the killing of Stringer Bell, having been directed to his location by Avon Barksdale in settlement of the debt for Mouzone's own shooting.

Avon Barksdale brings a New York enforcer to Baltimore to guard his high-rise selling territory from the robber Omar Little. When his own second in command has that enforcer shot and blames Omar for it, Avon later settles the debt by telling the man where to find the person actually responsible — his own partner.

Kenard is a corner child who was once filmed playing at being Omar Little in an alley game, and who watched the real man limp past on a crutch, unimpressed by what the legend had become. He followed Omar into a shop where he was buying cigarettes and shot him through the head — the most feared figure in West Baltimore killed by someone too young for anyone in the trade to have considered a risk, and a murder the police barely investigate.
Omar Little and Bunk Moreland keep an uneasy respect: Omar gives Bunk truthful statements, and Bunk tells him plainly what his career has done to the neighbourhood they both come from.

Proposition Joe runs Cheese Wagstaff as one of his crew chiefs, and vouched for him to Marlo Stanfield over the robbery of a co-operative package — proving Cheese's innocence by revealing his own connection to the Greek, which is the disclosure that gets Joe killed.
Cheese Wagstaff gave Marlo Stanfield the information needed to reach his own uncle, and stood by while Proposition Joe was killed for it.

At the final meeting of the city's drug wholesalers' association, Cheese argues that loyalty is bad business — moments after it emerges that he informed on his own uncle, the man who founded it. Slim Charles shoots him mid-sentence, then observes that it was for nothing.

The two never meet face to face. Omar Little, who makes his living robbing drug crews, holds up a private card game where Marlo Stanfield is gambling and later takes an entire wholesale shipment belonging to Marlo's suppliers. Marlo has him framed for a murder he did not commit and has his closest friend tortured to death as bait; Omar spends his last weeks shouting Marlo's name in the street trying to provoke him into the open.
Frank Sobotka is Nick's uncle and the union official who decides what work Nick gets, and he brings his nephew into the smuggling only as far as he must.
Frank Sobotka is Ziggy's father, able neither to protect his son from the docks' contempt nor to take him seriously himself.
Nick and Ziggy Sobotka are cousins raised almost as brothers, Nick perpetually clearing up after Ziggy's schemes until the last one is a killing.

Frank Sobotka had decided to tell the federal investigators everything — about the containers he waved through, and about the women who died in one of them. The Greek learned of it before the meeting, and had him killed under the interstate on his way to it, on the docks his union had worked for generations.
Frank Sobotka took the Greek's money for years and then resolved to inform on the organisation after the container deaths, a decision the Greek did not allow to stand.

Beadie Russell's container paperwork is what builds the case against Frank Sobotka's local, and the two arrive at a wary understanding once he decides to talk to the federal investigators rather than keep taking the Greek's money.
Stanislaus Valchek demanded a detail on IBS Local 1514 purely to punish its treasurer, and the investigation he wanted for spite uncovers an international smuggling operation.
Tommy Carcetti runs against Mayor Clarence Royce and beats him in the Democratic primary, an outcome Royce never seriously entertained.
Clarence Royce is succeeded as mayor by Tommy Carcetti, who inherits the school system deficit Royce had concealed through the campaign.

Norman Wilson, a reporter before he was an operative, runs Tommy Carcetti's campaign and then advises him in office: he is the one sent to leak the Daniels story to the papers, and the one who tells Carcetti to his face that leaving the governor's school money on the table is a choice about Annapolis rather than about Baltimore.
Steintorf exists to say the things Carcetti needs said and not recorded, which is how the demand for lower crime figures reaches a police commissioner without the mayor ever having issued it.
Michael Steintorf delivers the mayor's demand for lower crime figures to Cedric Daniels, and it is that demand Daniels resigns rather than meet.
Tommy Carcetti keeps Ervin Burrell on as commissioner for political cover and removes him once the crime figures fail to fall.
Tommy Carcetti elevates Cedric Daniels to commissioner as a reform gesture and then requires the falsified statistics that make Daniels quit.

Odell Watkins delivered his constituency for Clarence Royce until Royce ignored their joint proposal to match witness-protection funding, and until Watkins noticed the campaign was quietly running Marla Daniels's opponent in the districts where Daniels was weak. He confronted Royce, sat out the primary, and then endorsed Tommy Carcetti.

Odell Watkins's support on the campaign trail swings a tight primary to Tommy Carcetti after he breaks with Royce, and his first advice to the new mayor is that Ervin Burrell cannot simply be sacked in a majority-black city — counsel Carcetti takes and then works around.

Clay Davis raises and moves money for Clarence Royce and takes his cut; when Odell Watkins finally breaks with the administration he names Davis specifically, along with the developers, as what Royce has got into bed with at the expense of the neighbourhoods that elected him.
Tommy Carcetti uses Bunny Colvin's tolerated drug zones as a weapon against the sitting mayor during the campaign, and once elected has no more use for Colvin than the department did.

Prez gives Michael Lee detention for undone homework, Michael skips it to collect his brother Bug from school, and Prez learns the reason from Randy Wagstaff and Dukie Weems rather than from Michael, who will not discuss his home with any adult.
Prez teaches Dukie Weems, washes his clothes and feeds him at the school, and goes on giving him money long after the boy has left education for the corner.

Prez turns Randy's corridor sweet business into a maths lesson on wholesale pricing, and the boy works out he can buy cheaper online — then hits the obstacle that he has no credit card, which is the season's argument about ability and access in one exchange.
Prez teaches Namond Brice, whose disruption of the classroom is what gets him selected for the separate programme that saves him.

Parenti is a university academic with a research grant to study why some children become violent; Colvin is a police major just forced out after thirty years. Together they run a separate classroom for a school's most disruptive pupils, and find that asking the children how their neighbourhood actually works produces more than any lesson plan does.
David Parenti's separate classroom is where Namond Brice is asked questions rather than given orders, and where his complete unsuitability for the corner becomes plain to everyone but his mother.

Bunny Colvin, a police major forced out after thirty years, and his wife take Namond Brice into their suburban home — with the consent of Namond's imprisoned father, who overrules his own wife from the visiting room to make it happen. Of the four boys the fourth season follows, Namond is the only one who gets out, and this is the one clean rescue the series permits anybody.
Cutty Wise takes Namond Brice into the gym at his mother's insistence and tells him plainly that there is no fight in him, after watching him hold the heavy bag for other boys rather than use it.

Michael Lee shelters Dukie Weems in his flat and takes him off the corner to mind Bug rather than work a package — Kenard complains Dukie is not doing his job and does not know why. In the penultimate episode Michael leaves him at a scrapyard encampment and does not come back.

When a group of pupils corner Randy Wagstaff at school to beat him for snitching, Michael Lee fights them off and leaves their leader bloodied — Randy is badly beaten regardless. What isolates Randy is the neighbourhood and the group home, not the three boys he grew up with.

Namond Brice buys Chinese takeaway for Michael Lee, Randy Wagstaff and Dukie Weems in the one evening the four spend as children rather than as workers; later Michael beats him at Cutty Wise's gym for teasing Dukie, and is told by Cutty never to come back.

Randy Wagstaff confides what he knows about Lex's murder to Dukie Weems and to nobody else among the four, and Dukie never repeats it — which places the leak that destroys Randy's placement entirely with the police department rather than with his friends.
Randy Wagstaff told Ellis Carver what he knew about a murder on the understanding that it would go no further; when it did, Carver could not stop the boy losing his foster home.

Snoop had recruited Michael Lee into the Stanfield organisation at thirteen and trained him. When she drove him to a vacant lot on an errand that did not make sense, he understood he was the job, and shot her in the passenger seat — the pupil killing the teacher with what she had taught him.
The Deacon finds Cutty Wise work when he comes out of prison and then finds the money and the paperwork that turn a derelict building into a boxing gym.

The Deacon is a church elder whose judgement Colvin trusts more than his own commanders'. Shown the three tolerated blocks, he tells Colvin he has built a great village of pain and left it unattended — no clinics, no needle exchange, no help of any kind — which is the only criticism of the experiment Colvin takes seriously.

The Deacon steers a university researcher's grant toward a just-retired police major, on the reasoning that an academic proposing to study children from the drug corners needs someone who has actually policed them. The result is a separate school classroom for the most disruptive thirteen-year-olds.
Gus Haynes takes his doubts about Scott Templeton's sourcing to the managing editors and is told to drop it; Templeton keeps filing, wins a Pulitzer, and Gus is moved to the copy desk.
Gus Haynes edits Alma Gutierrez and teaches her the reporting Templeton does not bother with; she backs him against Templeton and is exiled to a suburban bureau for it.

Gus Haynes edits Scott Templeton from the city desk, asks him at the top of each shift what he is working on, and later demands he produce the homeless man he has quoted; Templeton takes the complaint over Gus's head to the managing editor instead.
Thomas Klebanow promotes and protects Scott Templeton, whose invented serial killer coverage brings the paper the prize its management wants.

Thomas Klebanow is Gus Haynes's managing editor; when Gus objects at the Burrell press conference that the reporter who could have worked those sources was bought out, Klebanow tells him to stay collegial and cut back on the profanity, and later moves him to the copy desk.

James C. Whiting III is the Sun's executive editor and Thomas Klebanow's superior; the two arrive from outside Baltimore together and share an appetite for prize-winning narrative over local reporting.
James C. Whiting III signs off on the decision to disbelieve Gus Haynes and keep the fabricated stories in the paper.

Alma Gutierrez files thirty-five inches on the Junebug triple homicide and finds it cut to twelve below the fold, while Scott Templeton's invented material runs at length; she backs Gus Haynes against him and is moved to a suburban bureau for it.

Bubbles, a heroin addict who knows every corner in West Baltimore, works as Greggs's paid informant. His method of identifying the dealers she cannot photograph is to walk the streets putting distinctive hats on the people he sees, so the surveillance team can match a face to a name.

Bubbles works as an informant for Jimmy McNulty as well as Kima Greggs, on terms the two detectives negotiate with him directly — five dollars an hour, thirty on a day, and as McNulty points out, no withholding.

Bubbles and Johnny Weeks steal and use together: the counterfeit-money scam on a Barksdale corner in the first episode that gets Johnny beaten nearly to death, and a short con stripping copper piping to sell. Johnny disapproves of Bubbles informing for the police and takes no part in it.

Johnny Weeks was beaten nearly to death by Bodie Broadus, Wallace, Poot Carr and other Pit dealers for trying to pass counterfeit money to D'Angelo Barksdale's crew in the first episode, and it is that beating that pushes Bubbles into working as a police informant.

Bubbles feeds Sherrod, gives him a bed on his cart round and walks him back into a school he has been out of for years, and the boy sits in a classroom several grades below where he should be without either of them naming it.
Bubbles prepared a capsule of doctored heroin for the addict who had spent months robbing and beating him, and Sherrod took it instead; the boy's death is what finally stops Bubbles using.
Walon is Bubbles's Narcotics Anonymous sponsor, turning up across the years it takes Bubbles to get clean and refusing to let him treat his own guilt as a reason to use again.
Kima Greggs is the police officer Bubbles trusts most, and she keeps checking on him long after he has stopped being useful to any case.
The closing montage puts Leander Sydnor in front of a judge complaining about a case his bosses will not let him work, precisely the position Jimmy McNulty occupied in the first episode.
As Bubbles finally gets clean and is allowed upstairs to eat with his family, Dukie Weems is shown taking his first shot in a scrapyard, the series handing the role on rather than closing it.

Michael Lee beat Kenard up for stealing a package, lying that the police had taken it, and insulting Namond Brice; by the fourth season finale Kenard is working Michael's new corner alongside Dukie Weems, and it is from there that he follows Omar Little into the shop.

Michael Steintorf displaces Norman Wilson as the mayor's closest adviser over the course of the fifth season: it is Steintorf who carries the demand for lower crime figures that Daniels resigns over, and Wilson who is still telling Carcetti that refusing the governor's school money is a decision about Annapolis.

McNulty is a homicide detective for most of the series, thrown out of the unit into the marine unit and the Western District and taken back each time, because Jay Landsman would rather have a detective who closes cases than one who behaves.
Bunk Moreland carries one of the unit's highest clearance rates, which is the currency that buys him the latitude to drink on duty and to refuse the work he considers beneath the squad.

Jay Landsman runs the squad's board, on which open cases are written in red and closed ones in black, and his objection to Lester Freamon opening the vacant houses is purely that a column of new red names destroy a year's arithmetic.
Santangelo is the squad's weakest detective, given the choice by William Rawls between informing on McNulty and being transferred to the property unit, and transferred anyway once he has done it.

Crutchfield catches several of the murders the series turns on, including Omar Little's, and works each at the pace the squad's only real measure rewards — the proportion of killings officially closed. A case that cannot be closed quickly gets the effort that reflects.
Holley rises to sergeant in the unit during the later seasons and inherits the squad's real caseload while its overtime budget is being consumed by a murder nobody committed.
Greggs transfers into homicide after years in narcotics, and it is from inside the unit that she works out what McNulty is doing with the homeless killings and reports it to Cedric Daniels.
Cole is a competent, unspectacular member of the squad whose death is marked with a wake at their bar, the detectives laying him out on the pool table under a sheet.
Rawls commanded homicide before rising to deputy commissioner, and the clearance-rate culture he enforced there outlives his promotion and shapes every squad decision after it.

Each squad staffs the new unit with the officers it least wants and then resents what it has lost. The homicide sergeant objects to opening the boarded-up houses where a drug crew has hidden its victims, on the plain arithmetic that thirty recovered bodies means thirty new unsolved murders on his board — the measure his squad is judged by.
Pearlman answers to an office whose caution about winnable cases repeatedly limits what the detectives she works with are permitted to build.
Nathan tries the organisation's murder cases and is the prosecutor who puts Omar Little on the stand in an ascot, a witness she knows the jury will either believe entirely or not at all.
Rupert Bond heads the State's Attorney's office and uses it to pursue the political case he thinks will make his name.
Rupert Bond took the Clay Davis case out of federal hands to try it himself in state court, and lost it when the senator talked the jury round.
Ilene Nathan prosecuted Bird Hilton for the murder of the witness William Gant, and won it on Omar Little's testimony.
Bird is the soldier the organisation uses when a witness needs removing, and his willingness to shoot William Gant on a public street is exactly the recklessness that eventually convicts him.
Bunk Moreland and his colleagues took Bird Hilton in for the Gant murder, and Bunk's interrogation of him is where the case begins.
Frank Sobotka arranged to give the FBI everything he knew about the smuggling through the port, and was killed before the meeting could take place.

Carcetti uses council hearings on police failures to build a public profile, calculating correctly that a white councilman cannot win the mayoralty on the council's own arithmetic without first being seen to be right.

Nerese Campbell presides over the Baltimore City Council, and it is from that seat that she brokers Ervin Burrell's quiet exit from the commissioner's office in exchange for his silence about Cedric Daniels's finances.
Gray sits alongside Carcetti as a colleague and friend, and is encouraged into a mayoral run that has no path to victory and every prospect of splitting the vote Carcetti needs split.

Royce's administration knew the size of the school system's shortfall and held it back through the primary; Carcetti inherits the number on taking office and then declines the governor's money to close it, so two mayors in succession decide the deficit is survivable and the schools are not their problem.
Donnelly has learned exactly which numbers the system checks and produces them, while telling a new teacher without sentiment which of his pupils will not be in the building next year.
Sampson explains to Prez in his first weeks that the job is not teaching mathematics but holding a room, and that the curriculum arrives only after that has been achieved.

Prez leaves the police department after a fatal mistake and becomes a mathematics teacher. He finds the school runs on the same logic he left behind: where commanders massaged the share of murders recorded as solved, the school suspends its curriculum for weeks to drill children on the single standardised test it is judged by.
David Parenti's research programme operates inside the city school system on a grant, and depends on the system's willingness to let a separate classroom exist.

Bubbles attends meetings for years without speaking, and the account he finally gives of Sherrod's death, in a church basement in the last episode, is the one confession in the series that is actually heard.
Walon works the fellowship's steps and sponsors others through them, and tells Bubbles that the shame he is carrying is not a reason to use but the reason to keep coming.

Johnny Weeks enters a treatment programme as part of the deal Kima Greggs arranges to get his possession charge dropped on Bubbles's behalf, and takes no part in the informing that Bubbles does for the same detectives.
Charles Marimow is installed over the Major Crimes Unit as a political favour and sets about dismantling the wiretap case and driving out the detectives who built it.
Charles Marimow orders Lester Freamon off the long case he has spent years building, and Freamon takes a transfer rather than comply.
Marimow's arrival costs the unit Greggs, who transfers to homicide rather than work under a commander who treats a wiretap as an excuse for not making arrests this week.
Ervin Burrell puts Charles Marimow over the Major Crimes Unit precisely because Marimow can be relied on to stop it producing anything politically inconvenient.
Colonel Ray Foerster oversees Cedric Daniels's unit and is among the few senior officers willing to shelter real casework from the command staff.
Ray Foerster commands the criminal investigation division the Major Crimes Unit sits within, and protects it for as long as his health allows.
William Rawls pressed Michael Santangelo to inform on McNulty in exchange for keeping his place in homicide, and exiled him anyway.
Michael Santangelo agreed under pressure from William Rawls to report on Jimmy McNulty's movements, and McNulty worked out who it was almost immediately.
Dennis Mello is Bunny Colvin's second in the Western District and helps run the tolerated zones knowing what it will cost them both.

Colvin commands the police district containing most of West Baltimore's drug corners, in the final year before his retirement, having concluded across thirty years that the arrests his superiors require have never once changed anything on those streets.

Mello runs the district's daily shift administration for Major Colvin, and helps operate three blocks in which no drug arrests are made — knowing exactly what will happen to both their careers when headquarters finds out, and keeping it off the paperwork anyway.
Carver polices the Western for the whole series and ends it running a shift there, applying to his own officers the lesson Colvin gave him about knowing the names on a post.

Herc works drug enforcement in the police district covering most of West Baltimore, where he loses a surveillance camera worth thousands of dollars and then invents an informant to justify a warrant — two failures that between them wreck a case the rest of the department has spent a year building.

Dozerman is shot in the face during an undercover drug buy in the district and his police weapon is taken at the scene. The manhunt for the gun, and the harder policing that follows, are what convince his commanding major that the arrests his officers keep making have never changed anything.
Colicchio patrols the Western with an appetite for confrontation that the district tolerates until he assaults a schoolteacher over a parked car in front of witnesses.
Ellis Carver supervises Anthony Colicchio and eventually writes him up rather than smooth over an assault on a schoolteacher, the clearest measure of how far Carver has come.

The three blocks bring the Western District a fourteen per cent fall in crime, a figure William Rawls calls insane, illegal and stone-cold brilliant in the same breath as noting that it will end both their careers.
Michael Crutchfield catches the investigation into Omar Little's killing, and the case is closed when a child is led away in handcuffs.
Stinkum is being promoted to run his own corner as a reward for expanding the organisation's territory, and is shot by Omar Little on the night he is due to take it up.
Savino takes a three-year sentence for the organisation rather than implicate anyone in the Orlando shooting, and comes out to find that the people he protected are gone.
Little Man is a soldier used for the Orlando ambush, and his panic in that car costs him his life within days once Avon Barksdale and Stringer Bell decide he cannot be trusted under police pressure.
Omar Little shot Stinkum dead in an alley on the night the Barksdale lieutenant was to take over a corner of his own, and wounded Wee-Bey Brice in the same ambush.

Wee-Bey Brice shot Little Man dead on orders from Avon Barksdale and Stringer Bell, because it was Little Man who had shot a police officer at the Orlando ambush and he was judged too unreliable to survive the crackdown that followed.

Avon Barksdale, with Stringer Bell, ordered Little Man killed after Little Man shot Detective Kima Greggs during the Orlando ambush and brought the full weight of the department down on the organisation.
Omar Little shot Savino Bratton after finding him working for the Stanfield organisation, having given him the chance to say he had no part in Butchie's death.

Tosha Mitchell robs with Omar Little's crew and works its setups — she is the one who draws Brother Mouzone's man Lamar away for Omar — and she asks the question the crew keeps asking: why it has to be Barksdale stashes when the city is full of them. She is shot in the head by Dante during the raid Omar insists on anyway.

Kimmy infiltrates targets in disguise — she poses as a nurse to Omar Little's fake disabled veteran — and leaves the crew after Tosha Mitchell's death on the plain ground that there are easier people in Baltimore to rob than the Barksdales. She comes back for the robbery of Proposition Joe's co-op shipment.
Dante robs with Omar Little in the middle seasons, and his capture by Brother Mouzone is the lever that brings the two men into the same room and ends Stringer Bell's life.
Omar Little and Dante were partners in the middle seasons, and it is Dante's capture by Brother Mouzone that brings Omar to the meeting that ends Stringer Bell's life.
Brother Mouzone seized and held Dante in order to reach Omar Little, and released him unharmed once the two men had come to an understanding.
Donette is the mother of D'Angelo Barksdale's son, and takes up with Stringer Bell while D'Angelo is serving his sentence.
Donette began a relationship with Stringer Bell while D'Angelo Barksdale was in prison, and her account of D'Angelo's state of mind is part of what convinces Stringer he is a risk.
Brianna Barksdale keeps Donette on the organisation's money as the mother of her grandson, and uses her as a channel to D'Angelo in prison.
Shardene dances at the club, and it is a friend's death from an overdose there, and the casual disposal of her body, that makes her willing to carry information out.
Shardene Innes agreed to work for the Major Crimes Unit from inside the Barksdale organisation's club after learning what had happened to a friend who danced there.

Lester Freamon persuaded Shardene Innes to inform from inside Orlando's, encouraged her into nursing school, and married her; she is with him at the finale wake and in the retirement the closing montage gives him.
Being put in charge of the club is D'Angelo's second demotion, a job with a title and no function, designed to keep him where he can neither earn nor do damage.
Fruit runs corners near the demolished towers and recruits directly from the neighbourhood's schoolchildren, which is how the fourth season's boys come into the organisation's orbit at all.

Andre's shop holds the organisation's money and package, and after Omar Little robs it Andre is made to swear a false statement placing Omar at a murder, then killed once the statement has served its purpose.
Omar Little robbed Old Face Andre's shop of the Stanfield organisation's money, and Andre's complaint to Marlo Stanfield is what sets the frame-up in motion.

Chris Partlow staged the robbery of Old Face Andre's shop himself, shooting a delivery woman dead inside it and beating Andre to make the story stand up, so that Andre could name Omar Little for a murder he had nothing to do with; Andre was killed once that account had served.

Marlo Stanfield had Old Face Andre used to frame Omar Little for the murder of a woman in Andre's own shop, then had him killed once the statement had served — after Bunk Moreland and Vernon Holley had already got Andre to admit the framing.
Fruit runs the corner Michael Lee first works, and it is Fruit's crew that the boy is drawn into before Chris Partlow takes him up.
The Stanfield organisation uses the vacant row houses of West Baltimore as its burial ground, sealing bodies behind the plywood with lime.

Chris Partlow devised the method — plastic sheeting, quicklime, the boards nailed back — which keeps the killings off the city's murder figures entirely, because a body sealed into a condemned row house is never found and so is never counted.
Snoop's contribution is the tool: the powder-actuated nail gun she buys after a long conversation in a hardware shop about the merits of the .27 calibre load.

Freamon works out that a drug crew has been sealing its victims inside boarded-up empty houses, and gets the authority to open them. Bodies are recovered from house after house across a single police district — each one a new unsolved murder on the department's books — so the discovery destroys the homicide squad's solved-case figures, and Freamon notes that they have so far searched only one sector of one district.

Nerese Campbell offers Tommy Carcetti her influence on the council and her standing with the ministers as a down payment on the mayoralty he will vacate when he runs for governor — and, not trusting the promise, keeps making herself the indispensable liaison until he honours it.

Nerese Campbell takes the mayoralty when Tommy Carcetti wins the governorship, and one of her first acts is to make Stanislaus Valchek police commissioner — the office passing to the department's most transactional operator by way of a deal struck years earlier.
Tony Gray and Tommy Carcetti are council colleagues and friends, and Carcetti encourages Gray's mayoral run knowing it will split the vote he needs split.
Tommy Carcetti used Tony Gray's mayoral candidacy to divide the black vote against Clarence Royce and had no further use for him once the primary was won.
Tony Gray ran against Clarence Royce in the mayoral primary, taking votes from him without ever being close to winning.
Theresa D'Agostino ran Tommy Carcetti's mayoral campaign, treating Baltimore as a set of numbers to be moved and delivering the win.
Theresa D'Agostino and Jimmy McNulty had a brief affair during the mayoral campaign, ended by her taking him to a party where it became clear how little either belonged in the other's world.
Andy Krawczyk took Stringer Bell's money into his downtown developments without asking where it came from, and was on the site with him the day Stringer was killed.

Andy Krawczyk's downtown developments depend on approvals granted at City Hall, which is why he is present at every administration's functions and takes money from Stringer Bell without asking its source.

Carcetti arrives at City Hall to find a school deficit his predecessor concealed, and takes the decision there that defines him: refusing the governor's money because accepting it would cost him the governor's job.
Royce runs City Hall on patronage and appearances, holding back the schools' deficit until after the primary and being surprised that the concealment is not enough.
Campbell trades her council votes and her standing with the ministers for a written understanding about the mayoralty, and collects on it the moment Carcetti moves up.

Norman Wilson works out of City Hall as the mayor's senior aide, having come to politics from a newsroom — which is why he is the one Carcetti uses when something needs to reach a reporter without the mayor's fingerprints on it.
Steintorf converts the mayor's ambitions into instructions nobody wants written down, including the demand for crime figures that Cedric Daniels resigns rather than produce.

Davis works City Hall and Annapolis as one circuit, taking money from developers, drug figures and his own constituents' campaign funds, and is protected for years by how many people would be implicated by his fall.
Jen Carcetti is Tommy Carcetti's wife, supports the mayoral campaign, and understands earlier than he admits it that the mayoralty was only ever a step toward Annapolis.
Grace Sampson takes Prez in hand during his first year at Tilghman and explains what the school can and cannot do for the children in it.
Marcia Donnelly is Prez's assistant principal, and the person who tells him plainly which of his pupils the building will not be seeing again.
Marcia Donnelly runs Edward J. Tilghman Middle School day to day, managing the test scores the system requires and the children it has given up on.
Grace Sampson teaches at Tilghman alongside Prez in his first year and is the colleague who tells him the job is holding the room before it is teaching mathematics.
Zenobia is moved out of the mainstream classroom as unteachable and, in the smaller room, turns out to be capable of an entirely different conversation about the life she is expecting to have.

David Parenti's separate classroom is where Zenobia Dawson, moved out of the mainstream as unteachable, gives the season its clearest statement of the argument: we got our thing, but it's just part of the big thing.

Bunny Colvin works with Zenobia Dawson in the separate classroom, where she objects during test practice to answering questions about asking a father for pocket money when she has neither the father nor the money.
Michael Lee raises his half-brother Bug in place of their mother, and every choice he makes about the Stanfield organisation is made to keep the boy safe.

Michael Lee and Bug are half-brothers, and Michael's insistence on raising the boy himself, rather than leaving him in their mother's household, is what makes Chris Partlow's offer of protection impossible for Michael to refuse.

Donut runs with Michael Lee's group of neighbourhood boys and is the one who steals the car they use to get around delivering campaign material for Randy Wagstaff on election day — the closest any of them comes to ordinary paid work.
Donut drives past Bunny Colvin's suburban house at the end of the fourth season and exchanges a nod with Namond Brice, the one thread left between Namond and the corner.

Fruit runs street corners whose takings are falling, and is given enforcers by Marlo Stanfield to drive a rival organisation's crews off them. Spider is one of the schoolchildren selling drugs on those corners while that dispute is settled several ranks above him.
Horseface works the cranes and knows the paperwork well enough to make a container vanish from the port's computer, which is the practical service Frank Sobotka is actually selling.
Nat Coxson backs the campaign for the canal and the grain pier at every union meeting and is left, after Frank Sobotka's death, to carry a fight the local can no longer fund.

Horseface is the man who actually makes Frank Sobotka's arrangement work, losing particular container numbers from the port computer, and he escalates the feud with Valchek by stealing the major's surveillance van and having it photographed around the world.
Glekas runs the warehouse where stolen goods from the port are received and priced, and his habit of short-changing the people bringing them in is what gets him shot behind his own counter.
Ziggy Sobotka shot George Glekas dead behind the counter of his warehouse after being cheated and humiliated by him once too often.
Nick Sobotka dealt with George Glekas over stolen goods and warned his cousin Ziggy repeatedly not to try to do business with him alone.
Business is done over coffee in a diner with a view of the water, chosen because a Greek man eating breakfast is the least remarkable thing on that stretch of waterfront.

The head of the port smuggling ring conducts business from a booth in an ordinary waterfront diner, in a cardigan, saying almost nothing while his second in command does the talking. Police surveillance photographs everyone at that table without ever establishing which of them they are actually looking for.
Vondas takes the meetings at the diner, including those with Proposition Joe, so that every arrangement can be made without the organisation's head being in the room.

Russell and the investigators put the waterfront diner under surveillance and photograph everyone using it, never establishing that the quiet older man in the cardigan is the one they want — a failure that lets the smuggling ring leave the city intact.
Mike Fletcher works the city desk under Gus Haynes and is the reporter Haynes trusts with the assignments that need time, which is why he is the one still standing when the desk changes hands.
Gus Haynes assigns and edits Mike Fletcher, and Fletcher's patiently reported work is the standing rebuke to Scott Templeton's inventions.
Mike Fletcher spent months reporting Bubbles's story for the Sun, and the resulting profile is the first time anyone puts Bubbles's account of himself into print.

Mike Fletcher spends weeks with a homeless veteran and produces the reported story the paper's management claimed to be asking for, while Scott Templeton invents his; in the closing montage Templeton collects a Pulitzer and Fletcher takes over the city desk Gus Haynes is removed from.
Elena McNulty is Jimmy McNulty's estranged wife and the mother of his two sons; their separation runs in parallel with everything his work costs him.
Marla Daniels is Cedric Daniels's wife, a lawyer with political ambitions who leaves him when it becomes clear he will not manage his career as she would.
Marla Daniels wins the council seat her husband would never have run for, pursuing directly the advancement she had spent years urging on him.
Cheryl is Kima Greggs's partner and the mother of their son; Kima's return to street work after being shot is what the relationship does not survive.

Gant was the one witness who testified truthfully at a Barksdale murder trial. Days after the acquittal, Bird shot him dead in the open — the organisation's demonstration of what testifying costs, and the killing that pushes a detective to complain to a judge that the police are ignoring these deaths.
William Gant's killing was ordered from inside the Barksdale organisation by Avon Barksdale, as the standing answer to anyone who testifies.
Jimmy McNulty recognised William Gant as the witness from D'Angelo Barksdale's trial when the body came in, and it is that recognition he takes to Judge Phelan.
Orlando holds the club's liquor licence because he has no record, and is beaten by Avon Barksdale for trying to deal on his own account before being set up and killed for informing.
Orlando's name is on the licence and nothing else; Avon Barksdale removes it the moment Orlando is arrested, which is the whole measure of what the club was ever giving him.
Orlando Blocker agreed to work for Kima Greggs after his arrest, and the undercover buy he arranged is the one at which Greggs was shot.
Avon Barksdale installed Orlando Blocker as the club's nominal owner and warned him explicitly to stay away from the drug side of the business.
Wee-Bey Brice and Little Man shot Wendell Orlando Blocker dead in the car at the staged buy, on Avon Barksdale's orders, for having agreed to inform.
Fitzhugh is the agent who explains, without much satisfaction, that the Bureau's resources went to terrorism and political corruption and that a city drug case is now nobody's federal priority.
Terrance Fitzhugh and Jimmy McNulty drink together and trade favours across the federal and city lines, and it is Fitzhugh who tells McNulty that the Bureau is protecting the Greek.

Terrance Fitzhugh is the Major Crimes Unit's named contact inside the Bureau, drinking with McNulty and running the checks nobody in the department can — including the query about George Glekas that reaches the Greek's own handler and clears the organisation out of Baltimore.
Terrance Fitzhugh handled the federal end of the approach to Frank Sobotka, and was waiting for the debriefing that never happened.
Stringer Bell, with Avon Barksdale, ordered Wee-Bey Brice to kill Little Man once Little Man's shooting of a detective had made him a liability the organisation could not carry.
Little Man took part with Wee-Bey Brice in the killing of Orlando Blocker at the staged buy.

Little Man panicked at finding an unexpected passenger in Orlando Blocker's car during a drug buy the police had arranged, and shot Detective Kima Greggs — a shooting nobody in the organisation had ordered. Wee-Bey Brice later told Stringer Bell he would have left her alive, and Little Man was killed within days for the mistake.
Jen Carcetti appears at City Hall for her husband's swearing-in and the public occasions that require a candidate's family.

Wee-Bey Brice, with Stinkum and Bird Hilton, took Brandon Wright by pretending to be police, tortured him for Omar Little's location and got nothing, and dumped the body where Wallace would have to look at it.
Stinkum took part with Wee-Bey Brice and Bird Hilton in the torture and killing of Brandon Wright, a job that came out of Stinkum's own grudge after Omar Little had robbed him at gunpoint.

During a daylight raid by Omar Little's crew on a house where the Barksdale organisation kept its drugs and money, Dante fired wildly and hit Tosha Mitchell, a member of his own crew, in the head. It is the death that ends Omar's willingness to keep robbing that organisation and drives him out of Baltimore.

After a detective complains privately that the police will not investigate a drug organisation's murders, Phelan telephones Deputy Commissioner Burrell. Judges do not run police departments but can embarrass them publicly, and the call forces Burrell to create the investigative unit the series follows — an intrusion he resents for five years.

Pearlman is the prosecutor who must draft each wiretap application and get it in front of a judge; Phelan is the judge who signs them. He is candid with her that a case generating newspaper coverage does his own re-election prospects no harm, which is one reason the applications keep being approved.

Renaldo drives and shoots alongside Omar Little through the robberies of Stanfield corners and stash houses, and it is his refusal to return from Puerto Rico that leaves Omar hunting Marlo Stanfield alone.
Renaldo carries messages and money between Omar Little and Butchie, and it is through Butchie's bar that the pair are reached in Puerto Rico with the news of his killing.
The Major Crimes Unit identifies Sergei Malatov off the port wiretap and takes him in the sweep, and he is one of the few people in the Greek's organisation the case ever manages to charge.
Sergei Malatov collects and enforces for the Greek's organisation and is arrested with the drugs coming off the docks, taking the charge without naming anyone above him.
Odell Watkins delivers Annapolis for whoever holds City Hall and expects to be consulted on appointments in return, which is the arrangement Carcetti breaks.
Colonel Ray Foerster shelters Lester Freamon's slow paper cases from commanders who want arrests, and Freamon loses his last senior protection when Foerster dies of cancer in post.

Officer Dozerman is shot in the face during a buy-and-bust — an operation where police buy drugs undercover and arrest the seller on the spot — run by Carver's squad. Carver has to account for sending an officer into it with no informant and no advance intelligence, and his commander responds by stopping such operations in the district altogether.
Dozerman's shooting is the last straw for Bunny Colvin, who announces to his squads that there will be no more buy-and-busts in the district for the rest of his command.

Colicchio and Herc are frequently paired in the Western District drug squad and share the same instinct for force. Both police the three blocks where their major has quietly suspended arrests, and it is Colicchio who supplies the mocking nickname the whole city then uses for it.
Anthony Colicchio calls Ellis Carver a rat to his face for writing him up, having expected the squad's usual protection and been refused it by a sergeant who came up in the same drug unit he did.

Mello handles the daily administration of the three blocks where drug arrests have been suspended — the rotas, the post assignments, the paperwork that does not mention what is actually happening — which makes him the officer who could end his commander's career at any moment and does not.

Mello relays Colvin's orders to Carver's squad and is one of the very few officers in the district let in on what is actually happening: that their commander has suspended drug arrests in three blocks without telling anyone above him, and is relying on his own men not to report it.

Vernon Holley had Bubbles brought in as a suspect for Kima Greggs's shooting, lost his temper when Bubbles could not answer him, and beat him until Landsman pulled him off — then claimed Bubbles had attacked him first. Bubbles asked for McNulty, who cleared it up.
Ilene Nathan puts Omar Little on the stand against Bird Hilton and wins the conviction, having decided that a jury will either take a self-declared robber at his word or not at all.

At the investigation's first meeting Pearlman divides the legal work: drug material comes to her, murder material to Ilene Nathan in the state's attorney's office. It is why the case against the drug organisation ends up prosecuted by two women who never appear in the same courtroom.
Rupert Bond heads the office Rhonda Pearlman works in, and it is his decision to pull the Clay Davis case into state court that turns her financial work into a public defeat.
Clay Davis walks out of Rupert Bond's state prosecution acquitted and is greeted on the courthouse steps as a man wronged, while Bond, who took the case for the profile, gets none of it.
Savino Bratton drove for the crew that killed Orlando Blocker, and it is because he was not directly implicated in the shooting of the detective in the same car that he faced only three years.
Savino Bratton takes work with the Stanfield organisation after his release, having found nothing left of the outfit he went inside for.

Kimmy robs Barksdale stash houses with Omar Little's crew and shoots a Barksdale man named Tank in the chest during the exchange that follows Tosha Mitchell's killing — the one occasion the crew answers a death directly.

Horseface Pakusa walked into the Southeastern District car park and drove off with Stanislaus Valchek's surveillance van, then had it photographed around the world, which is the escalation that turns Valchek's grudge into a full detail.

Nat Coxson is the man Frank Sobotka must ask to extend his term, the local rotating its leadership between a white and a black officer each year. The two visit the family of a stevedore whose leg is crushed on the docks and Frank hands over an envelope of cash; when Coxson asks where the money comes from, Frank will not answer him.
Donut is arrested repeatedly in the Western District for stealing cars, and released each time because nobody in the system can think what else to do with a boy that age and that size.

Elena McNulty and Jimmy McNulty conduct a custody fight through the middle seasons, and her account of him to a lawyer is one of the few outside assessments of McNulty the series lets stand unanswered.
Sherrod attends Tilghman exactly once, and spends the rest of the term working a corner for a dealer called Jojo while pretending to Bubbles that he is in class.
Nat Coxson works the same docks as Frank Sobotka and speaks for the men at the union hall, where the argument is always the same: no ships, no shifts, no local.

Bird Hilton was the third of the enforcers, with Wee-Bey Brice and Stinkum, who abducted Brandon Wright by posing as undercover officers, tortured him for Omar Little's whereabouts, and left the mutilated body on display.

Stringer Bell was the one told that Brandon Wright had been spotted at a west-side restaurant, and he sent Wee-Bey Brice, Stinkum and Bird Hilton to take him — an order Avon Barksdale's bounty had made inevitable but did not itself give.
Stringer Bell shared with Avon Barksdale the decision to have Bird Hilton shoot the state's witness William Gant, after attempts to intimidate and bribe Gant into silence had failed.
Jimmy McNulty works the Snot Boogie killing in the opening scene, sitting on a step taking an account from a witness who cannot explain why a craps game robbed every Friday kept letting the man play.
